pages.title: AI and Community Engagement
pages.excerpt: When AI eats the paperwork, people get their time back — and the question becomes what we do with that reclaimed energy.
pages.content:
> When AI eats the paperwork, people get their time back — and the question becomes what we do with that reclaimed energy.

## The Core Thesis

Every small organisation in Australia — every social enterprise, Indigenous community org, every two-person team doing meaningful work — has been drowning in compliance, reporting, acquittals, stakeholder management, grant applications, and data collection frameworks. **The administration of impact has been consuming the capacity for impact itself.**

The cruel irony: organisations closest to the ground, doing the most relational work, are the most burdened by administrative overhead. Funding models demand it. Government accountability frameworks were designed for institutions, not for humans sitting in living rooms having conversations that actually change lives.

## The Compression

What AI and automation now make possible is the compression of the administrative layer — from ~60% of a small team's energy to ~10%. That reclaimed 50% is the revolution.

A three-person team can now accomplish what previously required eight — not because people were replaced, but because the work that was never the *real* work gets handled differently.

### Practical Example

A community engagement worker in [[../communities/mount-isa|Mount Isa]] spends their week in relationship — yarning, listening, being present. AI handles case notes, data entry, reporting frameworks, and grant acquittal drafts. The human reviews and refines rather than creates from scratch.

[[../people/brodie-germaine|Brodie Germaine]]'s story illustrates this: "I'd rather Brodie here 'cause it's face to face," a young person says. That face-to-face presence is what gets lost when administration eats everything.

## The Government Argument

Government funds outcomes but measures compliance. These are not the same thing. The gap between what gets measured and what actually matters has been the open wound of social policy for decades.

The argument becomes: **If AI handles the compliance layer, the ratio of funding-to-engagement fundamentally changes.** Every dollar paying a coordinator to write reports can instead pay for that coordinator to be in community. Every hour on administrative accountability redirects to relational accountability — which is the kind that actually works.

> "Your reporting frameworks were designed for a world where human labour was the only way to track, measure, and report. That world is ending. Either redesign your accountability models or you're actively choosing to fund administration over engagement."

That's not a philosophical argument. That's a procurement argument. And it's one that Treasury understands.

## What Emerges

When people are freed from administrative machinery, what emerges isn't just "more engagement hours." It's the space for things that make communities resilient: **art, story, culture, play, exploration, the slow and ungovernable work of meaning-making.**

A young person who's been through the justice system doesn't need another case plan. They need someone who has time to sit with them. They might need a camera, a story to tell, a song to write, or a three-hour conversation with an Elder that covers everything and nothing. That work has never fit inside a logic model. It has never survived a grant acquittal. And it is the most important work there is.

## The Generational Shift

If machines handle the output — code, reports, logistics, optimisation — then what's the distinctly human contribution?

It's the things Indigenous cultures never stopped valuing: **relationship to place, obligation to kin, transmission of knowledge through story, the capacity to hold complexity without reducing it to a spreadsheet.**

It's the things that relieve anxiety and loneliness — not through consumption, but through genuine belonging. Through being known. Through having a role in something that matters beyond individual productivity.

## Connection to [[lcaa-method|LCAA]]

This thesis maps directly to ACT's methodology:
- **Listen** — AI can transcribe, summarise, cross-reference. Humans do the listening.
- **Curiosity** — AI can surface patterns and connections. Humans follow the threads with genuine curiosity.
- **Action** — AI handles logistics, compliance, reporting. Humans do the relational work.
- **Art** — irreducibly human. The highest expression of reclaimed time and energy.

## Sources

- Raw: `wiki/raw/2026-02-18-article-eating-the-paperwork-ai-community-engagement-renaissance.md`

pages.title: AI Ethics & Agent Strategy
pages.excerpt: The best AI output is the one that gets out of the way and lets the right voice be heard.
pages.content:
> The best AI output is the one that gets out of the way and lets the right voice be heard.

## Overview

ACT's approach to AI is built on a single principle: AI serves community voice, it never replaces it. Every AI capability in the ecosystem is gated by consent, aligned to [[alma|ALMA]], and subject to community override. Efficiency is never a sufficient reason to bypass these constraints.

This article covers the ethical framework, the internal agent roles, and what AI can and cannot do within ACT systems.

## Non-Negotiables

| Rule | Enforcement |
|------|-------------|
| **Cultural sovereignty is sacred** | OCAP enforced in code and practice |
| **No individual profiling** | System-level patterns only |
| **Sacred knowledge hard-blocked** | Cannot be processed, not just warned |
| **Community authority highest weight** | Overrides efficiency in decision paths |
| **Consent before analysis** | No opt-out model, explicit opt-in only |

## ALMA as Gatekeeper

All AI learning and ethics checks pass through [[alma|ALMA]]:

```
User/Community Input
        ↓
   ALMA Check
   - Consent verified?
   - Cultural sensitivity flagged?
   - Authority confirmed?
        ↓
   AI Processing (if permitted)
        ↓
   ALMA Review
   - Output safe?
   - Individual profiling avoided?
   - Value returned to community?
        ↓
   Community Review
        ↓
   Output
```

## What AI Can Do

| Task | Conditions |
|------|------------|
| Summarize meetings | Consent from participants |
| Map relationships between projects | System-level only |
| Check consent scope before release | Automated gatekeeping |
| Draft content for review | Human review required |
| Assist with research synthesis | Attribution maintained |

## What AI Cannot Do

| Task | Reason |
|------|--------|
| Profile, rank, or optimize individuals | Dignity violation |
| Override community voice | Authority breach |
| Process sacred content | Cultural sovereignty |
| Generate final narratives | Human authority required |
| Make consent decisions | Community authority only |
| Analyze without explicit opt-in | Consent violation |

## Internal Agent Roles

ACT uses named agent roles to make AI responsibilities explicit:

| Agent | Role | Guardrails |
|-------|------|------------|
| **Scribe** | Summarizes meetings, captures next actions | Consent from participants, no profiling |
| **Cartographer** | Maps relationships between projects, stories, signals | System-level patterns only |
| **Evidence Steward** | Checks consent scope and shareability | Cannot override community decisions |
| **Studio Assistant** | Supports drafting and editing | Never owns the narrative |
| **Farmhand** | Orchestrates tasks, turns messy inputs into actions | ALMA checks on all outputs |

### The Farmhand Role

Farmhand is ACT's primary AI layer — the infrastructure that reduces admin and holds context. It turns messy inputs into clear next actions across the Knowledge Hub.

**Farmhand can:**
- Turn messy inputs into clear tasks
- Protect consent and cultural boundaries in summaries
- Connect LCAA steps to real work
- Keep ALMA signals visible

**Farmhand cannot:**
- Profile individuals
- Override community voice
- Inflate claims or certainty
- Process without consent

> Intelligence without consent is just extraction. We would rather be slower than wrong.

## Implementation Checklist

For any new AI feature:

| Check | Required |
|-------|----------|
| OCAP principles respected? | Yes |
| ALMA gatekeeper integrated? | Yes |
| Individual profiling prevented? | Yes |
| Sacred content hard-blocked? | Yes |
| Community authority preserved? | Yes |
| Opt-in consent required? | Yes |
| Human review on outputs? | Yes |

## Future Development Principles

As AI capabilities grow, ACT maintains:

1. **Community veto** — Any AI use can be blocked by community decision
2. **Transparency** — What AI does is visible, not hidden
3. **Accountability** — Humans answer for AI outputs
4. **Reversibility** — AI decisions can be undone
5. **Locality** — Prefer local/open models where possible

## Backlinks

- [[alma|ALMA Framework]] — the impact and ethics model that gates all AI
- [[governance-consent|Governance & Consent]] — consent architecture AI must respect
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the platform where AI consent settings live
- [[ai-community-engagement|AI Community Engagement]] — broader AI use in community contexts

pages.title: ALMA — Authentic Learning for Meaningful Accountability
pages.excerpt: We do not measure people. We measure whether the system is learning.
pages.content:
> We do not measure people. We measure whether the system is learning.

## Overview

ALMA is ACT's shared impact-and-learning model. It reads signals at a system level, not an individual level, and feeds learning back into [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] practice. ALMA is a way of paying attention, not scoring. It protects against extractive data practices while enabling genuine learning from community experience.

ALMA is distinct from a reporting framework — its purpose is to keep ACT accountable to learning, not to generate proof for external audiences.

## How ALMA Works

```
Community Stories (Empathy Ledger)
         ↓
    ALMA Signals (system-level patterns)
         ↓
    Learning & Reflection
         ↓
    LCAA Practice Changes
         ↓
    Better Outcomes
```

Community stories live in Empathy Ledger with consent controls. ALMA reads signals from consented stories only. Individual identities are protected throughout — system-level patterns inform decisions, not individual profiles.

## The Six Signal Families

These are the lenses used to read system-level learning:

| Signal | What It Means | Scale |
|--------|--------------|-------|
| **Evidence Strength** | How reliable is the learning? What's the source? | 1 (anecdotal) → 5 (robust, triangulated) |
| **Community Authority** | Who holds authority here? Is consent in place? | 1 (external) → 5 (community-owned) |
| **Harm Risk** (inverted) | What could go wrong? Who might be harmed? | 1 (high risk) → 5 (no foreseeable harm) |
| **Implementation Capability** | Can this be done well? Is capacity ready? | 1 (beyond capacity) → 5 (ready) |
| **Option Value** | Does this open or close future possibilities? | 1 (limiting) → 5 (significant new options) |
| **Community Value Return** | Does value flow back to community? | 1 (extracted) → 5 (community-first) |

## ALMA in Reporting

Every piece of evidence should include four elements:

| Element | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Story** | A consented narrative or quote from Empathy Ledger |
| **Signal** | ALMA lens notes at system level (not individual) |
| **Shift** | What we changed or will change in practice (LCAA step) |
| **Scope** | What is shareable now vs internal-only |

## Capture Prompts

When gathering evidence, ask:

1. What did we hear, and who holds authority?
2. What system-level shift is emerging?
3. What harm risk or consent boundary must be held?
4. What practical change do we commit to next?
5. What should remain internal for now?

## ALMA Data Anchors

Every ALMA record should link to:
- Story record (Empathy Ledger ID)
- Consent scope and cultural sensitivity level
- Project slugs and place/Country
- ALMA signal tags and LCAA stage

## Reporting Template

```markdown
**Title:** [Story/learning title]
**Project:** [project slug]
**Place / Country:** [location]
**Consent scope:** [INTERNAL ONLY | EXTERNAL-LITE | EXTERNAL]

**Story (summary or quote):**
[Consented narrative from Empathy Ledger]

**ALMA Signals:**
- Evidence strength: [description]
- Community authority: [who holds it]
- Harm risk (inverted): [risks identified]
- Implementation capability: [readiness level]
- Option value: [future possibilities]
- Community value return: [how value flows back]

**LCAA shift (what we will change):**
[Practical change committed]

**Review status:** [pending | approved | restricted]
```

## What ALMA Is Not

| ALMA Is | ALMA Is Not |
|---------|------------|
| System-level learning | Individual profiling |
| Patterns across stories | Scoring or ranking people |
| Community-controlled | Externally imposed |
| Consent-first | Surveillance |
| Practice-changing | Report-generating |

## Field Notes

> "If a story cannot be told without harm, we do not tell it. The signal stays internal until it is safe."

> "Evidence serves relationships, not reports. We count what we can, but we listen to what we cannot."

> "ALMA is not about proving impact. It's about staying accountable to learning."

## Backlinks

- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — ALMA feeds learning back into LCAA cycles
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the platform that holds consented stories ALMA reads
- [[governance-consent|Governance & Consent]] — consent architecture ALMA operates within
- [[ai-ethics|AI Ethics & Agent Strategy]] — ALMA as gatekeeper for AI analysis
- [[vignette-workflows|Vignette Workflows]] — operational use of ALMA signals in story vignettes

pages.title: ALMA Intervention Portfolio
pages.excerpt: 1,766 youth justice interventions across Australia, scored on evidence, cultural authority, and replication readiness — JusticeHub's living evidence base.
pages.content:
> 1,766 youth justice interventions across Australia, scored on evidence, cultural authority, and replication readiness — JusticeHub's living evidence base.

## Overview

ALMA (the engine behind JusticeHub) maintains a structured catalogue of community-led, government, and philanthropic interventions in youth justice and adjacent sectors. As of April 2026, it holds **1,766 interventions** from **729 operating organisations**, scored against ten intervention types and four evidence levels.

The portfolio is the answer to the question funders keep asking: *"What works, who runs it, and what does it cost?"* It is also the answer to the question communities keep asking: *"Why does the funding go to the same people who already have it?"* — because the portfolio's top scores reveal exactly which small ACCOs are doing the highest-leverage work.

## Distribution by Intervention Type

| Type | N | Avg Portfolio Score |
|------|---|---------------------|
| Community-Led | 345 | 0.45 |
| Wraparound Support | 328 | 0.50 |
| Education / Employment | 213 | 0.42 |
| Prevention | 207 | 0.39 |
| Cultural Connection | 206 | 0.48 |
| Diversion | 140 | 0.47 |
| Therapeutic | 126 | 0.46 |
| Justice Reinvestment | 72 | 0.50 |
| Early Intervention | 72 | 0.43 |
| Family Strengthening | 57 | 0.45 |

**Wraparound Support** and **Justice Reinvestment** are the highest-scoring categories on average — both also the most under-funded relative to their evidence base. The largest category by count, **Community-Led** (345 interventions), captures the long tail of place-based programs that government funders typically don't see.

## The Top of the Portfolio

The 15 highest-scoring interventions reveal the pattern ACT and JusticeHub keep finding: **Indigenous-led organisations dominate the evidence**, but rarely have the formal evaluation infrastructure that Western funders demand.

| Rank | Name | Org | Score | Evidence |
|------|------|-----|-------|----------|
| 1 | Deadly Inspiring Youth Doing Good | DIYDG ATSI Corp | 0.86 | Indigenous-led |
| 2 | Central Qld Indigenous Development | CQID | 0.86 | Promising |
| 3 | Rumbalara Aboriginal Co-operative | Rumbalara | 0.80 | Untested |
| 4 | Mulungu Aboriginal Corp PHC | Mulungu | 0.78 | Indigenous-led |
| 5 | Youth Legal Aid Service | Legal Aid QLD | 0.78 | Untested |
| 6 | ATSI Wellbeing Services | ATSI Wellbeing | 0.78 | Promising |
| 7 | QATSICPP (Youth Justice Peak) | QATSICPP | 0.78 | Untested |
| 9 | Oochiumpa Youth Services | Oochiumpa | 0.77 | **Effective** |
| 10 | headspace | headspace | 0.77 | Promising |
| 12 | Mamu Health Service | Mamu | 0.77 | Indigenous-led |

**8 of the top 15** are Aboriginal community-controlled organisations (ACCOs). Only **Oochiumpa Youth Services** carries the highest evidence rating ("Effective — strong evaluation, positive outcomes"). This is not because the others don't work — it's because ACCO-scale programs rarely have $300K spare for an external evaluation. The portfolio score corrects for that by weighting community authority and Indigenous leadership alongside formal evaluation.

## Why This Matters

Two things:

1. **The funding doesn't follow the evidence.** [[justice-funding-landscape|$4.12B in QLD youth justice]] is spread across 7,004 organisations. The top-scoring interventions in ALMA's portfolio are typically funded for $50K–$5M each — orders of magnitude below the largest government and philanthropic recipients.

2. **The "untested" label is a funding category, not a quality category.** When [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] runs a 20-year program with intergenerational outcomes but no peer-reviewed RCT, Western evaluation frameworks call it "untested." ALMA's portfolio score is designed to make that distinction visible.

## How JusticeHub Uses This

- **Funder briefings:** "These 15 organisations are doing the strongest work and receive a fraction of available funding. Here's the evidence."
- **Community matching:** "If you want to fund cultural connection in QLD, here are the 206 interventions sorted by community authority."
- **Procurement intelligence:** Cross-reference top-scoring interventions against [[justice-funding-landscape|government contract pipelines]] to find under-resourced programs that match commissioning priorities.

## Live Impact (snapshot)

From `v_alma_current_impact` as of 2026-01-26:
- **25** stories told
- **150** lives touched  
- **42** art pieces created

These numbers are deliberately small. They're the slice ACT has direct line-of-sight to — the rest of the portfolio is community-owned data.

## Backlinks

- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — 20-year evidence base, "untested" by formal frameworks
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — only top-15 intervention with "Effective" evidence rating
- [[alma|ALMA]] — the methodology behind the scoring

Young men on an Oonchiumpa on-Country trip to Atnarpa Station learned more than they might in any classroom. Walking Country with Elders and cultural mentors, they learned:

pages.title: Barkly Backbone
pages.excerpt: A backbone organisation doesn't do the work — it makes the work possible. In the Barkly, that distinction is the difference between communities thriving and communities burning out.
pages.content:
> A backbone organisation doesn't do the work — it makes the work possible. In the Barkly, that distinction is the difference between communities thriving and communities burning out.

**Status:** Ideation | **Code:** ACT-BB

## What It Is

Barkly Backbone is an early-stage concept for a shared operational infrastructure serving community organisations in the Barkly region of the Northern Territory. The Barkly — centred on Tennant Creek, approximately 500km north of Alice Springs — is one of Australia's most remote and geographically dispersed regions, with a predominantly Aboriginal population spread across vast distances and served by a small number of chronically under-resourced organisations.

The concept draws from the "backbone organisation" model developed in collective impact theory: a dedicated entity that provides shared services — administration, technology, data, logistics, governance support — so that frontline community organisations don't have to build those capabilities themselves. Every hour a Tennant Creek youth worker spends on compliance paperwork is an hour not spent with a young person. Barkly Backbone is the concept that addresses that equation.

## The Barkly Region

Tennant Creek (Jurnkurakurr) is the largest town in the Barkly region, with a population of approximately 3,000. It is the administrative and service centre for a catchment that extends hundreds of kilometres in every direction. The region has some of Australia's highest rates of child welfare intervention, youth justice involvement, and housing instability — alongside a rich Aboriginal cultural landscape and a number of organisations working hard with minimal infrastructure.

Key facts grounding the concept:
- The Barkly is in the SPSP (Stronger Places Stronger People) network — confirmed in ACT project_knowledge (March 2026), which notes Tennant Creek as a SPSP site
- PLACE ($38.6M backbone fund, First Nations-majority board) specifically identifies Tennant Creek in its network — and has no data platform, a gap [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] is positioned to fill
- [[contained|CONTAINED]]'s national touring schedule includes a planned Tennant Creek stop (June 2026, $75K budget) — the highest per-stop budget, reflecting the cost of cultural safety and local facilitation in remote settings

## The Problem Barkly Backbone Is Designed to Solve

Small community organisations in remote Australia face a structural paradox: they are closest to the people who need support, and furthest from the administrative infrastructure that funders require. The result is a perpetual capacity trap — organisations spend disproportionate time on reporting, acquittals, and compliance rather than the relational work that actually produces outcomes.

This is not a problem unique to the Barkly. But the Barkly's remoteness amplifies it. There are no consultants down the road. Broadband is unreliable. Staff turnover is high. Organisations doing transformational work often can't demonstrate their outcomes in the formats funders require — which means they don't get funded, which means the work stops.

A backbone organisation in the Barkly would provide:
- **Shared technology infrastructure** — community-appropriate digital tools, data systems, reporting templates
- **Administrative capacity** — grant writing, financial reporting, acquittals
- **Data and evidence support** — helping organisations document outcomes in formats that funders and policymakers recognise
- **Logistics and connectivity** — practical support for organisations operating across vast distances

## Connection to ACT's Ecosystem

Barkly Backbone connects to several ACT workstreams in ideation:

### JusticeHub
[[justicehub|JusticeHub]] is the ACT platform built to document and surface what community programs actually achieve. In the Barkly, JusticeHub would function as the evidence layer for a backbone — helping local organisations prove their outcomes without building their own reporting infrastructure. The PLACE governance research (March 2026) explicitly identifies the Barkly as a target geography where JusticeHub fills a genuine gap.

### Oonchiumpa
[[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] operates across Central Australia from its base in Mparntwe (Alice Springs), with some reach toward the Barkly. Its model — community-led, Elder-governed, outcome-documented — is the type of organisation a backbone would serve. The Oonchiumpa evidence base (95% diversion, Operation Luna) shows what becomes visible when organisations get the support to document their work.

### Goods on Country
[[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] has identified Tennant Creek as a potential manufacturing site for containerised production. A backbone organisation in the Barkly could provide the local anchoring infrastructure that makes a Goods on Country node viable — shared admin, local relationships, governance capacity.

### CivicGraph
[[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] maps funding flows and organisational relationships across the Australian social sector. The Barkly, as a named geography in PLACE's SPSP network, is already embedded in the data layer. Barkly Backbone would be the field-level complement to that intelligence.

## The Backbone Model

The backbone concept comes from the collective impact framework developed by FSG and Kania & Kramer (2011). The argument: complex social problems require coordinated action across multiple organisations, and coordination requires dedicated infrastructure. Without a backbone, organisations work in parallel rather than together, duplicate effort, compete for the same funding, and lose the cumulative learning their work generates.

In the Barkly context, the specific backbone functions most needed are:
1. **Governance support** — helping community-controlled organisations meet their legal and compliance obligations without diverting frontline capacity
2. **Shared data** — consistent outcome measurement across organisations, feeding both internal learning and external accountability
3. **Funder interface** — aggregating the evidence base of multiple organisations to make the collective impact legible to government and philanthropy
4. **Local infrastructure** — the physical and logistical backbone for organisations operating in very remote settings

## Current Stage

This is a concept in early ideation. No funding has been committed. No organisational partner has been confirmed in available records. The wiki has not yet absorbed field research or community consultation for this project. What is documented here is the problem the concept addresses and the ecosystem logic that makes it coherent.

The project requires:
- Community consultation in Tennant Creek and the broader Barkly — this must be led by local organisations, not imposed by ACT
- Identification of existing backbone functions already operating in the region (to complement rather than duplicate)
- A governance model that keeps local organisations in control
- Funding — backbone infrastructure is chronically under-funded nationally, and the Barkly's remoteness multiplies costs

## Project Codes

| System | Reference |
|--------|-----------|
| Project code | `ACT-BB` |
| Status | Ideation |
| Geography | Tennant Creek / Barkly region, Northern Territory |

## Backlinks

- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — community-led model in Central Australia; Barkly-adjacent geography
- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — evidence platform that backbone organisations would feed into
- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — Tennant Creek identified as potential manufacturing node
- [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] — data layer; Barkly in SPSP network already mapped
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — Tennant Creek stop on national tour (June 2026); highest per-stop budget

pages.title: Beautiful Obsolescence
pages.excerpt: Our ultimate success metric: "ACT? We don't need them anymore. We run this ourselves now."
pages.content:
> Our ultimate success metric: "ACT? We don't need them anymore. We run this ourselves now."

## Overview

Beautiful Obsolescence is ACT's design discipline of building toward its own irrelevance. Every tool, platform, and engagement is designed with handover in mind from day one. The goal is not to grow ACT's reach — it's to transfer ownership, capability, and governance so completely that communities no longer need ACT to maintain what was built together.

This is not a brand line. It is a delivery discipline that shapes architecture decisions, documentation, training approaches, and governance structures.

## The Tractor Metaphor

The name A Curious Tractor comes from the Power Take-Off (PTO) mechanism — the connection point that transfers engine power to implements like balers, augers, and pumps. The tractor provides power; the farmer directs it.

Applied to ACT's work:

1. **Attach** to any implement a community needs
2. **Power** the work without owning the work
3. **Be unhitched** when the community is ready
4. **Be repaired locally** without depending on us
5. **Be left behind** as a working tool, not a relic

The tractor serves the farm. It doesn't become the farm.

## What It Looks Like

Beautiful Obsolescence shapes every domain of ACT's work:

| Domain | How It Shows Up |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Architecture** | Open source, exportable data, no vendor lock-in |
| **Documentation** | Playbooks and guides for self-maintenance |
| **Training** | Capacity building embedded in every engagement |
| **Governance** | Community decision-making structures |
| **Agreements** | Sunset clauses with expected handover timelines |

### Documentation as Deliverable

Documentation and training are deliverables, not extras. If work cannot be handed over, it isn't finished. Every project includes a handover plan, playbooks for ongoing maintenance, training for local caretakers, and clear pathways for independence.

### Sunset Clauses

Partnership agreements include:
- Expected handover timeline
- Capability transfer milestones
- Community readiness criteria
- Exit conditions

## The Test

Ask of any project:

| Question | Required |
|----------|----------|
| Can they run this without us? | Yes |
| Can they modify it for their needs? | Yes |
| Can they export their data anytime? | Yes |
| Do they own the decisions? | Yes |
| Is there a clear handover plan? | Yes |

If any answer is no, there is more work to do before calling the project complete.

> "If we cannot hand it over, we are still in Curiosity." — LCAA field note

## Beautiful Obsolescence vs. Abandonment

| Beautiful Obsolescence | Abandonment |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| Planned transition | Unplanned exit |
| Capability transfer | Knowledge loss |
| Community readiness | Community scrambling |
| Systems that work | Systems that break |
| Ongoing peer support | Gone without trace |

We don't disappear. We become unnecessary.

## Why Traditional Tech Creates Dependency

Most technology relationships are structured to create dependency:
- Proprietary systems that can't be forked
- Locked-in data that can't be exported
- Expert reliance that doesn't transfer
- Ongoing fees that shift power to the vendor

Beautiful Obsolescence inverts this by design:
- Community capacity grows throughout the engagement
- Transferable knowledge is the goal
- Local ownership is the measure of success
- Self-determination is the endpoint

## Examples Across ACT Projects

### Empathy Ledger
Full data export for communities, open source codebase, training for community storytellers, platform designed for forking, community-controlled consent settings.

### Goods on Country
Local manufacturing capability built into program design, maintenance training included in every production run, supply chain documentation shared openly, community ownership of inventory and decisions.

### JusticeHub
Research accessible without ACT intermediaries, community governance structures from day one, local coordination capacity built in, knowledge that stays local by design.

## Backlinks

- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Action phase is where handover planning lives
- [[governance-consent|Governance & Consent]] — governance as handover discipline
- [[alma|ALMA Framework]] — learning model that feeds capacity transfer
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — primary platform designed for obsolescence

pages.title: Benjamin Knight
pages.excerpt: Co-founder of A Curious Tractor — photographer, technologist, and community practitioner building infrastructure for justice reinvestment and sovereign storytelling.
pages.content:
> Co-founder of A Curious Tractor — photographer, technologist, and community practitioner building infrastructure for justice reinvestment and sovereign storytelling.

## Overview

Benjamin Knight is co-founder of [[../concepts/act-identity|A Curious Tractor (ACT)]] alongside Nicholas Marchesi OAM. He is the architect of the ACT technology ecosystem and the primary field practitioner behind [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] and [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]].

Ben grew up in Muswellbrook, NSW. His practice spans photography, community engagement, and technology — shaped by a long apprenticeship in empathy, innovation, and resilience learned "by standing close to people's lives and letting their stories teach me what change actually takes."

## Formative Experiences

### Orange Sky (3 years)
Three years as photographer with Orange Sky Australia, sitting with people experiencing homelessness across Australia and New Zealand. This work taught the discipline that carries into justice work: "Earn trust slowly; don't take stories — receive them."

### South America
An encounter inside a prison in Bolivia, listening to men talk about hope. "That encounter didn't flatter me with the feeling of helping; it humbled me with the responsibility to keep learning."

### Mount Isa — Ground Truthing
NAIDOC week in Mount Isa crystallised the case for JusticeHub. Walking alongside families, Elders, and young people — meeting [[brodie-germaine|Brodie Germaine]] and witnessing the web of relationships, gyms, camping trips, and cultural practices that already change trajectories. The insight: "The answers live in community already. Our job is not to arrive as saviours but to remove friction, fund the intelligence that's there, and help it circulate."

### Minjerribah / North Stradbroke Island
The Minjerribah Moorgumpin Elders-in-Council modelled governance that holds culture at the centre, not the edge. "When Elders lead, young people feel the ground under their feet."

### Palm Island
[[../communities/palm-island|PICC]] demonstrated community control at scale — 200+ workforce spanning health, family services, and more. Evidence that "when you invest in capacity where people live, the system gets smarter and trust deepens."

### Spain — Diagrama
Visiting [[diagrama|Diagrama]]'s youth justice centres to learn what parts of that ecosystem might translate to Australia — and what must be adapted by, with, and for First Nations communities.

## Core Beliefs

- The solutions to youth justice are **community from community**
- Our role is to **resource without prescribing** — pay for intelligence that already exists and help it flow
- The work isn't to build new monuments; it's to **unblock the paths communities are already walking**
- **Evidence travels fastest as a human story** — funders and policymakers change their minds when they can see and feel what a young person experiences
- "Presence over surveillance" works — relationship-based approaches outperform compliance-based ones

## Why JusticeHub

> "JusticeHub sits at the intersection of everything I've learned: that stories move resources; that community wisdom gets lost without lightweight infrastructure; that innovation is social before it's technical; that change sticks when it's owned locally."

## Sources

- Raw: `wiki/raw/2025-11-05-article-walking-toward-justice-a-personal-journey-267823.md`

pages.title: BG Fit
pages.excerpt: A culturally grounded fitness, healing, and mentorship program addressing the overrepresentation of Indigenous youth in the justice system — using movement and country to disrupt the punitive cycle.
pages.content:
> A culturally grounded fitness, healing, and mentorship program addressing the overrepresentation of Indigenous youth in the justice system — using movement and country to disrupt the punitive cycle.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-BG | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

BG Fit operates in Mount Isa and Doomadgee, communities where Indigenous youth face disproportionate contact with the justice system. The program works from a premise that physical fitness, cultural connection, and Elder mentorship — not punishment — are the most effective interventions. By grounding health and wellbeing in culture and country, BG Fit creates conditions for young people to build identity, purpose, and community belonging.

The results are striking: participating youth have reduced their average police contact from approximately 5 incidents per year to less than 1.

## Key Details

- **Locations:** Mount Isa and Doomadgee, Queensland
- **Target cohort:** Indigenous youth at risk of or with prior justice system involvement
- **Key partners:** Local Elders, community organisations, local police
- **Target:** Full community ownership by 2027
- **Current need:** Sustained funding, strengthened Elder partnerships

## Program Structure

The BG Fit model runs across three connected phases:

1. **Pre-camp fitness** — structured physical training building readiness and trust with participants
2. **On-country cultural camps** — annual camps with Elders integrating cultural knowledge, ceremony, and land connection
3. **Post-camp recovery and integration** — follow-up support maintaining the gains made on country

## Proof Points

- Youth police contact reduced from average 5 incidents per year to less than 1 per participant
- Annual on-country camps demonstrating measurable behaviour change
- Elder-led partnerships sustaining cultural credibility and community trust

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — direct programming through fitness, camps, and mentorship — with deep roots in **Listen**, expressed through ongoing Elder partnerships and community co-design.

- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — another ACT initiative working with remote Indigenous communities

pages.title: Black Cockatoo Valley
pages.excerpt: Conservation-first. We work with Country, not on it. The land sets the pace; we do not scale beyond what the land and community can carry.
pages.content:
> Conservation-first. We work with Country, not on it. The land sets the pace; we do not scale beyond what the land and community can carry.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-BCV | **Tier:** Place

## What It Is

Black Cockatoo Valley is a 150-acre property on Jinibara Country near Witta, Queensland. It is the land holding that grounds ACT's entire physical practice — the site where residencies, R&D, habitat restoration, and community programs take place.

Together with [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] (the former nursery in Witta town), Black Cockatoo Valley forms ACT's "Place" cluster — the land base that makes all the digital and social enterprise work legible.

## Land Practice Philosophy

### Conservation-First

The land is the teacher and the limiter. Conservation-first is the baseline, always.

> Field note: When the creek is low or the grass is tired, we slow down. Capacity is a land decision before it is a calendar decision.

### Key Commitments

| Commitment | Implementation |
|------------|----------------|
| **Low-impact activity** | No extractive tourism, limited-volume operations |
| **Revenue reinvested** | Residencies and workshops fund restoration, weed management, monitoring |
| **Long-term stewardship** | Community co-stewardship and beautiful obsolescence as the goal |
| **Conservation boundaries** | Scale to land capacity and community readiness, not demand |

## The Site

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Size** | 150 acres |
| **Country** | Jinibara |
| **Location** | Near Witta, Queensland |
| **Focus** | Conservation, land practice, R&D, residencies |

The site includes:
- Pasture under regenerative grazing
- Food forest and orchard
- Native corridor restoration
- Water catchment systems
- Studio and gathering buildings

## Activities

### What We Do

| Activity | Purpose | Frequency |
|----------|---------|-----------|
| **Residencies** | Creative practice on Country | Seasonal |
| **Workshops** | Skills, making, land practice | Regular |
| **Restoration** | Weed management, habitat care | Ongoing |
| **R&D** | Regenerative practice research | Continuous |
| **Community programs** | Retreats, learning | By capacity |

### What We Don't Do

- Extractive tourism
- High-volume events
- Activities beyond land capacity
- Operations that harm habitat

## How Land Practice Connects to Ecosystem Projects

Every project should explain how it strengthens land practice:

| Project | Land Practice Connection |
|---------|-------------------------|
| **[[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]]** | Manufacturing and maintenance grounded in place |
| **[[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]** | Stories from and about Country |
| **[[justicehub|JusticeHub]]** | On-Country healing as justice alternative |
| **[[the-harvest|The Harvest]]** | Local enterprise supporting land care revenue |
| **[[act-studio|ACT Studio]]** | Technology serving conservation goals |

## Country Sets the Pace

> If a project asks for more than the land can give, we redesign the project, not the land.

We plan residencies, harvest shares, and enterprise activity to seasons and capacity. When capacity is limited we reduce, not push through; we wait, not accelerate; we learn, not force.

### Conservation Boundaries

The land has veto power:
- No activities during sensitive seasons
- Habitat areas are protected
- Water systems respected
- Wildlife corridors maintained

## 2026 Focus

Balance land management with studio innovation, product development, and enterprise delivery:

1. **Protect land capacity** — Conservation-first guardrails maintained
2. **Run The Harvest in Witta** — Small, practical enterprise hub (separate site)
3. **Push Goods** toward manufacturing and operational maturity
4. **Treat stories and technology** as core instruments of stewardship, not add-ons

## Co-Stewardship Vision

Long-term aim: community co-stewardship and beautiful obsolescence. This means:
- Preparing governance structures for shared ownership
- Building relationships over years, not months
- Transferring capability and authority gradually
- Being ready to step back when community is ready

## Field Notes

> "We do not scale beyond land capacity or community readiness."

> "The creek tells us more than the calendar."

> "If we're too busy to notice the birds, we're too busy."

pages.title: Brodie Germaine
pages.excerpt: Founder of BG Fit, CAMPFIRE, and BAIL — transforming youth empowerment in Queensland through fitness, cultural connection, and mentorship on Kalkadoon Country.
pages.content:
> Founder of BG Fit, CAMPFIRE, and BAIL — transforming youth empowerment in Queensland through fitness, cultural connection, and mentorship on Kalkadoon Country.

## Overview

Brodie Germaine is a community leader and youth mentor based in Mount Isa on Kalkadoon Country. He founded BG Fit, a fitness and mentoring program, and leads two major youth initiatives: the CAMPFIRE Project and BAIL (Be an Indigenous Leader). His work sits at the intersection of physical wellness, cultural identity, and community-led justice alternatives.

Brodie's own story arcs from youth crime to community service. He is open about this trajectory, using his lived experience as the foundation for authentic mentorship: "Unfortunately I was part of youth crime growing up and I'm now in a position giving back."

## Programs

### BG Fit
A community gym and mentoring space in [[mount-isa|Mount Isa]] that serves as the hub for Brodie's youth work. Young people describe it simply: "He keeps us away from trouble." The gym functions as much as a relational space as a fitness facility.

### CAMPFIRE Project
A holistic, community-led program prioritising cultural connection, ancestral wisdom, and personal growth. Rooted in Elder guidance, it provides young people in the child protection system with tools for resilience and identity-building through:
- On-Country camping trips
- Yarning circles with Elders
- Fitness activities and mentorship
- Trauma-informed cultural immersion

### BAIL (Be an Indigenous Leader)
Combines fitness with cultural teachings for youth aged 12-17. Activities include touch football, fishing, yarning circles, and on-Country experiences. Target: 100+ young people per year. Goal: reduce reoffending by providing constructive alternatives and strengthening cultural connection.

## Community Recognition

Uncle Warren King, Kalkadoon Elder, on Brodie: "He comes from good stock... and he'll continue." The pride in Uncle Warren's endorsement carries the weight of cultural approval — success understood not as individual triumph but as continuation.

Nigel Tain (Men's Rugby Union): "We collaborated with Brodie last year to do a bit on country stuff... to see the growth in the kids... Brodie does an absolute amazing job for the community."

Young people: "I'd rather Brodie here 'cause it's face to face" — the irreplaceable value of presence over distance-based service delivery.

## Approach: Presence Over Surveillance

Brodie's methodology embodies a principle shared across ACT's ecosystem partners: that relationship-based intervention works where compliance-based intervention fails. He invites police officers on camping trips — transforming them from enforcers into human beings in the eyes of young people.

His mother Danielle Germaine articulates the intergenerational philosophy: "We just got to keep going, be resilient and not to give up. Even though at times where we think we can't do enough for these kids, we just gotta keep trying so they know that they've got someone there to listen out and look out for."

## Vision

Brodie envisions a comprehensive wellness centre integrating fitness, cultural education, and community support — a safe, inclusive space for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to strengthen physical, mental, and emotional health.

## ACT Connection

Brodie is a key figure in [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] storytelling and a proof point for community-led youth justice alternatives. His work is referenced in the [[ai-community-engagement|Eating the Paperwork]] thesis as an example of what becomes possible when practitioners are freed from administrative burden to focus on relational work.

**Project code:** ACT-CF (CAMPFIRE)

Uncle Dale's vision for youth justice reform doesn't start with detention facilities or court processes. It starts with Country, culture, and care.

His vision: cultural healing centres where young people in the justice system can reconnect with identity, learn from Elders, and find pathways forward that don't require incarceration. These aren't programs bolted onto the existing system — they're alternatives that address root causes.

Key elements of the vision:
- **On-Country healing** — Connection to land as foundation

## Context

**Place:** Platform-wide, serving multiple communities
**Voice Owner:** Platform founder and community collaborators (consented internal)
**Consent Status:** INTERNAL ONLY — review required for external use

## Story

Empathy Ledger began with a question: how do we create infrastructure for storytelling that respects community sovereignty? The platform was built through deep listening with communities who had experienced extractive research and media practices.

The design centres on:
- **Consent at every level** — Who can see, who can share, who can use
- **Cultural protocols** — Elder review, sacred content protection, ongoing consent
- **Data sovereignty** — Communities own their data, can export anytime
- **40% value return** — If stories generate value, communities share in it

Every feature reflects what communities told us they needed: control, visibility, and the ability to change their minds.

pages.title: CAMPFIRE
pages.excerpt: A cultural immersion, fitness, and mentorship program for Indigenous youth in Mount Isa and surrounding communities, founded by Brodie Germaine.
pages.content:
> A cultural immersion, fitness, and mentorship program for Indigenous youth in Mount Isa and surrounding communities, founded by Brodie Germaine.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-CF | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

CAMPFIRE is not just a program — it is a passage. Founded by Brodie Germaine, a Pitta Pitta and Wakka Wakka man from Kalkadoon Country in Mount Isa, CAMPFIRE integrates cultural reconnection to Country, physical fitness, and mentorship to interrupt the cycles of youth crime and disconnection that plague Northwest Queensland.

The program's name reflects both method and metaphor: the campfire as a gathering place where stories are shared, wisdom is passed down, and communities remember who they are. It stands as a counter-narrative to the dominant response — approximately $1 million per year to keep a single young person in youth detention — arguing instead that transformation happens through belonging, not punishment.

## Founder: Brodie Germaine

Brodie's own story is inseparable from what CAMPFIRE became. Born in Mount Isa, he grew up navigating the complexity of life in housing commission homes with family members cycling through the justice system. Athletic prowess in rugby league carried him to Queensland state representation and a scholarship to Ignatius Park College in Townsville. At 18, he encountered drugs for the first time and spiralled through a period of addiction and lost purpose.

The turning point came through an invitation — reluctantly accepted after surviving a suicide attempt — to a men's camp led by Aboriginal Elder Ernie Dingo. In a yarning circle on Country surrounded by sixty men, Brodie found his voice for the first time. Under Ernie's mentorship, he began facilitating Camping on Country programs throughout the Gulf. His parallel passion for fitness grew from personal training sessions in a shed during COVID into Brodie Germaine Fitness — a community gym in Mount Isa that functions as a sanctuary away from lateral violence and substance abuse.

Today these twin vocations have merged into CAMPFIRE.

## The Three Pillars

### Cultural Immersion: Remembering Who We Are

The centrepiece of CAMPFIRE is the "Camping on Country" expeditions — seven-day immersions in remote areas without phone reception or modern distractions, conducted with proper cultural protocols and always involving Elders from the specific Country being visited. Activities include traditional hunting, fishing, tool-making, didgeridoo-making (which supports anxiety through breath control), and storytelling.

"Something about Country, that spiritual feeling that really, really helps the mind, body, and soul when you reconnect to land," Brodie shares.

These camps model respect, reciprocity, and relationship with land and community in ways no bureaucratic consultation process can replicate. Brodie notes: "As Aboriginal people, we do consultation naturally. When you meet someone, it's 'Hey, where are you from? Who are your mob? Who's your totem?'"

### Physical Fitness: Embodying Strength and Discipline

The community gym in Mount Isa provides structured fitness programs that build physical strength while developing discipline, goal-setting, and healthy stress management. The gym serves as a doorway — a safe space where young people can belong regardless of circumstances, and a pathway into deeper cultural programs.

"Exercise doesn't always have to be the gym," Brodie says. "It can be going out taking your dog for a walk, walking up a hill, or doing anything. The gym is a good tool to get people in the doors, and then from there we can offer a lot more like our on-Country programs."

### Mentorship: Walking Alongside on the Journey

Each young person is matched with a dedicated mentor who provides consistent support, guidance, and advocacy. The mentoring relationships formed often become lifelines for young people with few positive adult connections in their lives. The intergenerational exchange of knowledge helps heal historical fractures while ensuring cultural wisdom flows forward.

## Program Ecosystem

CAMPFIRE is part of a broader vision for an integrated ecosystem of care:

- **School-based support** — in-class mentoring and fitness activities to keep young people engaged in education
- **Cultural exchange** — exchanges between Mount Isa youth and urban communities
- **Wellness Centre** — Brodie's five-year vision: a 24-hour facility with a gym, recovery space, youth program delivery, education, and a safe space for anyone "feeling low"

All initiatives employ a trauma-informed approach that recognises intergenerational trauma while emphasising cultural pride as a pathway to healing.

## Context

Mount Isa's watchhouses overflow with young Indigenous people. The Queensland government allocates $1.2 billion toward enforcement and incarceration while preventative cultural programs struggle for a fraction of those resources. CAMPFIRE exists in this gap — a living testimony, operating in the same geography as the problem, funded on goodwill and community relationships, and outperforming the system.

Brodie reflects: "As an Aboriginal person, I still don't understand how you measure 'healing' on paper. But maybe the way to measure a young person's healing stages would be... if I take them out bush, and then when they return to community, they start to make changes with their personal lives, with their family, the way they communicate, the way they listen."

## Connection to ACT Ecosystem

CAMPFIRE features in [[contained|CONTAINED]] as one of the community-led programs that fill the "Solutions Room" — evidence that the system can be different. BG Fit (Brodie Germaine Fitness / CAMPFIRE's gym infrastructure) is cited in the Queensland Making Safer Bill submission as a program worth replicating, alongside Oonchiumpa and the Diagrama model.

CAMPFIRE is also one of the programs that [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] tracks as an evidence-based intervention, with documented reductions in youth police contact in the Mount Isa region.

## Published Writing

- "From Trouble to Transformation: The CAMPFIRE Journey" (2025-10-11) — narrative account of Brodie Germaine's founding story and the CAMPFIRE model
- "Spotlight on Changemaker Brodie Germaine" (2025-10-11) — JusticeHub profile of the founder

pages.title: Caring for Those Who Care
pages.excerpt: A sector sustainability initiative identifying and filling the wellbeing gaps for NFP leaders and workers — research-led, storytelling-powered, and grounded in the conviction that sustaining the carers is inseparable from sustaining the communities they serve.
pages.content:
> A sector sustainability initiative identifying and filling the wellbeing gaps for NFP leaders and workers — research-led, storytelling-powered, and grounded in the conviction that sustaining the carers is inseparable from sustaining the communities they serve.

## Overview

Caring for Those Who Care addresses a structural blind spot in the social sector: the people who dedicate their working lives to holding communities together are themselves underserved, under-supported, and often operating at significant personal cost. NFP leaders in particular carry a particular burden — responsible for organisations, staff, and communities, expected to model resilience, and often without the peer support or institutional backing that leaders in other sectors take for granted.

The project combines rigorous research, community storytelling, and practical recommendations to identify the gaps and build the case for systemic change in how the sector cares for its own.

## NFP Leaders Interview Project

The research centred on the **NFP Leaders Interview Project**, conducted in partnership with **Bond University**. This multi-phase research project:

1. **Research Design** — developing interview frameworks that could surface the real experience of NFP leaders, including the dimensions of isolation, moral injury, financial precarity, and emotional labour that are rarely discussed publicly
2. **Data Collection** — in-depth interviews with NFP leaders across the sector, gathering qualitative evidence of the support gaps
3. **Analysis** — systematic analysis of themes, patterns, and the structural conditions that generate them
4. **Recommendations** — translating findings into actionable recommendations for funders, peak bodies, government, and the sector itself

The Bond University partnership brings academic rigour and credibility to findings that might otherwise be dismissed as anecdote or advocacy.

## Storytelling as Method and Output

Beyond the formal research, Caring for Those Who Care uses storytelling to communicate findings in ways that build empathy and shift the conditions for change. Stories from NFP leaders — told with care and appropriate consent — make visible the human cost of sector underinvestment in worker wellbeing.

This connects the project to ACT's broader storytelling infrastructure, particularly [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]].

## Relationship to Junes Patch

[[junes-patch|June's Patch]] is a natural companion to this project: where Caring for Those Who Care identifies the problem and builds the evidence base for healthcare worker wellbeing needs, June's Patch delivers a direct nature-based response. Together they represent ACT's commitment to both knowing and acting.

## LCAA Phase

**Listen** — The project's primary work is listening: to NFP leaders, to their experiences, to what the sector needs that it isn't getting. Research and storytelling are both forms of deep, structured listening. The recommendations that follow are grounded entirely in what was heard.

pages.title: Cars and Microcontrollers
pages.excerpt: Making things with your hands is not a hobby. For some young people, it's the first time their intelligence has been recognised.
pages.content:
> Making things with your hands is not a hobby. For some young people, it's the first time their intelligence has been recognised.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-MC | **Tier:** Studio

## What It Is

Cars and Microcontrollers is an ACT project at the intersection of maker culture, electronics, and hands-on learning. The project puts young people in contact with physical machines — cars, engines, circuits, microcontrollers — and treats the work of understanding and building those machines as a legitimate site of learning, identity, and creative practice.

The Notion project record confirms status as Active (as of February 2026). Operational detail in the wiki is thin — this project has not yet had its full source material ingested. What follows frames Cars and Microcontrollers within the ACT ecosystem and its underlying logic, based on confirmed status and ecosystem positioning.

## The Logic Behind the Project

ACT returns consistently to one insight: that engagement follows relevance, and relevance in marginalised communities often looks like practical things that work.

A microcontroller is a small programmable chip embedded in everything from cars to washing machines to Arduino projects. Learning to wire one, program it, and watch it control something physical is — for a young person who has never been told they're the kind of person who does that — a significant event. Not because of the technology. Because of what it proves about them.

Cars occupy a different register. In many communities where ACT works — remote NT, outer suburban Queensland, Western Sydney — mechanical knowledge is intergenerational, practical, and status-bearing. Knowing how engines work is not abstract. It connects to work, to independence, to the skills of fathers and uncles and older brothers. Cars and Microcontrollers plants one foot in that world and extends the other into electronics and computational thinking.

## Ecosystem Position

Cars and Microcontrollers sits in ACT's Studio tier — the category for creative practice and experimental projects that don't fit the satellite community-program model, but that embody ACT's core belief that making produces engagement where institutional programs fail.

The making-as-pathway pattern runs through ACT's other Studio projects:

| Project | What They Make | Why It Works |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| [[resoleution|ReSOLEution]] | Custom sneakers | Identity, creative ownership, commercial possibility |
| [[deadlylabs|DeadlyLabs]] | STEM experiments in sports science | Familiar domain (sport) opens unfamiliar domain (science) |
| [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] | Functional goods for remote communities | Making things community actually needs |
| Cars and Microcontrollers | Mechanical and electronic systems | Practical intelligence, intergenerational relevance |

The common thread across all of these: young people learn best when they're building something real, with materials they can touch, toward an outcome they understand.

## Relationship to ACT's Technology Thesis

Microcontrollers — the Arduino, the Raspberry Pi, the ESP32 — are the entry points into the physical computing world. They sit at the border between digital and physical: code that makes things move, sense, respond. For ACT, which builds technology platforms (JusticeHub, Empathy Ledger, CivicGraph) alongside community programs, a project that introduces young people to this same layer is meaningful beyond its immediate community impact.

The long-term question Cars and Microcontrollers implicitly poses: what if the young people in the program eventually build the technology that helps their own communities? This isn't a stated outcome — it's an aspiration encoded in the design.

## Current Evidence

Evidence in project_knowledge is sparse. The Notion sync (February 2026) confirms the project is Active. Financial tracking in Xero under `ACT-MC — Cars and Microcontrollers` confirms it has incurred costs. No published articles, partner organisations, or specific community contexts have been ingested yet. The wiki has not yet absorbed deeper sources for this project.

pages.title: Civic Transparency Movement
pages.excerpt: The emerging practice of using AI to make government legible to citizens — reversing the historical flow where states made societies legible to themselves.
pages.content:
> The emerging practice of using AI to make government legible to citizens — reversing the historical flow where states made societies legible to themselves.

**Status:** Active research  
**Compiled:** 2026-04-06  
**Related:** [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]], [[civic-world-model|Civic World Model]], [[third-reality|The Third Reality]], [[global-precedents|Global Precedents]]

---

## Karpathy's Thesis

In 2025, Andrej Karpathy (co-founder of OpenAI, creator of Andrej Karpathy's Neural Networks course, and one of the most-followed AI researchers globally) articulated a compelling vision for AI's role in civic life:

> AI agents will be able to process the full corpus of government procurement, lobbying disclosures, campaign finance filings, and legislative text — creating a persistent watchdog that no individual journalist or NGO could sustain.

The core insight: **governments produce enormous volumes of machine-readable public data** (procurement, legislation, corporate registrations, grant disclosures, court filings) but that data is functionally inaccessible to most citizens because the volume and complexity exceed human processing capacity. AI removes that constraint.

This is not about replacing investigative journalism. It is about enabling a new kind of **structural accountability** — one that catches patterns across thousands of contracts, tracks the same entity through multiple regulatory disclosures, and surfaces relationships that only become visible at scale.

---

## "Seeing Like a State" — The Reversal

The political theorist James C. Scott's 1998 book *Seeing Like a State* described how modern states make society *legible* in order to govern it:

- Cadastral land surveys that convert complex communal land use into clean property titles
- Standardised surnames that make individuals trackable across administrative systems
- Scientific monoculture farming that maximises measurable yield at the cost of ecological complexity
- Urban planning grids that prioritise administrative clarity over the organic logic of communities

Scott's argument was that this "high modernist" simplification destroys the local, practical knowledge (*metis*) that makes communities actually function. The state gains legibility; the people lose complexity.

**The civic transparency movement inverts this dynamic.**

AI can now process government's own administrative outputs — the procurement databases, the company registrations, the grant disclosures, the legislative text — and make them navigable by the people those governments are meant to serve. Instead of the state making society legible to administrators, **society can now make the state legible to itself**.

This is not just a technical capability. It is a democratic rebalancing.

---

## What Gets Made Legible

The volume of public government data that is technically available but practically inaccessible is extraordinary:

**Procurement and contracts**
- Federal and state government procurement records: who won, what amount, which department
- Subcontracting relationships that obscure beneficial ownership
- Contract variations and extensions that increase total value without fresh competition
- Patterns of awards to connected entities

**Legislative complexity**
- Omnibus bills that bundle hundreds of unrelated provisions into a single vote
- Amendment histories that show what was added, removed, or watered down and by whom
- Regulatory impact statements vs actual outcomes
- Sunset clauses and review triggers that are quietly allowed to lapse

**Political finance**
- Donation flows from corporate entities to political parties and candidates
- The timing of donations relative to policy decisions or procurement outcomes
- Shell company structures that obscure the ultimate donor
- Third-party campaigning and issue advertising expenditure

**Lobbying disclosures**
- Which entities lobbied which ministers on which legislation
- Revolving door: former officials who now lobby their former departments
- The gap between disclosed lobbying and actual policy outcomes

**Local government**
- Development application approvals and who benefits
- Council procurement and who receives contracts
- Councillor pecuniary interest registers vs their voting records
- Rates, valuations, and exemptions

---

## CivicGraph: Already Implementing This

[[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] is ACT's implementation of civic transparency at scale. As of early 2026:

- **587,000 entities** — organisations, people, government bodies, projects
- **1.5M+ relationships** — funding, employment, governance, geographic
- **$74 billion in contracts tracked** across federal and state procurement
- **Political donation flows** mapped between corporate donors and recipients
- **Justice funding streams** visible including ACCO sector funding (see [[acco-sector-analysis|ACCO Sector Analysis]])

CivicGraph does not just aggregate data — it makes the *relationships* visible. The same entity appearing as a contractor, a donor, and a board member of a peak body is not visible in any single dataset. It only becomes visible when those datasets are joined and the entity resolution problem is solved. That is the hard technical work CivicGraph has done.

The [[civic-world-model|Civic World Model]] is the conceptual framing: a continuously-updated, AI-maintained model of how civic power flows in Australia — who funds whom, who employs whom, who influences policy and how.

---

## Global Precedents

The civic transparency movement is not unique to Australia. Several practitioners are building equivalent systems in other jurisdictions:

**Harry Rushworth — UK "Machinery of Government"**  
Rushworth's project maps the organisational structure of the UK government as a living, navigable document — not a static org chart but a queryable model of which department does what, who leads it, what its budget is, and how it connects to quangos, contractors, and arm's-length bodies. The project draws on Companies House data, civil service publications, and parliamentary disclosures. It is the structural complement to the financial data layer: understanding *how* government is organised is a prerequisite for understanding *where* money flows.

**Michael Adams — US City-Level Mapping**  
Adams is building equivalent infrastructure for US cities — the municipal level that is often the most opaque and the most directly impactful on daily life. City procurement, zoning decisions, police budgets, and school board contracts are governed by a patchwork of disclosure rules that vary dramatically between jurisdictions. Adams' work is notable for prioritising the city scale: where federal data is messy but plentiful, city data is often genuinely inaccessible.

**OpenSecrets / FollowTheMoney (US)**  
Long-established campaign finance tracking, now being extended with AI-assisted entity resolution and relationship mapping.

**Who Funds You? (UK)**  
Media ownership and funding transparency project — who owns the outlets that shape public discourse.

See [[global-precedents|Global Precedents]] for broader international examples of civic accountability infrastructure.

---

## ACT's Unique Angle: The Third Reality

Most civic transparency projects focus on making structural data legible: the numbers, the entities, the flows. This is necessary and valuable. But it is not sufficient.

Data without human meaning is just evidence waiting to be weaponised by whoever controls the narrative.

ACT's contribution to the civic transparency movement is the [[third-reality|Third Reality]] — the methodology that insists on connecting structural data (what government does, what money flows where) with experiential data (what communities feel, what outcomes look like at the human level).

The Third Reality is not a rebuke of data-driven accountability. It is its completion. A procurement record that shows a contract awarded to a connected entity is concerning. A procurement record *plus* a community story about what happened when that contractor arrived — that is accountability with teeth.

This is where [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] enters the civic transparency picture. EL is not just a storytelling platform — it is a structured, consent-governed repository of community experience that can be linked to the structural data in CivicGraph. The combination is what distinguishes ACT's approach from pure transparency infrastructure.

---

## Indigenous Funding Flows and the ACCO Sector

One of the most opaque areas in Australian civic data is **funding to and through the ACCO sector** — Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations.

The structural problem:
- Federal and state government funding for Indigenous programs flows through dozens of different programs, departments, and mechanisms
- ACCO funding is often bundled into broader program categories in procurement data
- Many ACCOs receive funding from multiple government sources simultaneously, making total funding hard to reconstruct
- The distinction between direct funding to ACCOs vs funding to non-Indigenous organisations *for* Indigenous programs is rarely visible in raw procurement data

CivicGraph is beginning to make these flows visible. This matters for:

- **Community self-determination**: communities being able to see what is being spent in their name
- **Policy advocacy**: evidence base for arguing that direct ACCO funding produces better outcomes than mainstreamed service delivery
- **Accountability**: tracking whether government commitments to community-controlled organisations are actually being met
- **The Closing the Gap framework**: connecting expenditure data to outcome data

This is the specific intersection where [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] connects to ACT's broader mission of supporting community control and Indigenous sovereignty.

---

## The AI Advantage

What makes this moment different from previous civic transparency efforts (FOI requests, parliamentary budget offices, investigative journalism) is the combination of:

1. **Scale**: AI can process the full corpus, not a sample
2. **Persistence**: AI watchdogs don't burn out, don't change beats, don't get reassigned
3. **Entity resolution**: AI can identify that "Acme Pty Ltd", "Acme Services", and "Acme Group" are the same beneficial owner across different datasets
4. **Relationship mapping**: AI can surface n-hop relationships (A funds B which employs C who is a board member of D which received a contract from A's department)
5. **Temporal analysis**: AI can track how an entity's relationships, funding, and activities change over time
6. **Natural language interface**: AI makes the data accessible to citizens, journalists, and community organisations without requiring technical expertise

The limiting factors remain data access (not all public data is machine-readable), entity resolution quality (names are messy), and the political will to act on what is surfaced.

---

pages.title: Civic World Model
pages.excerpt: Replacing the "middle management" of the state and philanthropy with an interconnected intelligence layer.
pages.content:
> Replacing the "middle management" of the state and philanthropy with an interconnected intelligence layer.

## Origin

Inspired by Block's "[From Hierarchy to Intelligence](https://block.xyz/inside/from-hierarchy-to-intelligence)" thesis, which describes replacing traditional corporate hierarchies (where middle management routes information slowly) with AI-coordinated systems.

CivicGraph is building the **Civic World Model** — the social sector equivalent. Instead of relying on government bureaucrats, grant managers, and delayed annual reports to route information, CivicGraph deterministically maps entities, capital flows, and social outcomes in real time.

## Four Architectural Principles (from Block)

### 1. The "Honest Signal"
Block views transaction data as the most honest signal. In social impact, traditional signals are subjective grant applications and marketing spin. CivicGraph redefines the honest signal by tracking actual money flows (procurement, donations, grants) cross-referenced with verified outcome data from ALMA.

### 2. Humans at the Edge
The system handles intelligence and coordination. Human roles shift to the "edge" — community leaders running diversion programs, storytellers on Empathy Ledger, designers of Goods on Country. Administrative burden removed from grassroots organizations.

### 3. Capabilities vs. Interfaces
CivicGraph is the underlying **Capability and Intelligence Layer** — the atomic data primitive. JusticeHub, Empathy Ledger, and government dashboards are **Interfaces** that surface this civic intelligence to different audiences.

### 4. Building the "Company World Model"
A machine-readable state of operations, priorities, and roadblocks in real time. CivicGraph does this for the public sector — 566,522 entities connected by 1,536,626 relationships across 254 tables and 29.5M records.

## CivicGraph Platform Stats (Live)

| Domain | Tables | Records |
|--------|--------|---------|
| Registries | 9 | 23.5M |
| Entity Graph | 9 | 3.4M |
| Procurement | 12 | 1.1M |
| People & Governance | 4 | 357K |
| Influence & Accountability | 10 | 340K |
| Funding & Grants | 25 | 248K |
| Social & Disability | 14 | 479K |
| Evidence & Outcomes | 35 | 127K |
| **Total** | **254** | **29.5M** |

## Entity Linkage

The ABN (Australian Business Number) is the universal join key. 559K+ entities resolved from 8 government data systems using ABN matching and normalized name fuzzy-matching.

Key linkage rates:
- Justice Funding: **86%** (146K records)
- Federal Contracts: **85%** (791K records)
- Foundations: **100%** (10.8K records)
- Political Donations: **59%** (313K records)
- ALMA Interventions: **56%** (1.4K records)

## Data Coverage Gaps

- NSW, VIC, WA, SA, TAS, NT, ACT lack org-level funding data (only QLD has granular per-recipient grants)
- 94,162 funding records still unclassified by topic
- 873 LGAs identified as funding deserts

## The Product Vision

CivicGraph is not a data dashboard — it's a **replacement for the archaic, top-down hierarchy** of traditional grant-making and policy-creation. Transitioning social impact from bureaucratic hierarchy to decentralized, verifiable intelligence.
