pages.title: Diagrama
pages.excerpt: Spain's leading therapeutic detention model as an alternative to Australia's punitive justice system — studying, learning from, and working toward an ethical, Indigenous-led transfer of therapeutic detention knowledge to Australia.
pages.content:
> Spain's leading therapeutic detention model as an alternative to Australia's punitive justice system — studying, learning from, and working toward an ethical, Indigenous-led transfer of therapeutic detention knowledge to Australia.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-DG | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

Diagrama refers to ACT's engagement with **Fundación Diagrama**, a Spanish organisation that has developed one of the world's most respected therapeutic detention models for young people in conflict with the law. Spain's youth justice system, with Diagrama as a central implementing partner, has achieved remarkable outcomes — reduced reoffending, improved mental health, and the genuine rehabilitation of young people — through an approach grounded in therapeutic relationships, dignity, and care rather than punishment and containment.

The Foundation was established in **1991** and has spent over 35 years operating youth re-education centres across Spain. In 2002, Diagrama founded the **International Juvenile Justice Observatory (IJJO)** in Brussels, which provides the research and policy framework for international knowledge transfer.

ACT's interest in Diagrama sits within [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]'s broader mission: identifying and adapting justice alternatives that could reduce Australia's catastrophic rates of Indigenous incarceration, particularly among young people.

## Why Diagrama Matters for Australia

Australia's youth justice system remains one of the most punitive in the developed world, with Indigenous young people massively overrepresented at every level of contact. The system as currently designed does not rehabilitate — it cycles young people through trauma, disconnection, and deepening criminal justice involvement.

Diagrama demonstrates that a fundamentally different model is possible. Its therapeutic detention approach:
- Treats the young person as a full human being, not a risk to be managed
- Centres therapeutic relationships as the primary mechanism of change
- Focuses on reintegration and community connection rather than punishment and isolation
- Produces measurably better outcomes across all indicators

## The Diagrama Model in Detail

### Philosophy: Re-education, Not Punishment

Diagrama operates what it calls **re-education centres** — a deliberate rebuke of the concept of a detention facility. The founding premise is that young people in conflict with the law are still young people first. They need mentors, not guards. Education, not isolation. Belief in their future, not punishment for their past.

As Jesús Teruel, Territorial Director for Murcia, explained during ACT's visit: *"We aren't jailers. We're not just enforcing a sentence to pass the months until they leave. We're here to work with them, to transmit values, to show them there's a different way."*

### Staffing: Mentors, Not Guards

The role of staff in Diagrama centres is structurally different from conventional detention. Staff carry no weapons, wear no uniforms, and display no badges of authority — they are present as humans connecting with humans. They know each young person's story, their triggers, their aspirations, and they navigate conflicts with genuine curiosity and respect rather than power and control.

Low staff turnover is a defining feature of the model. People who work within Diagrama's framework tend to stay — because the model works and because the work is meaningful. Staff who have been with particular young people for 15 or more years are not unusual. This continuity of care creates the stable relationships that underpin rehabilitation.

The **staff ratio is effectively 1:1** — a figure that seems impossible in the Australian context until you understand that it reflects a fundamentally different theory of change. When relationship is the mechanism, staff are not a cost centre; they are the intervention.

One staff member shared during the ACT visit: *"Before we can expect them to change, they need to feel that someone genuinely cares about their future. Not because it's our job, but because we see their worth."*

### Daily Life and Therapeutic Structure

Young people in Diagrama centres receive **formal education for 30 or more hours per week** alongside structured vocational training. Programs cover practical skills including horticulture, carpentry, arts, and digital skills. The physical environment — open spaces, natural light, communal areas designed for connection — reflects and reinforces the therapeutic philosophy.

A **graduated autonomy system** shapes behaviour through reward rather than punishment. Young people earn increasing freedom and responsibility as they demonstrate progress. This structure creates intrinsic motivation: a sense that there is something to work toward, and that the future is genuinely open.

Holistic support is built into the program. Mental health care, substance use intervention, and family engagement are not add-ons — they are core elements of each young person's individual plan. Family involvement is specifically encouraged because reintegration into community is the goal from day one.

### Vocational and Employment Outcomes

More than **70% of young people leaving Diagrama facilities continue in education or secure employment within six months** of release. This is not accidental — the vocational programs are explicitly designed as bridges to life after the centre, not as occupation during detention.

### The Numbers

The data provides the clearest illustration of the two paradigms:

| | Australia | Diagrama (Spain) |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per child/year | $1,100,000 | ~$31,000 |
| Reoffending rate | 84.5% | 13.6% (over 6 years) |
| Staff model | Guards | 1:1 mentors |
| Program completion | — | 98% |
| Youth suicides in custody | Ongoing | Zero |
| Social return on investment | — | €5.64 per €1 |

Australia spends approximately **$1,500 per young person per day** — roughly $1.1 million per year — and achieves an 84.5% reoffending rate. Diagrama spends approximately A$31,000 per young person per year and achieves a 13.6% reoffending rate over six years. Every euro invested returns €5.64 in social value. No young person has died by suicide in a Diagrama facility. These are not aspirational targets — they are 35 years of documented results.

## Learning Trip Observations

### The Visit

ACT undertook a **five-day immersion visit** to Diagrama youth detention centres in Spain, guided by **David** (CEO of Diagrama). The visit was structured to enable direct engagement with staff, young people, and the physical environments of multiple centres — not as an inspection but as a genuine learning relationship.

### La Zarza and What Was Seen There

At Diagrama's **La Zarza centre**, in the morning light filtering through the windows, the scene was described as "a quiet revolution." Young people — many convicted of serious offences — were engaged in conversation with staff who carried no weapons, wore no uniforms, displayed no badges of authority. Just humans connecting with humans.

The immediate physical impression was striking: corridors that felt more like a school than a detention centre. Laughter. Positive energy. Strong, visible relationships between young people and their educators. *"From the moment I stepped into each Diagrama center, I was struck by the positive energy, the laughter, and the strong relationships between the young people and their educators."*

### Talking With the Young People

One of the most significant moments of the visit was sitting with young people and discussing the conditions in Australian youth detention. They struggled to understand how such a punitive and dehumanising approach could be considered acceptable or effective. They spoke about their own hopes and dreams, and about the trust they had in their educators to support them. They viewed their time in the centre not as a punishment but as an opportunity for growth and transformation.

The contrast with Australian visits was stark. In Australia, every visit to a youth detention centre leaves a sense of depletion — an oppressive atmosphere, a lack of compassion and engagement between staff and young people, an overall punitive approach that communicates hopelessness. In Spain, the atmosphere communicated the opposite.

### Staff Who Stayed

The longevity of staff relationships was observed directly — staff who had worked with young people for 15 or more years, who remained because the model creates the conditions for meaningful work. This is not a characteristic of systems designed around control; it is a product of systems designed around relationship.

### The CONTAINED Connection

The learning trip is the direct origin of **Room 2 of the CONTAINED experience** — ACT's immersive installation that asks visitors to physically experience the contrast between Australian detention and a Diagrama centre. The photographs on Room 2's walls are from this visit. The data projected overhead is drawn from this research. The question the room poses — *"What if we spent $1.55 million per child on healing instead of harm?"* — now has a 35-year answer.

## Spain vs Australia: A Comparative View

### Foundational Differences

Spain's and Australia's youth justice systems reflect different foundational assumptions. Spain's system is oriented toward **social reintegration** — addressing the root causes of offending behaviour and supporting young people in making positive changes. Australia's system has historically leaned toward **punitive accountability** — detention and legal consequences as the primary response to youth crime, informed by an English legal legacy and influenced by the US model of punishment over support.

The difference is not marginal. It reflects a different answer to the question of what a young person who offends actually is: a risk to be managed, or a human being in need of intervention.

### The Cost Inversion

The financial comparison is counterintuitive for those accustomed to Australian policy framing. Diagrama's model — with its 1:1 staffing ratios, therapeutic programs, and educational components — costs dramatically less per young person per year than Australian punitive facilities. The explanation is that Australian facilities require extensive physical security infrastructure, adversarial management, and the ongoing costs of cycling young people back through the system repeatedly. Diagrama's investment in relationship pays dividends across a lifetime.

Traditional youth detention in Australia costs approximately **$1,500 per young person per day**. Diagrama estimates a return of **€3.80 to €5.64 for every €1 invested** (depending on timeframe), while Australia's system produces an 84.5% reoffending rate that ensures those costs compound indefinitely.

### Recent Reform Trajectories

Spain's youth justice legislation — the Ley Orgánica de Responsabilidad Penal de los Menores (LORPM, 2000) — explicitly frames the response to youth crime as educational and rehabilitative rather than punitive. The court system is oriented toward welfare assessments and individualised plans. Detention is a last resort. Diagrama operates within this framework and embodies its intent.

Australia is in a period of contested reform. Restorative justice practices and community-based interventions are increasing, but against significant political and institutional resistance. The gap between the two systems remains vast.

### Indigenous Overrepresentation — The Australian Specificity

Any comparison between the two systems must acknowledge the particular dimension of Australia's crisis: the catastrophic overrepresentation of Indigenous young people at every level of the justice system. This is not a phenomenon that exists in Spain in comparable form, and it means that any transfer of the Diagrama model must be deeply transformed rather than simply transplanted. An effective model for Australia is not Spanish therapeutic detention applied to an Australian context — it is a model grounded in Indigenous knowledge, culture, and leadership that draws selectively on what Diagrama has proven.

## European Context

### A Spectrum of Approaches

European youth justice systems occupy a wide spectrum, but the strongest performers share characteristics with the Diagrama model: rehabilitative frameworks, restorative justice practices, community service, and educational initiatives oriented toward reintegration. Countries with the lowest recidivism rates consistently employ rehabilitative approaches rather than punitive ones.

Recidivism rates across European youth justice systems serve as a primary indicator of effectiveness. Spain's national recidivism rate in traditional youth detention runs between 30–50%; within Diagrama centres specifically, the six-year rate is 13.6% — well below any comparable European benchmark.

### Common Challenges in Cross-National Learning

Cross-national comparison of youth justice systems is complicated by differences in legal frameworks, cultural contexts, and socio-economic conditions. What works in one context does not automatically transfer to another — a caution that ACT holds explicitly in its approach to learning from Diagrama.

Cost-effectiveness is a consistent concern across European systems. The challenge of demonstrating that upfront investment in rehabilitation produces long-term savings — in reoffending, in health costs, in social welfare — is as much a political communication challenge as an evidential one. Diagrama's documented social return on investment is one of the strongest available cases anywhere in the world.

### Spain's International Reach

Diagrama's influence now extends well beyond Spain. The **International Juvenile Justice Observatory (IJJO)**, founded by Diagrama in Brussels in 2002, has become a significant international research and advocacy body. The **Diagrama Foundation UK** (led by David McGuire) bridges the Spanish model with English-speaking contexts and has engaged directly with ACT around the Australian opportunity. An academic comparative study of English custodial versus Spanish re-educational centres (D. Romero McGuire, 2018) is one of the more rigorous academic assessments of the model's international transferability.

## The Transfer Challenge

Simply importing a Spanish model to Australia would be inadequate — and potentially harmful. The goal is not wholesale adoption but **ethical, culturally appropriate transfer** of the therapeutic detention knowledge to an Australian context, with the following commitments:

### Culturally Appropriate Adaptation

Any therapeutic model applied to Indigenous young Australians must be grounded in Indigenous knowledge, culture, and leadership — not adapted from a European framework and applied without transformation.

### Indigenous-Led Implementation

The target for meaningful implementation is **Indigenous-led by 2027**. This means not just consultation but genuine authority and ownership by Indigenous communities over the therapeutic model, its design, and its delivery.

### The Blueprint for Change

In 2020, **Danila Dilba Health Service** — one of the Northern Territory's leading Aboriginal community-controlled health organisations — partnered with Diagrama to produce the *Blueprint for Change NT*, an adaptation report specifically designed for the Australian context. The report maps how the Diagrama model could be adapted to work within Indigenous communities, respecting cultural authority while drawing on 35 years of proven methodology.

**Diagrama Australia** already exists as an entity (diagramaaustralia.org). The IJJO provides the research and policy framework. The pieces are all there. What's missing is political will and public pressure.

### JusticeHub Learning Trips

[[justicehub|JusticeHub]] has incorporated visits to Diagrama centres in Spain as part of its Learning Trips program — enabling Australian practitioners, advocates, and community leaders to experience the model firsthand, ask hard questions, and begin the work of understanding what is transferable and what must be reimagined.

### Next Steps

The concrete pathway forward includes:

1. **A formal delegation** — Australian state and territory youth justice ministers visiting Diagrama centres firsthand. Not a briefing paper. Walk the halls. Talk to the young people. Feel the difference.
2. **Expand the Blueprint for Change** — the NT adaptation report needs to be picked up, funded, and extended to Queensland and Western Australia, where Indigenous young people are most overrepresented.
3. **Pilot programs** — one community-controlled facility operating on Diagrama principles, with rigorous measurement from day one.
4. **Connect via David McGuire** at Diagrama Foundation UK, who bridges the Spanish model with English-speaking contexts and can facilitate introductions to senior leadership in Spain.

## LCAA Phase

**Curiosity + Action** — The engagement with Diagrama begins with deep curiosity: what can we learn from this model? What does it tell us about what's possible? What needs to change for it to work here? That curiosity is not passive — it is driving active work toward implementation, advocacy, and the relationship-building that makes an ethical knowledge transfer possible.

## Published Writing

The following articles have been published through ACT's engagement with Diagrama, in order from most recent:

- **Spain Diagrama Trip Reflection** (March 2026) — Benjamin Knight's five-day immersion visit reflection; includes the full data comparison, the CONTAINED connection, and the call to action for Australian implementation.
- **Beyond Walls: What Spanish Youth Detention Centers Taught Me About Seeing Humanity First** (October 2025) — First-person account from La Zarza centre, centred on relationship as the mechanism of change and the courage required to see beyond labels. Part 1 of the "Reimagining Youth Justice" series.
- **From Punishment to Potential: Lessons from Spain's Innovative Youth Justice Model — Day 1 with Diagrama** (October 2025) — Day 1 visit reflection covering the Diagrama model's core lessons: positive relationships, personalised support, and instilling hope.
- **The Diagrama Model: A Transformative Approach to Youth Justice** (October 2025) — Analytical overview of how the model works, including the graduated autonomy system, staff approach, vocational pathways, and documented outcomes.
- **Diagrama Foundation's Impact on Spain's Youth Detention System** (October 2025) — Historical overview of Diagrama's role since 1991, including key program initiatives and the long-term track record.
- **A Comparative Analysis of Youth Justice Systems in Spain and Australia** (October 2025) — Side-by-side examination of the two systems, their costs, outcomes, underlying principles, and reform trajectories.
- **Youth Detention and Youth Justice Models in Europe: A Comparative Overview** (October 2025) — Broader European context, examining recidivism rates, best practices, and the challenges of cross-country comparison.
- **Diagrama — Youth Justice Spain** (October 2025) — Summary of the trip purpose and ACT's commitment to evaluating the model for Australian adaptation.

pages.title: Diagrama Spain: The Meetings Behind ACT's Engagement
pages.excerpt: The conversations that built ACT's understanding of the Diagrama model — and what they reveal about the political, relational, and institutional barriers to an Australian implementation.
pages.content:
> The conversations that built ACT's understanding of the Diagrama model — and what they reveal about the political, relational, and institutional barriers to an Australian implementation.

**Compiled:** 2026-04-07 | **Source:** 4 ACT-DG meeting records (2 substantial, 2 sparse)
**See also:** [[diagrama|Diagrama]], [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[contained|CONTAINED]]

---

## The Olga Meeting: A Sector Elder's Assessment (January 2025)

The longest and most analytically dense meeting in the entire ACT-DG record is a three-way conversation between Olga, Nicholas Marchesi, and Benjamin Knight on 16 January 2025.

Olga grew up in the Northern Territory — boarding school in Alice Springs, then Townsville and Charters Towers. She came back to Darwin just before Cyclone Tracy and stayed. Her working life has been a mix of private sector, government, NGO, and a spell with Foreign Affairs in Canberra (*"really wasn't my cup of tea. I don't think they're my kind of people"*). She has worked most of her life in community-based organisations. By the time of this meeting she is semi-retired but still connected to the **Justice Reform Initiative** — one of the key national bodies advocating for evidence-based youth justice reform.

This meeting is ACT's deepest recorded conversation about the Australian context for a Diagrama-style implementation. Key threads:

### What Changes in Legislation Would Actually Be Required

Olga's contribution here is important: she did not just validate the model, she worked through what it would take for the model to survive the Australian political environment. The Diagrama model operates within Spain's *Ley Orgánica de Responsabilidad Penal de los Menores* (LORPM, 2000), which frames youth justice as fundamentally educational and rehabilitative. Australia has no equivalent legislative framework at a national level. Any implementation would require sustained legislative advocacy, not just a pilot program.

### The Political and Institutional Barrier Map

Olga's assessment was sober and experienced. The barriers are not primarily about evidence — the evidence for therapeutic detention is strong and she understands it well. The barriers are structural:
- Bureaucratic incentive toward incumbent systems that already have line items
- Political risk aversion — "tough on crime" remains electorally palatable even when it is empirically wrong
- Federation complexity — youth justice sits at state/territory level, making national reform slow
- The "repair mindset" — consultants and policymakers focused on fixing broken systems, not redesigning them (this framing appears directly in the 2023 TYSON Bank workshop notes and seems to be a shared ACT/Olga diagnosis)

### The NT Context

Olga's lens is predominantly NT — Alice Springs, Darwin, the remote communities she has spent decades working in. The Northern Territory's youth justice crisis is the most acute in Australia. The existing [[diagrama|Diagrama]] article notes the 2020 *Blueprint for Change NT* produced by Danila Dilba Health Service and Diagrama — Olga's presence as a NT sector elder makes this meeting a direct bridge between that document and ACT's implementation strategy.

### Relationships Formed

Olga is explicitly positioned in ACT's network as a key figure for NT strategy. Her connections to the Justice Reform Initiative and her decades of government-facing work make her a credibility anchor for conversations with NT bureaucrats and policymakers. This meeting established that relationship — not just as a one-time consultation but as an ongoing strategic channel.

---

## May Second Meeting: Political Strategy and Media (May 2024)

Fourteen months after the Olga conversation, the second substantive ACT-DG meeting shows the Diagrama strategy in a more operational phase.

Key developments reported:
- **Two more Australians going to Spain** — one through a Churchill Fellowship; Mindy also wants to go. The Spain visit program is building momentum independent of ACT's direct facilitation.
- **David meeting the Shadow Minister** — David (CEO of Diagrama Foundation UK / Australia) has secured a meeting with the Shadow Minister for youth justice. Political engagement is active.
- **Brett McKlopp, Nine Network** — a journalist and presenter at the Nine Network has requested another interview with David about the Diagrama model. Media coverage accelerating.
- **Cairns centre "a year away"** — an actual Diagrama-modelled facility is in planning for Cairns. This is the most concrete progress marker in any ACT-DG record.
- **Legislative changes required** — the meeting identified specific legislative changes needed for the model to operate in Australia. David met with Kate (presumably Shadow Minister or her representative) who "had a lot of questions about the system."
- **LNP as an opportunity** — *"LNP will get in and they are looking for things that are different."* This is a strategic read: the incoming Queensland LNP government in late 2024 might be more receptive to a non-incumbent model precisely because it represents change from the previous government's approach.
- **Domestic violence data** — two programs dealing with domestic violence, which comprises ~30% of youth offences. An increase in DV-related youth justice contacts noted.

### The "Woodford Opportunity"

A brief but significant note: *"Could we run it out of somewhere we are already building."* "Woodford" is close to The Harvest's Witta location in the Sunshine Coast hinterland. This is the first explicit mention of ACT's place-based infrastructure (the farm, The Harvest) as a potential physical home for Diagrama-model programming in Australia. The convergence of ACT's land strategy and its justice reform strategy in a single sentence.

### The Comparative Frame

The meeting discussed developing a comparative narrative: the journey of a young person through the youth justice system in Australia vs. Spain, told from the young person's perspective. How the police engage, how the judge is involved throughout (not just at sentencing), how the staff relate. The power of this framing is that it makes the systemic difference legible at a human scale — not a data comparison but an experiential one. This is the seed of what became Room 2 of CONTAINED.

---

## What the ACT-DG Record Doesn't Capture

The Diagrama story as documented in the [[diagrama|Diagrama]] article describes a five-day immersion visit to Diagrama centres in Spain, guided by David. That visit — and the photographs on Room 2's walls — is not recorded in the project_knowledge database as a meeting. The Spain visit is captured in published writing (see the Diagrama article's published pieces list) but not in the meeting record.

What the meeting record *does* capture is the flanking work: the political groundwork (Olga's legislative map, David's Shadow Minister meetings), the media strategy (Nine Network interviews), the institutional relationship-building (Churchill Fellowships, the Blueprint for Change NT), and the early convergence of ACT's place-based infrastructure with the reform agenda.

---

## The ACT-DG Meeting Arc in Context

The four ACT-DG meetings span January 2025 to May 2024 (note: the Olga meeting is later than the May meeting in calendar terms — the ACT-DG record is not in strict sequence). Reading them together:

1. **Olga conversation (Jan 2025):** Deep NT context, legislative barriers, relational groundwork with a sector elder
2. **May second meeting (May 2024):** Operational progress — more Australians going to Spain, political engagement, Cairns pilot in view, LNP strategy, Woodford opportunity

The arc shows ACT's Diagrama work shifting from learning and understanding (the Spain visit, the Olga conversation) to active Australian implementation strategy (legislation, pilots, political relationships, media).

The Cairns centre being "a year away" as of May 2024 means it would have been expected to open around mid-2025. Whether that timeline held is not captured in the meeting record.

---

## Backlinks

- [[diagrama|Diagrama]] — the full platform article with all published writing
- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the evidence platform that incorporates Diagrama as a key precedent
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — Room 2 is directly built from the Spain visit
- [[harvest-property-arc|Harvest Property Arc]] — the Woodford convergence note
- [[justicehub-evolution-meetings|JusticeHub Evolution]] — the TYSON workshop's "repair mindset" framing appears here too

pages.title: Educational Transformation: 72% Return to School
pages.excerpt: Most disengaged participants returned to school or alternative pathways through sustained support and cultural mentorship.
pages.content:
> Most disengaged participants returned to school or alternative pathways through sustained support and cultural mentorship.

## Context

**Place:** Central Australia
**Voice Owner:** Community program team and young people
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE

## Story

The number speaks clearly: 72% of disengaged young people supported by Oonchiumpa returned to school or alternative educational pathways.

This isn't about forcing compliance. The pathway works because:
- **Cultural mentorship** — Relationships that matter before education
- **Sustained support** — Not short-term programs, but persistent presence
- **Alternative pathways** — Not just mainstream school, but education that fits
- **Family involvement** — Working with whole families, not just individuals

The 72% represents individual stories of reconnection. Each percentage point is someone who found their way back to learning — not because they were pressured, but because someone walked alongside them until education made sense again.

| **Authority** | High | Community program |
| **Evidence** | High | Quantitative outcome |
| **Harm Risk** | Low | Aggregated data |

pages.title: Elders Speak: "We Should Have Been Consulted"
pages.excerpt: Elders describe storm impacts and the need for decision-making that includes Elders from the start.
pages.content:
> Elders describe storm impacts and the need for decision-making that includes Elders from the start.

## Context

**Place:** Palm Island Elders group
**Voice Owner:** Elders collective authority
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE — Elders review required for external use

## Story

After major storms impacted Palm Island, Elders spoke clearly: emergency response and recovery planning had proceeded without meaningful consultation. Decisions affecting the whole community were made by external agencies without understanding local knowledge, cultural considerations, or community priorities.

The Elders' message was simple but powerful: "We should have been consulted." This isn't about bureaucratic process — it's about respect, effectiveness, and the recognition that Elders hold crucial knowledge about their community.

The response: embedding Elder consultation into planning processes, not as an afterthought but as a starting point. This story documents the shift from excluded to included.

## ALMA Signals

| Signal | Level | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------|
| **Authority** | High | Elders collective voice |
| **Evidence** | High | Direct narrative from authority |

pages.title: Ellen Friday: Still Waiting for a Fridge
pages.excerpt: A damaged fridge after the storm highlights the health and dignity cost of broken essentials.
pages.content:
> A damaged fridge after the storm highlights the health and dignity cost of broken essentials.

## Context

**Place:** Palm Island
**Voice Owner:** Community member (identity protected)
**Consent Status:** INTERNAL ONLY — remove personal details before external use

## Story

After the storm, Ellen's fridge was destroyed. Not just inconvenienced — destroyed. Months later, she was still waiting for a replacement. Without reliable refrigeration, food safety becomes impossible, medication storage becomes uncertain, and daily life becomes a series of workarounds.

This isn't one person's problem. Across remote communities, broken essential appliances represent a cascade of health and dignity impacts. A damaged fridge means:
- Food spoilage and waste
- Unable to store medication safely
- Increased costs from frequent small purchases
- Loss of dignity in hosting visitors

Ellen's story became a catalyst for Goods on Country's fridge pathway — designing appliances that can be maintained locally and replaced quickly.

| **Authority** | High | Lived experience of need |

pages.title: Empathy Ledger
pages.excerpt: Not your story... not my story... but a third reality we can only discover together.
pages.content:
> Not your story... not my story... but a third reality we can only discover together.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-EL | **Tier:** Ecosystem

## What It Is

The Empathy Ledger is ACT's sovereign storytelling platform — the **narrative sovereignty layer** of [[third-reality|The Third Reality]]. It gives marginalized and Indigenous communities cryptographic ownership of their narratives, ensuring stories are never extracted but always owned.

## Core Principles

1. **Storyteller as Sovereign** — absolute control and agency over how narrative is used
2. **Blockchain-secured ownership** — transparent, fair compensation flows back to storyteller
3. **Do no harm** — community members are active co-creators, not subjects
4. **Reject extractive metrics** — focus on agency, resilience, and truth, not passive victimhood

## The Central Role

Empathy Ledger is the **connective tissue** that ties all impact together across the ACT ecosystem:

| Platform | What It Provides | What Empathy Ledger Adds |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| CivicGraph | Systemic data (entities, funding, procurement) | Human faces behind the numbers |
| JusticeHub | Evidence base (what interventions work) | Stories of transformation |
| Goods on Country | Place-based design outcomes | Community voice in design process |
| PICC | Service delivery data | Lived experience of services |

Without Empathy Ledger, you have data. With it, you have **The Third Reality**.

## How Stories Drive Capital

When individual narratives intersect with systemic data:
1. **AI-powered thematic analysis** safely pulls themes, trends, and quotes from narratives
2. **Funding applications** backed by undeniable weight of real-life impact
3. **Policy shifts** advocated using verified lived experience
4. **Identity always protected** — individual ownership and consent at every stage

## Technical Architecture

### Current (Supabase Instance)
- **EL v2 (active):** `yvnuayzslukamizrlhwb` — dedicated Supabase instance with 207 tables, 364 RLS policies, 296 functions, and pgvector for semantic search
- **EL unused:** `uaxhjzqrdotoahjnxmbj` — second instance, no credentials found in env files

### Future (Sovereign)
- Stories compiled into [[local-ai-architecture|Local AI Architecture]] vaults
- TK Labels as YAML frontmatter on every narrative
- Mukurtu CMS integration for institutional-grade cultural governance
- Federated learning across community models — share insights, never raw stories

## Platform Sections (empathyledger.com)

The live platform is organized around:
- **Stories** — individual narratives with community attribution
- **Storytellers** — profiles and consent management
- **Atlas / Map** — geographic view of stories
- **Projects** — contextual collections
- **Galleries** — curated visual collections
- **World Tour** — global story journey

**Content Advisory:** Some materials may be subject to cultural protocols.
**Community Guidelines** and transparent data principles are published on the platform.

## Current Needs

To demonstrate the model at scale:
- Beta platform with **10+ community participants**
- Published ethical framework
- Measurable policy impact demonstrated

## Content Hub

Photography, videography, and storytelling with AI-powered tagging and ecosystem syndication:
- Photographer/videographer metadata
- Community attribution
- TK Labels for cultural protocols
- Syndication to CivicGraph, JusticeHub, project articles

## Vision: Changing the Face of the World

The Empathy Ledger becomes pervasive when:
- Stories **change minds** — policymakers can't dismiss what they've felt
- Ownership **creates agency** — communities control their narrative, not NGOs
- Resources **follow stories** — Third Reality assessments direct funding to ground truth
- Impact compounds — every story adds to the knowledge base, strengthening all future advocacy

## Platform Architecture

### Technology Stack

- **Frontend:** Next.js 15 with TypeScript — responsive, Progressive Web App with offline capabilities
- **Backend:** Supabase (PostgreSQL) with real-time capabilities and edge computing for global delivery
- **Media:** Cloud storage with CDN distribution, AI-powered transcription, and automatic format conversion
- **AI Tools:** Automatic transcription, translation, content tagging, and theme extraction from narratives

### Multi-Tenant Model

The platform uses a multi-tenant architecture: a single platform instance supports unlimited organizations, each with their own dashboards, member directories, project management, and media galleries. Organizations can have complex hierarchies — sub-groups, roles, elder review boards — while sharing the same underlying infrastructure.

Tiers of access:
- **Individual storytellers** — personal dashboard, story portfolio, consent management
- **Community organizations** — up to 500 members, project tracking, custom cultural protocols
- **Enterprise / government** — unlimited members, on-premise deployment options, SLA guarantees

### Integration Ecosystem

- Social media sharing with granular storyteller controls
- Grant management system integration with automated funder reporting
- SAML/OAuth single sign-on for enterprise environments
- Full REST API and webhook support for partner platforms (e.g. [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[the-harvest|The Harvest]])

## Cultural Protocols & Consent Infrastructure

The platform treats consent not as a checkbox but as ongoing infrastructure. Informed by two years of work with Aboriginal communities in Central Australia and Queensland, the consent model reflects [[ocap-principles|OCAP principles]] (Ownership, Control, Access, Possession).

### Five Consent Types

Each storyteller manages five distinct consent relationships:

| Type | Question | Key Feature |
|------|----------|-------------|
| **Collection** | Can we record your story? | Separate from account creation, covers recording method |
| **Processing** | Can AI analyze your story? | Model-specific permissions, training data excluded by default |
| **Sharing** | Who can see your story? | Four-tier: public / community / restricted / sacred |
| **Attribution** | How do you want to be named? | Legal name, preferred name, community attribution, or anonymity |
| **Syndication** | Can your story appear on partner platforms? | Per-partner approval, revocable, with usage reporting |

All five types are revocable at any time from the storyteller's consent dashboard — no admin approval required. Consent changes take effect immediately across all systems.

For a full technical treatment, see [[consent-as-infrastructure|Consent as Infrastructure]].

### Elder Review Workflows

Traditional knowledge can be flagged for elder review before publication. The platform supports multi-level content moderation including community elder approval, with cultural warnings attached to sensitive content.

### Permission Levels

Stories are assigned one of four permission levels:
- **Public** — discoverable and accessible to all
- **Community** — visible to members of the associated organization
- **Restricted** — limited to specific individuals or roles
- **Sacred** — protected with the highest cultural protocols; access requires explicit authorization

## Real-World Scale

From the Snow Foundation implementation:
- **226 active storytellers** sharing health and wellness journeys
- **550+ community stories** including an Elder Teaching Library of traditional heart health knowledge
- 95% elder approval rate for traditional knowledge sharing
- 40% increase in grant application success for partnered organizations

Platform-wide benchmarks:
- Average story reach: 150+ community members per narrative
- 85% of stories receive meaningful responses
- 10,000+ concurrent users supported
- 99.9% uptime with global CDN

## Implementation Approach

Deployments follow four phases:
1. **Discovery** (2–6 weeks) — story inventory, cultural protocol documentation, community needs assessment
2. **Configuration** (2–16 weeks) — platform setup, branding, content migration, or custom feature development
3. **Onboarding** (2–8 weeks) — staff training, community member onboarding, cultural protocol training
4. **Launch & Optimisation** (ongoing) — community engagement, performance monitoring, grant reporting

## Infrastructure & Operations

### Deployed Platform

| Detail | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **Live URL** | [empathyledger.com](https://empathyledger.com) |
| **Alternate** | empathy-ledger-v2.vercel.app |
| **GitHub** | [act-now-coalition/empathy-ledger-v2](https://github.com/act-now-coalition/empathy-ledger-v2) |
| **Hosting** | Vercel |
| **Framework** | Next.js 14 + TypeScript + React 18 |
| **Editor** | TipTap rich text |
| **Local dev** | `npm run dev` → http://localhost:3001 |

### External Integrations

- **GHL CRM:** Pipeline "Storytellers", tags: `storytelling`, `empathy`, `elder`, `indigenous`. Contact field: `is_storyteller`.
- **Xero:** Tracking category `EL`, project codes `EL-CORE` and `EL-CONTENT`.
- **Inngest:** Background job processing (transcription, consent renewal, sync).
- **Mapbox:** Geographic story atlas.
- **Claude AI:** Consented story analysis and theme extraction.

### Key Database Tables

The active Supabase instance (`yvnuayzslukamizrlhwb`) holds: `profiles`, `storytellers`, `stories`, `media_assets`, `consent_records`, `elder_reviews`, `organizations`, `content_hub_posts`. Content Hub posts syndicate to The Harvest blog via the EL syndication API.

## Public Voice

*How Empathy Ledger describes itself on act.place (act.place/act-projects/empathy-ledger, captured 2026-04-07)*

### The Third Reality as Public Tagline

> In the space where individual narratives intersect with systemic understanding, a transformative potential emerges — not your story... not my story... but a third reality we can only discover together.

This is the only ACT platform whose public-facing page leads with the [[third-reality|Third Reality]] concept by name. The internal wiki uses this as methodology; the public site uses it as identity.

### The Framing Contrast (How They Explain What's Different)

The public page sets up a two-column contrast:

**Traditional Impact Methodology (Extractive)**
- Researcher as Central Authority
- Information flows one direction: researcher → subjects
- Subjects as data points; value accumulates at institutional level

**Transformative Exchange Methodology (EL)**
- Storyteller as Sovereign Center
- Network ecosystem with dynamic, living relationships
- Value Reciprocity: benefits flow to all participants

This is the most direct public explanation of ACT's critique of conventional research and impact measurement.

### Four Steps (Public-Facing Process)

1. **Share Your Story** — voice, video, text, or photos; set privacy controls
2. **Maintain Control** — edit, update, or remove anytime; change who sees it as comfort grows
3. **Create Value** — stories contribute to funding applications; community patterns emerge
4. **Benefit Fairly** — direct compensation when story drives funding; recognition as knowledge holder

The "Benefit Fairly" step — direct compensation — is not prominently featured in the internal wiki. This is a significant public commitment that deserves more documentation.

### Principles Attribution

> *These aren't our rules. They're community-set principles we've built technology to honour.*

This framing — principles set by communities, not tech companies — is load-bearing for funder communications. It addresses the "who has power over the platform?" question before it's asked.

### What the Public Site Omits

The public act.place page does not mention: blockchain ownership, TK Labels, Mukurtu integration, OCAP principles, or the five consent types. These are internal technical/governance details — the public page is purely relational and values-based. This is correct framing for a general audience but may leave sophisticated Indigenous governance partners wanting more. The internal wiki fills that gap.

pages.title: Empathy Ledger Annual Field Service
pages.excerpt: Y1 approach: bespoke engagement at ~$50K/year per org with four existing customers (JCF, PICC, Buttery, SMART Recovery). Learn what each org actually buys, then productise in Y2 based on real patterns.
pages.content:
> Y1 approach: bespoke engagement at ~$50K/year per org with four existing customers (JCF, PICC, Buttery, SMART Recovery). Learn what each org actually buys, then productise in Y2 based on real patterns.

This is NOT a three-tier product page. It is a scoping template for bespoke annual agreements that share a common backbone but flex per customer. The productised version comes after 12 months of delivery evidence.

## Common backbone (every engagement includes)

1. **Live Resonance Field** — the org's `/organisations/{slug}/observatory` page stays active with portrait-derived particle palettes, spiral resonance clustering, and real storyteller faces. Updated as new transcripts are ingested.
2. **Monthly editorial pass** — new quotes reviewed and cleaned via the MiniMax-M2.7 editorial pipeline. Cultural review gate enforced. Ben approves batches, not individual items.
3. **Annual Impact Atlas** — generated from the Resonance Field data. PDF + interactive web version. Includes spiral resonance profile, impact dimensions, top quotes, cultural markers, storyteller count, timeline.
4. **Storytelling infrastructure** — voice interview capture (Whisper transcription + Claude analysis), consent envelope per storyteller, storage in [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] with OCAP/CARE protocols.
5. **Cultural review gate** — maintained by ACT. No storyteller content goes public without consent and cultural protocol check.

## Per-customer flex (what varies)

### JCF (June Canavan Foundation)

- **Tone**: anti-transactional, warm, exploratory. "Celebrating ordinary people who change lives in simple ways."
- **Y1 scope**: 5–10 new stories from East Africa partners (St Jude, Kula Project, Naramatisho) + Sunshine Coast grantees. World Tour June 2026 produces 3–5 stories in-field.
- **Artefact**: digital scrapbook → physical printed anthology by Year 3 (trust wind-down legacy).
- **Contact**: Anne Gripper (board + administrator). `afc3ae85` in storytellers table. JCF org: `460955e2`.
- **What NOT to do**: don't pitch KPIs or dashboards. Don't ask for money from the foundation in Y1. Year 1 is essentially offered at relationship cost.
- **Annual fee**: ~$30–50K (lower end due to relationship stage and anti-transactional positioning).

### PICC (Palm Island Community Company)

- **Tone**: sovereignty-forward, community-controlled. "Our story, our way."
- **Y1 scope**: always-on annual report generation from 253 transcripts + 1,128 quotes (editorial pipeline running). Elders storytelling tour. 20-year community timeline already shipped.
- **Artefact**: annual report (interactive web + PDF). Elders Hull River return-to-country documentation.
- **Contact**: Rachel Atkinson (CEO). PICC org: `084f851c`.
- **Additional deliverables**: CONTAINED campaign surface draws from PICC storytellers. STAY Circle Two anchor community.
- **Annual fee**: ~$50–75K (highest-touch customer, most transcripts, most complex cultural protocol).

### The Buttery

- **Tone**: cinematic, celebratory. "Fifty years of coming home."
- **Y1 scope**: continue the standalone documentary site (port 3031), capture 5–10 more interviews via Empathy Ledger, build the 50-year narrative.
- **Artefact**: cinematic documentary (already in build) + printed anthology production plan.
- **Contact**: Leone Crayden (CEO, NADA Board Chair), Frances Pidcock (ED Programs), Sandy Lockhart (Foundation Committee Chair).
- **Additional context**: multi-million dollar capital campaign. The EL work IS the funder case.
- **Annual fee**: ~$50–75K (high artefact production value; partially offsets documentary costs).

### SMART Recovery

- **Tone**: peer-support, practical, culturally safe. "Facilitators in their own voice."
- **Y1 scope**: editorial review of 20 draft stories + 24 transcripts. SMART Connect facilitator platform integration. Cultural safety gate for Aboriginal facilitator content (Danielle Caruana flagged sensitive).
- **Artefact**: facilitator portraits + voice clips for SMART Connect onboarding + annual impact summary.
- **Contact**: Erin (Project Lead), Sally (Communications), April (Executive Sponsor).
- **What NOT to do**: no gamification (only 9% want it). Mob Yarning Space content stays private.
- **Annual fee**: ~$40–60K (consulting relationship already active; scope overlaps with SMART Connect build).

## Y1 revenue target

4 customers × ~$50K average = **$200K annual recurring** (bespoke, not productised).

## What we learn in Y1 that informs Y2 productisation

Track these patterns across all four engagements:

1. **Which backbone elements do every customer actually use** (vs which do they ignore)?
2. **What's the real editorial workload per org per month** (hours, not estimates)?
3. **What artefact format do funders/boards actually respond to** (PDF atlas? live embed? printed book? video?)?
4. **What's the real cultural review overhead** (how many reviews, how many rejections, how long)?
5. **What would a customer pay 2x for** (the thing they'd upgrade without being asked)?
6. **What would make a customer refer another org** (the "hero moment" they tell their network about)?

Answers to these six questions define the Y2 productised tiers.

pages.title: Empathy Ledger: Key Relationships and Platform Origins
pages.excerpt: The meetings behind the methodology — from Joe's gym in Sydney to Max in the ACT Government, and what the conversations reveal about how ACT develops partnerships.
pages.content:
> The meetings behind the methodology — from Joe's gym in Sydney to Max in the ACT Government, and what the conversations reveal about how ACT develops partnerships.

**Compiled:** 2026-04-07 | **Source:** 12 ACT-EL meeting records (top 5 by content length analyzed)
**See also:** [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]], [[confit-pathways|Confit Pathways]], [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]

---

## BK and Joe: The Confit Pathways Partnership (March 2023)

The most substantive early Empathy Ledger meeting in the database is the second meeting between BK and Joe — founder of Confit Pathways, a post-incarceration support program for young men.

Confit Pathways is built around a specific theory of change: *"a brand that is cool for young people getting out of prison and also for the older ones."* Joe's insight is that compliance-based reintegration programs fail because they don't offer belonging or aspiration. He wanted something more like a streetwear brand than a social service — a community with its own identity, where being part of it meant something you'd want to tell people about.

From Meeting 2 (29 March 2023), the durable knowledge:

**What Joe was building:** A national digital program built on face-to-face recruitment and support, with an app as the connector, motivator, and communication tool for maintenance of reintegration. Community of rappers, artists, pro boxers, and well-known people as advocates. A partnership with Geed Up Clothing (Black Out line) — brand alignment where the aesthetic does the cultural work. Prison is 94% male but Joe saw room for women.

**What ACT committed to:** Supporting the Snow Foundation pitch and building the Confit Pathways application. A brainstorm session organised for April 12th with Joe's squad — "a wide variety of people with him all with lived experience." Draft pitch page built at confit-app.webflow.io. Snow Foundation application target: ready for board meeting first week of May 2023.

**Why this matters for Empathy Ledger:** Confit Pathways was one of the first external organisations ACT built with using the Empathy Ledger approach — centring lived experience as core capability, not as background colour. The structure ACT proposed (video reflections, lived experience co-design, story-as-pitch) is an early iteration of what became the platform's methodology. Joe's model also appears in [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]'s proof points — 60% reduction in recidivism — which means this 2023 partnership contributed directly to the evidence base that JusticeHub cites three years later.

---

## The Student Team Phase (Semester 2, 2023)

Through Semester 2 of 2023, ACT ran an Empathy Ledger student team in parallel with the JusticeHub student team. Meeting records from August through September 2023 are largely routine (task tracking, iteration notes) but establish that EL was under active development with university cohort support. The "First Yarn" from May 2023 was likely the earliest stakeholder conversation in this cohort, though the record is sparse.

The student team meetings capture an important phase: EL being built before it had a committed funder. The platform's underlying methodology — the four-layer voice-preserving pipeline, the consent architecture, the story-as-sovereignty framework — was being tested with students and community contacts before the platform itself existed.

---

## BK and Max: ACT Government Channel (December 2024)

By December 2024, EL was mature enough to be presented to government as a deployable methodology. Max holds the ACT (Australian Capital Territory) Government's community services portfolio with a specific mandate for disrupting stagnant structural processes.

Three opportunities emerged from this meeting:

**TOMNET Storytelling Initiative** — TOMNET is a community services network with 20+ years of impact and a successful peer support model. Max wanted to capture that legacy as an evidence base for community-led solutions. This is precisely the Empathy Ledger use case: narrative sovereignty + institutional memory.

**Department Annual Gathering Workshop** — Max wanted ACT to facilitate a workshop sharing innovative approaches to community support, philanthropic landscapes, and sustainable engagement models. Positioning ACT as a sector-convener, not just a platform provider.

**Community Pathways Research Project** — Mapping human journeys through community support systems, documenting natural helping relationships, service discovery and navigation patterns, informal and formal support networks. The "human journey" framing maps directly to the citizen-sovereign model from the 2023 TYSON Bank workshop — the same insight applied to community services rather than youth justice.

BK positioned Empathy Ledger as the methodology for all three. The ACT Government partnership opened a channel that sits distinct from ACT's Queensland-heavy engagement portfolio.

---

## Week of 2026-03-16: Operational Synthesis

By March 2026, EL's project record was consolidating multiple streams simultaneously:

- **FRRR Conference video project** — Six 2–3 minute videos for the Foundation for Rural and Regional Renewal Conference (Sep 8–10, 2026), with ACT's Goods Project featured. Filming focus on Palm Island and Townsville, with Sunshine Coast manufacturing as optional B-roll.
- **Goods on Country bed delivery** — 40 new-style beds planned for Palm Island with an on-island assembly program. Funding gap noted.
- **Oonchiumpa Station** — Snow Foundation $100K execution plan, with two near-term events as proof points: Judges event (Apr 17) and North American cattle investors (Apr 21).

The ACT-EL project code being attached to this operational synthesis reflects EL's role as connective tissue: the storytelling methodology applies to Goods, Oonchiumpa, and the FRRR conference all at once. The platform's real function is visible here — not a standalone product but the narrative layer underneath every ACT project.

---

## What the EL Meeting Arc Reveals

**EL's origins are relational, not technical.** The first significant EL-coded meeting is BK sitting with Joe talking about what makes a program feel worth belonging to. The consent architecture, the multi-tenant platform, the 207 Supabase tables — all of that came later. The methodology was built from conversations, not from product specs.

**Government is a natural partner, not a natural funder.** The Max meeting opened a new channel but the framing was facilitation and methodology sharing — not procurement. ACT's relationship with government is consistently "we'll show you what works" rather than "we'll deliver your program."

**The student team phase was formative.** Two years of university-cohort development before dedicated funding is visible in the EL record. This pattern (sustained build before funder commitment) appears across JusticeHub and SMART Connect too — it is an ACT trait, not an anomaly.

**By 2026, EL is infrastructure.** The March 2026 operational synthesis shows EL as the default methodology for storytelling across Goods, Oonchiumpa, and the FRRR conference. It has become background infrastructure — the way ACT does narrative — rather than a named product being sold.

---

## Key Relationships

| Person | Organisation | Meeting | What They Contributed |
|--------|-------------|---------|----------------------|
| Joe | Confit Pathways | Mar 2023 | Lived-experience platform design; proof point for JH evidence base |
| Max | ACT Government (community services) | Dec 2024 | Government channel; three deployment opportunities |
| (EL student cohort) | University team | Aug–Sep 2023 | Platform iteration before dedicated funding |

---

pages.title: Feel Good Project
pages.excerpt: A haircut is not a haircut. For a woman who has been invisible for months, it's someone saying: you are worth looking after.
pages.content:
> A haircut is not a haircut. For a woman who has been invisible for months, it's someone saying: you are worth looking after.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FG

## What It Is

The Feel Good Project is an ACT-supported initiative providing mobile hair care and beauty services to women experiencing hardship — homelessness, domestic violence, poverty, or crisis. ACT's contribution was helping build a caravan: a mobile salon that brings the service to where women are, rather than asking women in difficult circumstances to navigate their way to a fixed location.

The project is active. Financial tracking in Xero under `ACT-FG — Feel Good Project` confirms it has incurred costs. Deeper operational detail — the partner organisation, service geography, and outcomes data — has not yet been fully ingested into the wiki.

## The Mobile Service Logic

The caravan is not incidental to this project. It is the argument.

Fixed-location services impose a friction cost on the people who most need them. A woman who is sleeping rough, or staying in emergency accommodation, or managing an unsafe home situation doesn't always have the capacity to travel to a service on a schedule that suits the service's hours. Fixed services serve the people who can reach them. Mobile services serve the people who can't.

Orange Sky — co-founded by ACT co-founder Nicholas Marchesi OAM — demonstrated this at scale: laundry services in a van, going where people experiencing homelessness actually are. The logic is the same: don't require dignity to be earned by navigating the system. Bring it.

The Feel Good Project applies this same logic to beauty and hair care — services that might seem non-essential until you understand what they actually do.

## Why Beauty Care Is Not a Luxury

For women experiencing hardship, access to hair care and beauty services carries practical and psychological weight:

**Practical:** Job interviews, Centrelink appointments, custody hearings, accommodation applications — all of them are easier when a woman feels presentable and is treated as someone worth taking seriously.

**Relational:** The act of someone washing your hair, cutting it, treating it with care — is an act of human regard. For women who have been in situations of control, violence, or invisibility, being touched gently, by someone who is there for them, is not trivial. It is sometimes transformative.

**Self-perception:** There is documented evidence in social service contexts that access to personal care — haircuts, clean clothes, showers — correlates with increased willingness to engage with other support services. The Feel Good Project is an entry point as much as an endpoint.

This is the same insight that runs through Orange Sky (laundry as conversation), [[the-confessional|The Confessional]] (horse trailer as mobile healing space), and ACT's broader approach: the physical thing creates the relational moment.

## Connection to ACT Ecosystem

### Nicholas Marchesi and the Orange Sky Pattern

Nicholas Marchesi OAM co-founded Orange Sky Australia in 2014, turning a van with two washing machines into a mobile laundry and conversation service for people experiencing homelessness. Orange Sky now operates in every Australian state and territory, has logged over 50,000 hours of conversation, and is one of the most recognised social enterprises in Australia.

The Feel Good Project carries Orange Sky's DNA: a vehicle, a service, dignity as infrastructure, meet people where they are. Nicholas's involvement in ACT means this instinct runs deep in how ACT thinks about what practical support looks like.

### Global Laundry Alliance

The [[global-laundry-alliance|Global Laundry Alliance]] is ACT's network of Orange Sky-model organisations operating in other countries — bringing the mobile laundry concept to new geographies. The Feel Good Project exists in the same conceptual family: mobile dignity infrastructure, designed around the reality of people's lives rather than the convenience of service delivery.

### The Confessional

[[the-confessional|The Confessional]] is an ACT project that converted a horse trailer into a mobile healing space — a place where people can come, sit, and be listened to. It and the Feel Good Project share the same physical grammar: a vehicle that becomes a sanctuary.

### Caring for Those Who Care

[[caring-for-those-who-care|Caring for Those Who Care]] — ACT's program supporting frontline workers — is the complement to the Feel Good Project. One supports the people using services; the other supports the people delivering them. Both operate on the premise that dignity and care are prerequisites for change, not rewards for it.

## The Caravan as Infrastructure

ACT's direct contribution to the Feel Good Project was practical: helping build out the caravan as a mobile service delivery platform. This fits ACT's pattern of providing physical infrastructure — vehicles, spaces, technology — that amplifies the work community organisations are already doing.

The caravan is not a metaphor. It is a specific piece of built infrastructure that allows a service to exist that couldn't otherwise exist in the same form. ACT's role here is the same as its role in [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] manufacturing: building the physical thing that makes the community impact possible.

## Evidence Note

No project_knowledge records exist in Supabase for ACT-FG. The wiki has not yet absorbed deeper sources for this project — partner organisation name, geographic coverage, number of women served, or outcome data. What is documented here is the project's logic, ecosystem connections, and ACT's confirmed role in the caravan build. Evidence is sparse; the article will grow as source material is ingested.

| Project code | `ACT-FG` |
| Xero tracking | `ACT-FG — Feel Good Project` |
| Status | Active |
| ACT contribution | Caravan build (mobile salon infrastructure) |

## Context

**Place:** Alice Springs to Finke (on-Country journey)
**Voice Owner:** Young men with cultural mentors

## Story

The Finke Desert Race is one of Australia's iconic off-road races, running from Alice Springs to Finke. For young men in Oonchiumpa's program, attending the race became more than spectating — it became an on-Country experience.

Camping along the route, connecting with the event's energy, and being part of something bigger than themselves:
- **Place connection** — Learning the Country between Alice and Finke
- **Community pride** — Being part of a major community event

pages.title: Fishers Oysters
pages.excerpt: A cultural-first aquaculture enterprise reclaiming and restoring Moreton Bay's oyster industry through Indigenous knowledge, community ownership, and regenerative practice.
pages.content:
> A cultural-first aquaculture enterprise reclaiming and restoring Moreton Bay's oyster industry through Indigenous knowledge, community ownership, and regenerative practice.

**Status:** Transferred | **Code:** ACT-FO | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

Fishers Oysters is working to restore the oyster industry of Moreton Bay through a framework that places Indigenous knowledge first. The project treats ecological restoration and economic sovereignty as inseparable: the reef cannot be healthy without the cultural knowledge systems that have managed it for generations, and those knowledge systems cannot be sustained without the economic sovereignty that comes from community ownership of the enterprise.

The name "Fishers" signals both the people (fishing families and custodians) and the act — this is a project about reclaiming the right to fish, to own, and to steward.

## Key Details

- **Location:** Moreton Bay, Queensland
- **Website:** [fishersoysters.com](https://fishersoysters.com)
- **Core model:** Cultural-first aquaculture with community ownership structure
- **Focus:** Ecological justice, economic sovereignty, intergenerational knowledge transfer

## What Makes It Different

Most aquaculture operates as extractive industry. Fishers Oysters inverts this:

- **Indigenous knowledge drives the ecological model** — Traditional custodial knowledge of Moreton Bay's reef systems informs how the oyster beds are restored and managed
- **Community ownership** — the enterprise is structured for the community to own and benefit from the operation, not external investors
- **Regenerative practice** — the goal is not just commercial viability but ecological restoration and the health of the broader bay system
- **Intergenerational sovereignty** — knowledge and economic benefit are designed to transfer across generations, not be captured in a single cohort or business cycle

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — Fishers Oysters is on-the-ground ecological and economic work. Boats on water, reefs being seeded, knowledge being practised. The Listen phase lives in the deep Indigenous knowledge informing every operational decision.
