pages.title: Five-Year Plan — Voice, Flow, Ground
pages.excerpt: Decision: ACT builds a revenue-generating machine over five years across three layers — Voice (Empathy Ledger bespoke storytelling), Flow (CivicGraph as the commercial trading arm), and Ground (ACT Farm + The Harvest residency and eco-tourism revenue). Both founders invoice retroactively for FY26 R&D work. CivicGraph is positioned as the exit lever for Years 6–10 art and activism. Founder sustainability is treated as a structural requirement, not a nice-to-have.
pages.content:
> Decision: ACT builds a revenue-generating machine over five years across three layers — Voice ([[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] bespoke storytelling), Flow ([[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] as the commercial trading arm), and Ground ([[act-farm|ACT Farm]] + [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] residency and eco-tourism revenue). Both founders invoice retroactively for FY26 R&D work. CivicGraph is positioned as the exit lever for Years 6–10 art and activism. Founder sustainability is treated as a structural requirement, not a nice-to-have.

This plan extends [[2026-04-founder-lanes-and-top-two-bets|Founder Lanes and Top Two Bets]] with a financial arc and operational rhythm. The Founder Lanes decision narrowed what we do. This decision says how long, for how much, and toward what personal and institutional outcomes.

## Why This Exists

The Founder Lanes decision diagnosed the problem: too many projects, low closure, blurred boundaries. This plan answers the question that decision left open: *what does success look like in five years, and how do we fund the art and activism phase that follows?*

Three structural truths drive the plan:

1. **ACT's FY26 revenue is $1.89M invoiced through March 2026.** The studio is already bigger than the documented projections ($350K–$1.2M mature in `visual-strategy.md`). The plan can be built from actual numbers, not aspirations.
2. **Both founders have under-invoiced.** Benjamin has $0 FY26 invoices despite 2,151 commits at 95% R&D allocation. Every $100K of founder invoicing generates ~$43.5K of ATO R&D refund to ACT. This is free money sitting in the tax code.
3. **Story must be the primary use of founder time.** Everything else — admin, invoicing, reconciliation, customer support, bookkeeping — either gets automated via AI agents or owned by an operations hire. The plan protects founder creative energy as a structural priority, not a luxury.

## The Three Layers

Instead of Soul / Wallet / Place, ACT's products map to three layers named in ACT's own vocabulary:

| Layer | What it means | Products | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Voice** | The listening substrate | [[empathy-ledger\|Empathy Ledger]], [[the-brave-ones\|Brave Ones]], STAY journals | Consent-first storytelling. Never sold, always operated. Revenue from bespoke annual engagements. |
| **Flow** | Where capital, evidence, and attention move | [[civicgraph\|CivicGraph]], [[justicehub\|JusticeHub]], [[goods-on-country\|Goods on Country]], [[contained\|CONTAINED]] | Commercial engine. CivicGraph SaaS + Goods retail + JusticeHub grants + CONTAINED tour stops. |
| **Ground** | Where it lands in place | [[act-farm\|ACT Farm]], [[the-harvest\|The Harvest]], STAY anchor communities | Residencies, workshops, eco-tourism, CSA subscriptions. Revenue from land-based experience. |

[[lcaa-method|LCAA]] weaves through all three: Listen is how we enter Voice. Curiosity is how we move through Flow. Action is how we land on Ground. Art is how we make all of it visible.

## Three Commitments

### 1. Both founders invoice FY26 retroactively

$100K each, 95%/40% R&D allocation, through the family trust structures being set up. Combined: ~$87K refundable R&D tax credit back to ACT annually. Compounding: ~$400K recycled cash over 5 years. This is the single highest-leverage financial move available and requires zero product work.

**Deadline:** Invoices issued by end of April 2026. CPA booked within 2 weeks for RDTI claim strategy.

### 2. CivicGraph is the commercial trading arm

[[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] keeps its Stripe tiers ($79–$1999/mo), grows its data moat (100K entities, 672K contracts, 312K donations), and is explicitly positioned as the product that funds the other products' community handover.

The [[beautiful-obsolescence|Beautiful Obsolescence]] language stays on [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]], [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]], [[the-harvest|The Harvest]]. It is never applied to CivicGraph publicly. CivicGraph exists to be commercially valuable and, in Y5, potentially sold to a strategic acquirer ($4–10M EV range at 3–6x ARR) to fund the Years 6–10 art and activism phase.

### 3. Empathy Ledger stays bespoke in Y1

Four existing customers — [[picc|PICC]], JCF, [[the-buttery|The Buttery]], [[smart-connect|SMART Recovery]] — at roughly $50K each annual bespoke engagement. That is $200K recurring from work already in flight, formalised into scoped annual commitments and invoiced on a schedule.

We do not productise into a three-tier SaaS yet. We learn from the actual bespoke work first. Productised version designed in Y2 once we know what the customers actually buy.

## Five-Year Revenue Arc

| Year | Voice (EL bespoke) | Flow (CivicGraph + JH + Goods) | Ground (Farm + Harvest) | Other grants | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Y1 FY27** | $200K (4 × $50K) | $400K MRR + $850K Minderoo H2 | $150K | $1M | $2.6M |
| **Y2 FY28** | $400K (6–8 bespoke) | $700K MRR + $1.14M Minderoo | $350K | $1M | $3.6M |
| **Y3 FY29** | $600K (10 bespoke) | $1.1M MRR + $1.14M Minderoo | $600K | $1M | $4.4M |
| **Y4 FY30** | $800K (productised) | $1.6M MRR | $900K | $1.2M | $4.5–5.5M |
| **Y5 FY31** | $1M | $2M MRR + possible exit | $1.2M | $1.3M | $5.5–6.5M + exit |

## Founder Sustainability

Founder burnout is a structural risk to the entire ecosystem. This plan treats founder financial stability as a requirement, not a side-effect.

Both founders aim to purchase land in the Witta area within 5 years — near [[act-farm|ACT Farm]], near [[the-harvest|The Harvest]], inside the valley the studio is already invested in. Target: $1M deposit each. This is funded through salary + R&D refund recycling + performance bonus from the 60% reinvestment allocation, not from the 40% community share.

| Year | Founder salary each | R&D refund to ACT | Est. personal savings/yr | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Y1 | $180K + $100K retro | ~$87K combined | $80–100K | $80–100K |
| Y2 | $220K | ~$87K | $100–130K | $180–230K |
| Y3 | $240K + bonus | ~$90K | $140–170K | $320–400K |
| Y4 | $260K + bonus | ~$95K | $200–250K | $520–650K |
| Y5 | $280K + bonus | ~$100K | $250–350K | $770–1M |

This is achievable on salary alone without requiring CivicGraph exit proceeds. The exit becomes the Y6–10 art/activism endowment rather than the house deposit.

## The Daft Punk Communication Rule

ACT's marketing is the work itself. The studio follows the Daft Punk discipline:

- Never explain when you can show. The Resonance Field, Brave Ones portraits, STAY journals, the World Tour documentary — these ARE the marketing. Nothing else.
- No daily posting, no founder-thought-leadership content, no personal brand hustle.
- Release cadence over content cadence. Major bodies of work 2–3 times a year. Each release gets one campaign push, then silence until the next.
- When press asks who runs ACT, the answer is "the studio". When a conference asks for a keynote, we send a film instead.
- Portfolio as album art. act.place looks like an artist's portfolio, not a consultancy website.
- Mystery is a feature. Under-describe. Let curiosity do the work.

This protects the founders from becoming the brand. The work is the brand.

## Six-Months-Ahead Operating Rhythm

The studio works **six months ahead**, always. Every quarter, half the effort delivers work prepped 6 months ago. The other half prepares deliverables for 6 months from now. Nothing gets done in the week it is due.

| Quarter | Delivering | Preparing |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 (Apr–Jun) | Minderoo response, CONTAINED, Brave Ones Phase 1, World Tour | Y1 Annual Atlases for JCF/PICC/Buttery/SMART |
| Q2 (Jul–Sep) | Tour documentation, annual atlases, Brave Ones gallery | R&D tax filing, Y1 customer renewals, Brave Ones Phase 2 |
| Q3 (Oct–Dec) | Customer renewals, R&D filing, Phase 2 outputs | New customers, Field Service productisation v1 draft |
| Q4 (Jan–Mar) | Productisation, new customer onboarding | Minderoo Year 2, Brave Ones Phase 3, farm residency season |

For CivicGraph exit specifically: if Y5 (FY31) is the target window, Y4 Q3 (October 2030) is when informal acquirer conversations start. Six months of prep before the deal opens.

## Automation Target List

Any task either founder does more than three times becomes an agent.

| Task | Agent | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Xero reconciliation | Dext capture → Claude categorisation → auto-match | Partially live |
| Invoice generation | Template invoices from Field Service contracts | Not started |
| R&D tax tracking | Git commits → tag R&D-eligible → AusIndustry app draft | Not started |
| Customer support triage | Claude email triage for EL customers, Ben approves exceptions | Not started |
| Content publishing | Resonance Field auto-publish to org observatories | Live (today's work) |
| Residency bookings | GHL form → triage → calendar → contract → deposit | GHL form live, rest manual |
| Grant pipeline | CivicGraph surfaces likely fits, drafts pitch letters | Not started |
| Weekly digest | Monday morning: what landed, what is due, one decision needed | Not started |

Target: 15–20 hours/week of admin reclaimed by end of Y1. That is the time budget for story work.

## Ground Revenue — Farm + Harvest + Eco-Tourism Ideation

The residency, workshop, eco-tourism and subscription revenue streams that build toward $1.2M/yr by Y5:

- **Philanthropy-sponsored residencies** — foundations pay $15–30K per residency spot × 20–25/yr = $300–750K
- **Corporate innovation retreats** — 3-day immersives at $15–25K per group × 10–14/yr = $150–350K
- **Innovation workshops** — 1–2 day facilitated workshops at $5–10K × 18–24/yr = $100–240K
- **Eco-tourism stays** — premium $300–500/night × 120 nights/yr = $40–60K
- **Harvest CSA + dining events** — subscriptions $600/season × 200 members = $120K + seasonal events $120K
- **June's Patch healthcare wellness** — hospital-funded staff programs, scaling to $120–200K/yr

The 40% community profit share applies to net, after costs. Founders draw salary as a cost, not a profit distribution.

## Art Projects — Y1 Release Program

Eight art projects to lean into across Y1, as the first application of the Daft Punk release cadence:

1. [[the-brave-ones|Brave Ones Phase 1]] — 5 portraits, ~$15K, pre-CONTAINED
2. *Extraordinarily Ordinary* (JCF) — 10–15 portraits of "ordinary people who change lives", $15–30K
3. Resonance Field gallery installation — projected field on walls, 1–2 nights Brisbane/Sydney, $20–50K
4. STAY Journal Chapter 01 — one community (Oonchiumpa or PICC), $20–40K
5. *Fifty Years of Coming Home* anthology (The Buttery) — 200-page hardcover, $50–80K
6. The Buttery 50-year cinematic documentary — already in build
7. World Tour travelogue — Ben's photographs from June trip → film/book/exhibition, $20K
8. Resonance Field public embed campaign — 5 orgs embed their field, no production cost

Budget ~$200K. Funded from: existing grant runway + a Y1 Art Program application to Ian Potter / Creative Australia / Copyright Agency.

## What This Changes Practically

1. Both founders invoice for the work they have already done. The R&D refund compounds.
2. CivicGraph engineering time increases. Every hour widening the entity graph is an hour toward exit value.
3. [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] stays bespoke until the customers teach us what to productise.
4. Act-Farm and Harvest shift from "40% flows back / beautiful obsolescence" messaging to **"regenerative capital engine — every dollar generates more residencies, more accommodation, more places for artists and communities."** The values of community stewardship stay. The growth-limiting framing goes.
5. The co-founder operating agreement from [[2026-04-founder-lanes-and-top-two-bets|Founder Lanes]] is ratified with financial specifics.
6. Marketing becomes release-driven, not content-driven.
7. Admin automation becomes a structural priority equal to product work.

## Proof Required

### Q2 2026 (immediate)

- Both FY26 invoices issued
- CPA booked for RDTI strategy
- PICC annual report delivered
- Minderoo STAY pitch submitted and responded to
- CONTAINED Mount Druitt launched
- At least 2 of 4 EL customers locked into formal $50K annual scope

### Q4 2026

- R&D tax claim filed for FY26
- CivicGraph MRR at $30–40K/month
- Act-Farm residency season complete, Y1 revenue confirmed
- Brave Ones Phase 1 exhibited
- World Tour debrief documented
- 6-months-ahead rhythm demonstrably running

### Q2 2027

- EL bespoke expanding to 6–8 customers
- CivicGraph data moat measurably wider
- Automation layer reclaiming 15+ hours/week
- Second residency/workshop season sold out before it opens
- Y1 art program complete, Y2 planned

## Review Triggers

Review this plan if any of the following happen:

- Minderoo says no AND no replacement funder materialises within 90 days
- CivicGraph MRR stalls below $20K/month for two consecutive quarters
- Either founder's personal savings trajectory falls below $60K/year for two consecutive years
- A community partner raises concern that the CivicGraph trading-arm framing compromises ACT's consent posture
- The 6-months-ahead rhythm collapses for two consecutive quarters
- The Pty Ltd / family trust legal structure is not finalised by end of Q2 2026

## Years 6–10 — The Art Phase (Sketch Only)

If the base works, Years 6–10 redirect founder energy from product building to art, activism, and systems change:

- Story World Tours (biennial, funded from CivicGraph exit proceeds or stable ACT revenue)
- Published works: books, documentaries, printed anthologies
- Systems-change campaigns: youth justice federal reform, child protection, poverty
- Residency portfolio at 3–5 sites (partnership model, not purchase)
- Ben's role: board chair + storyteller/advocate, not primary operator
- Nic's role: field practice + art direction, not operational delivery

This phase is only sketched. It earns detail once the Y1–Y5 base is proven.

pages.title: Funding Transparency
pages.excerpt: The principle that public money flows — government contracts, grants, charitable subsidies, political donations — should be legible to the citizens and communities they are meant to serve.
pages.content:
> The principle that public money flows — government contracts, grants, charitable subsidies, political donations — should be legible to the citizens and communities they are meant to serve.

## Overview

Australia has no single system connecting its public money flows. $107 billion in government funding flows to the charitable sector annually. 672,000+ federal contracts are awarded through AusTender. $312 million+ moves through political donations. $8.86 billion in grants were distributed by charities in 2023 alone.

The data exists — scattered across AusTender, ACNC returns, AEC disclosures, ATO statistics, state grant portals, and foundation annual reports — but it has never been assembled into a coherent decision layer accessible to ordinary citizens, community organisations, or journalists.

Funding transparency is the civic infrastructure requirement that [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] is built to address.

---

## Why It Matters

### The information asymmetry problem

When public data is fragmented, access to it becomes itself a form of power. Large foundations, corporate advisors, and government agencies can employ researchers to navigate complexity. Community organisations, small businesses, journalists, and citizens cannot.

The result: those who most need to understand funding flows — communities competing for grants, journalists investigating procurement, small organisations benchmarking their grant success — have the least access to the information required.

### Tax subsidies deserve public scrutiny

When the government foregoes **$2.26 billion** in revenue annually to subsidise charitable giving, and **82% of that benefit** flows to the top income decile, that is a policy choice deserving informed public debate. The debate cannot happen if the data is locked in ATO statistics tables, Treasury working papers, and ACNC annual reports that few people read.

### Procurement transparency reveals structural patterns

**140 entities** in Australia donate to political parties AND hold government contracts. They donated $80M and received $4.7B in contracts — a 58x correlation. Both major parties benefit. Government procurement officers currently have no tool to check this cross-reference.

**87.5%** of federal procurement value goes to just **10 entities**. SMEs win 52% of contracts by number but only 35% by value. These structural patterns are invisible without a unified procurement intelligence layer.

---

## What Civic Intelligence Means

Funding transparency is not just about publishing data. It is about making data **navigable** — turning fragmented public records into answers that ordinary people can use:

- Who funds what, where, and does it work?
- Which postcodes are most underserved relative to their disadvantage level?
- Which organisations donate to political parties AND hold government contracts?
- Which foundations fund issues that communities say they need addressed?
- Are government programs actually reaching the communities they target?

This kind of **civic intelligence** — the ability to ask meaningful questions of public money data — is what [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] calls decision infrastructure.

---

## The Legibility Ladder

Making funding transparent requires moving through layers:

1. **Publication** — data is published somewhere (AusTender, ACNC, AEC)
2. **Accessibility** — data is in usable formats with clear licensing
3. **Linkability** — records from different systems can be joined (ABN as universal key)
4. **Searchability** — a person can find what they need without a data science background
5. **Intelligibility** — the data is presented with context that makes it meaningful
6. **Accountability** — findings can be acted on (advocacy, policy, funding decisions)

Most Australian public data sits at step 1 or 2. CivicGraph works to reach step 5 and 6.

---

## The Double-Counting Problem

A critical structural reality: philanthropic flows are counted multiple times across different systems. A high-net-worth individual's donation appears in their tax return, then in the PAF's accounts, then in the recipient charity's revenue, and later in that charity's program expenditure. There is **no single official "total philanthropy" figure** in Australia that avoids double-counting.

This isn't just a measurement problem — it is a power problem. When data is fragmented, those with resources to navigate the complexity have information advantages over those who need funding most.

Assembling all fragments into one decision layer doesn't solve the double-counting problem. But it makes the landscape navigable for everyone — not just those with research budgets.

---

## Funding Transparency vs. Grants Databases

Funding transparency is not the same as a grants database. Grants databases show funding opportunities. Funding transparency shows:

- Who received what funding, not just what is available
- Whether funding correlates with community need or with political relationships
- Whether the same organisations appear across contracts, donations, and grants
- Whether communities getting funding are the ones saying they need it

This is the distinction between a **reactive tool** (find grants to apply for) and **civic intelligence infrastructure** (understand and hold accountable the system that allocates public resources).

---

## International Context

Other countries have advanced further on civic intelligence:

- **OpenSecrets** (US) — tracks political money flows, 40+ staff at peak, laid off a third in 2024
- **Sunlight Foundation** (US) — government transparency platform, closed 2020
- **360Giving** (UK) — grants data standard, 275 funders, £265B in grants, foundation-funded and fragile
- **GrantConnect** (AU) — government grants register but no outcome tracking, no cross-reference

The pattern: funding transparency platforms struggle financially because the institutions that benefit most from opacity (donors, procurement winners, political donors) don't fund them, and the institutions that should (government, philanthropy) are inconsistent funders.

CivicGraph's response to this is the **cross-subsidy model**: institutional users (procurement officers, compliance firms, foundations) pay, and community organisations get free access. Revenue comes from the value of the data, not from charitable goodwill.

---

## Related Concepts

- **[[civic-world-model|Civic World Model]]** — the architectural vision for how civic data should be structured
- **[[power-dynamics-philanthropy|Power Dynamics in Australian Philanthropy]]** — empirical findings about money concentration
- **[[civicgraph|CivicGraph]]** — the platform implementing funding transparency for Australia

---

- Raw: `wiki/raw/2026-04-07-gs-mission.md`

pages.content:
> A day on Country with Traditional Owners builds confidence, cultural authority, and the belief that young women can lead.

## Context

**Place:** Standley Chasm (on-Country visit with Traditional Owners)
**Voice Owner:** Young people and cultural mentors
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE

## Story

A group of young women visited Standley Chasm with Traditional Owners and cultural mentors through Oonchiumpa. What might look like a simple outing was actually something deeper: a day of cultural empowerment.

On Country, with Elders who welcomed them:
- Young women learned about place and story
- They were told they could be leaders
- They practiced cultural protocol
- They experienced belonging

The confidence built on days like this carries forward. Young women who might have doubted their place in leadership conversations began to see themselves differently.

| **Authority** | High | Traditional Owners hosting |
| **Evidence** | High | Narrative documentation |
| **Harm Risk** | Medium | Youth photos need care |
| **Capability** | Medium | Repeatable program |
| **Option Value** | High | Model for cultural experiences |
| **Community Value Return** | High | Young women empowered |

## Connections

pages.title: Global Laundry Alliance
pages.excerpt: A dignity-centred international network connecting community laundry hubs — advocating for policy change that recognises clean clothing and access to basic hygiene as a matter of human dignity, not charity.
pages.content:
> A dignity-centred international network connecting community laundry hubs — advocating for policy change that recognises clean clothing and access to basic hygiene as a matter of human dignity, not charity.

**Status:** Transferred | **Code:** ACT-GL | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

The Global Laundry Alliance grows from one of the most unexpected and powerful social innovations of recent Australian history: Orange Sky Laundry, co-founded by ACT co-founder [[nicholas-marchesi|Nicholas Marchesi]] OAM. Orange Sky demonstrated that a mobile laundry service for people experiencing homelessness was not primarily about clean clothes — it was about dignity, belonging, and the five-minute conversation that happened while the washing was on.

The Global Laundry Alliance takes that insight international: building a network of organisations running community laundry hubs worldwide, sharing knowledge and practice, and collectively advocating for the policy conditions that make this work sustainable and scalable.

## Origin: Orange Sky

Nicholas Marchesi co-founded Orange Sky Laundry in 2014 at age 20. What began as two friends with a borrowed washing machine and a van grew into a national service reaching tens of thousands of people experiencing homelessness across Australia and New Zealand. The insight at the heart of Orange Sky — that the laundry is a pretext for community — became foundational to how ACT thinks about service design more broadly.

See [[nicholas-marchesi|Nicholas Marchesi]] for the full founding story.

## The Alliance Model

### Community Hubs
The laundry hub is not just a utility — it is a community gathering point. The physical act of waiting together, of having the laundry done for you without judgment, creates conditions for trust, conversation, and connection that more formal services struggle to generate.

### Global Network
By connecting organisations running community laundry programs worldwide, the Alliance enables knowledge exchange, shared innovation, and collective advocacy that individual organisations cannot achieve alone. What works in Brisbane, London, or Nairobi can inform practice everywhere.

### Policy Change
The Alliance's advocacy work pushes toward systemic recognition: that access to clean clothing and basic hygiene is not a luxury or a charitable extra but a dimension of human dignity that public systems should support. This includes lobbying for funding models, public infrastructure, and social policy that treats hygiene as a right.

### Dignity as the Frame
Every element of the Alliance's work is oriented by dignity — not gratitude, not charity, not the transaction of service delivery, but the unconditional recognition of every person's inherent worth. This is the legacy of Orange Sky and the common thread connecting all member organisations.

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — The Alliance is network-building, hub-connecting, and policy-advocating. The listening happened in the years of Orange Sky operations that demonstrated what people actually need. The Global Laundry Alliance is the systemic action that follows.

pages.title: Global Precedents
pages.excerpt: International models that validate and inform The Third Reality, CivicGraph, and ACT's approach to community-led civic intelligence.
pages.content:
> International models that validate and inform The Third Reality, CivicGraph, and ACT's approach to community-led civic intelligence.

## Spain & Holland: Data Commons and Digital Democracy

### Barcelona — DECODE Project & Decidim
- **DECODE:** Massive decentralized data infrastructure — citizens possess absolute data sovereignty, choosing what data they "donate" to improve public services
- **Decidim** ("we decide" in Catalan): Digital democracy platform for direct citizen participation in allocating millions in municipal budgeting
- **Lesson for ACT:** Successfully branded the "Data Commons" concept. CivicGraph and JusticeHub can be positioned as a public digital commons, not private software

### Amsterdam — Commons Network
- Civil society think-tank promoting "the commons" — communities collaboratively stewarding resources, separate from both market and state
- Works directly with policymakers to build networks and defend the category
- **Lesson for ACT:** "The Third Reality" should be treated like the Commons Network treats "the commons" — a philosophical standard, not just a product feature

## Sweden: Indigenous Data Sovereignty (Sapmi Region)

### Sami Parliament & GIDA-Sapmi Network
- Sami people's traditional territory spans northern Sweden, Norway, Finland
- Through GIDA, pushing institutions to adopt CARE Principles as mandatory global standard
- Sami Parliament actively formalizing data rights into national policy
- **Lesson for ACT:** Sovereign storytelling and data control can be institutionalized in law. Use CARE principles as the foundational certification for Third Reality assessments

## Kenya & Tanzania: Catalytic Capital

### Miamba Yetu Program (Kenya-Tanzania Coast)
- "Blended finance" model deploying capital directly into local, environmentally positive businesses while delivering verified community benefits
- Bypasses slow bureaucratic philanthropy

### African Transition Acceleration Fund (ATAF)
- "Catalytic capital" for early-stage infrastructure that traditional grant-makers deem too risky
- **Lesson for ACT:** Reframe JusticeHub's Impact-Weighted Quadratic Funding as "catalytic capital" — high-leverage investment that unlocks massive downstream savings for the state

### East Africa M-Pesa Precedent
- Leapfrogged traditional banking infrastructure entirely
- Proves communities can bypass slow-moving bureaucracies to route capital directly
- **Lesson for ACT:** CivicGraph can be the M-Pesa of social impact — leapfrogging grant bureaucracy

## Holland & Europe: Rewriting Narrative

### Commons Network (Netherlands)
- Realized Europe needed a new story to orient its future
- Aggressively branded "the commons" — collaborative, democratic resource stewardship
- Works with policy makers to build networks and defend the new category
- **Lesson for ACT:** Category design requires narrative infrastructure, not just technology

## Existing ACT Infrastructure That Maps to These Models

| Global Model | ACT Equivalent | Status |
|-------------|---------------|--------|
| Barcelona's Decidim | CivicGraph transparency dashboard | Live (566K entities) |
| DECODE data commons | JusticeHub open evidence base | Live (1,004 programs) |
| Sami data sovereignty | Mukurtu + TK Labels integration | Planned |
| Miamba Yetu blended finance | ImpactQF via Allo Protocol | Conceptual |
| ATAF catalytic capital | JusticeHub capital routing | Conceptual |
| Commons Network advocacy | Third Reality certification | Branding phase |

## Outreach Strategy

For each region, tailored outreach connecting ACT's work to local precedents:

### Spain/Holland Angle
"We are inspired by DECODE and Decidim. CivicGraph maps 566K+ entities like Decidim brings transparency to budgets. We want to share notes on institutionalizing citizen-led data platforms."

### Sweden Angle
"Your Sapmi work establishing CARE Principles is the gold standard. We've built the Empathy Ledger for cryptographic narrative ownership. Let's explore how you translated Indigenous data rights into national policy."

### Kenya/Tanzania Angle
"East Africa leapfrogged banking — we're building similar pipelines for social justice. Through JusticeHub, we're implementing Impact-Weighted QF as catalytic capital. BG Fit reduced police contact from 5 incidents to <1. Oonchiumpa achieved 95% reduction in anti-social behavior."

## Travel Exploration Plan

Ben wants to visit all these places to build direct relationships. Priority contacts:
- DECODE/Decidim teams (Barcelona)
- Commons Network (Amsterdam)
- GIDA-Sapmi researchers (Sweden)
- Miamba Yetu / ATAF leaders (Kenya/Tanzania coast)

pages.title: Glossary
pages.excerpt: Terms and concepts used across ACT. This is a living document — update as language evolves.
pages.content:
> Terms and concepts used across ACT. This is a living document — update as language evolves.

## Core Concepts

### A Curious Tractor (ACT)
A regenerative innovation studio based in Queensland, Australia. Named after the tractor's Power Take-Off (PTO) mechanism — we transfer power to communities driving their own futures, rather than driving the futures ourselves.

### Beautiful Obsolescence
The design principle of building toward our own irrelevance. We aim to transfer ownership, capability, and governance to communities so completely that ACT eventually becomes unnecessary. Not failure — success. See [[beautiful-obsolescence|Beautiful Obsolescence]].

### Empathy Ledger
ACT's platform for story sovereignty. Communities own their narratives, control who sees them, and receive 40% of any commercial value generated. The core consent and impact infrastructure across the ecosystem.

### LCAA (Listen, Curiosity, Action, Art)
ACT's methodology for ethical innovation:
- **Listen:** Sit with community voice before acting
- **Curiosity:** Ask "what if?" without assuming answers
- **Action:** Build, test, iterate based on listening
- **Art:** Make it visible, shareable, cultural

See [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]].

### ALMA (Adaptive Learning for Meaningful Accountability)
ACT's impact model that reads system-level signals without profiling individuals. Uses six signal families to guide learning and decision-making. ALMA protects against extractive data practices while enabling genuine learning. See [[alma|ALMA]].

### Power Take-Off (PTO)
A tractor mechanism that transfers engine power to implements. ACT's founding metaphor: we provide power that communities direct, not the other way around.

---

## Data & Consent

### Consent Scope
The shareability level assigned to content:
- **INTERNAL ONLY:** Team only, not for external sharing
- **EXTERNAL-LITE:** System-level learnings, no identifiers
- **EXTERNAL:** Explicit consent, culturally reviewed, safe to share

### Elder Review
Required cultural review process for content touching Indigenous knowledge, stories, or protocols. Part of consent architecture, not optional. Elder decisions are final on cultural matters.

### OCAP Principles
Ownership, Control, Access, Possession — Indigenous data sovereignty principles developed by the First Nations Information Governance Centre:
- **Ownership:** Community owns data about them
- **Control:** Community controls how data is used
- **Access:** Community has right to access their data
- **Possession:** Data stays with community where possible

See [[consent-as-infrastructure|Consent as Infrastructure]].

### Sacred Content Protection
Technical and governance measures preventing sacred or culturally sensitive content from being shared without appropriate authority. Hard blocks, not soft warnings.

---

## Places

### Black Cockatoo Valley (BCV)
150-acre property on Jinibara Country near Witta, Queensland. Conservation-first land practice, Nature Refuge designation. Home to residencies, workshops, and habitat restoration.

### The Harvest
Enterprise hub in Witta supporting local makers, therapeutic horticulture, and community-led business. Tests sustainable enterprise models at human scale.

### ACT Farm
The studio practice — where methodology becomes action. Prototyping, learning, iteration, and handover preparation. The farm metaphor shapes daily operations.

### June's Patch
Healthcare worker wellbeing program at Black Cockatoo Valley. Therapeutic horticulture, "prescription to nature," research partnership with USC.

---

## Projects & Platforms

### JusticeHub
Network for community-led justice programs. Forkable models, cross-community learning, alternative approaches to youth justice and accountability. See [[justicehub|JusticeHub]].

### Goods on Country
Circular economy manufacturing for remote communities. Essential goods (beds, washing machines) built for local repair, maintenance, and ownership. 40% profit-sharing to communities. See [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]].

### Registry API
Standardized `/api/registry` endpoint exposed by each project. Enables ecosystem-wide content aggregation while each project maintains data sovereignty.

---

## ALMA Signal Families

See [[alma|ALMA]] for the full framework.

| Signal | What It Measures |
|--------|-----------------|
| Evidence Strength | How reliable is the learning? |
| Community Authority | Who holds authority? Is consent in place? |
| Harm Risk (Inverted) | Potential for harm if shared (higher = safer) |
| Implementation Capability | Can this be acted on? |
| Option Value | Does this open or close future possibilities? |
| Community Value Return | How much value flows back to community? |

---

## Technical Terms

### Multi-Tenant Architecture
Shared database infrastructure with Row Level Security (RLS) ensuring data isolation between organizations while enabling cross-tenant analytics.

### Row Level Security (RLS)
PostgreSQL feature that enforces data access policies at the database level. Users can only see data they're authorized to access.

### Edge Functions
Serverless functions running at the network edge (close to users). Used for real-time processing without cold starts.

### pgvector
PostgreSQL extension enabling vector similarity search. Powers semantic search across stories and content.

### SSG / SSR / CSR
- **SSG (Static Site Generation):** Pages built at deploy time
- **SSR (Server-Side Rendering):** Pages built on each request
- **CSR (Client-Side Rendering):** Pages built in the browser

---

## Governance Terms

### Sunset Clause
Built-in endpoint for tools and systems. Every ACT product has a plan for when it should end or transfer to community ownership. See [[beautiful-obsolescence|Beautiful Obsolescence]].

### Co-Stewardship
Shared governance between ACT and community partners. Pathway toward full community ownership and beautiful obsolescence.

### Community-Majority Governance
Decision-making structure where community members hold majority of seats/votes. The endpoint of governance handover.

### 40% Profit-Sharing
ACT's commitment to return 40% of commercial value from community stories and products to those communities. Tracked, auditable, distributed.

---

## Farm Metaphors

| Metaphor | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| Soil | The knowledge network, community wisdom, foundational relationships |
| Seeds | Projects, ideas, initiatives in early stages |
| Tending | Ongoing care, attention, maintenance work |
| Harvest | Impact, results, value returned to community |
| Compost | Learning from failure, turning setbacks into nutrients |
| Seasons | Natural rhythms and timing — don't force growth out of season |
| Farmhand | ACT's AI layer — infrastructure that reduces admin without replacing human judgment |

---

## Voice & Brand

### ACT Voice
Warm, grounded, humble, visionary, professional yet rebellious. Uses regenerative metaphors with restraint. Avoids corporate jargon and savior framing. See [[voice-guide|ACT Voice Guide]].

### Deficit Framing
Language that focuses on what communities lack rather than what they have. ACT avoids this — we center capability and agency.

### Extractive Language
Terms like "harvesting data," "capturing value," "mining insights" that treat people as resources. ACT doesn't use these.

---

## Acronyms

| Acronym | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| ACT | A Curious Tractor |
| ALMA | Adaptive Learning for Meaningful Accountability |
| BCV | Black Cockatoo Valley |
| CSA | Community Supported Agriculture |
| GHL | GoHighLevel (CRM platform) |
| LCAA | Listen, Curiosity, Action, Art |
| MCP | Model Context Protocol |
| OCAP | Ownership, Control, Access, Possession |
| PTO | Power Take-Off |
| RLS | Row Level Security |
| SSG | Static Site Generation |
| SSR | Server-Side Rendering |
| USC | University of the Sunshine Coast |

---

- [[beautiful-obsolescence|Beautiful Obsolescence]] — handover design principle

pages.title: Gold.Phone
pages.excerpt: A random connection voice platform and community installation tackling social isolation through authentic, unscripted human conversation — open-source, privacy-focused, and designed for local replication.
pages.content:
> A random connection voice platform and community installation tackling social isolation through authentic, unscripted human conversation — open-source, privacy-focused, and designed for local replication.

## Overview

Gold.Phone addresses the social isolation crisis with a deceptively simple intervention: connect two strangers by voice, at random, with no social media profile, no metrics, and no agenda. The platform creates conditions for genuine human connection that algorithmic social networks cannot — and deliberately will not — provide.

The project operates as both a digital platform and a physical community installation, making it accessible in contexts where smartphone apps are not the right interface. Its open-source foundation means any community can replicate and own their own version.

## Key Details

- **Format:** Voice platform + community installations
- **Technology:** Open-source, designed for local community replication
- **Core values:** Privacy-first, accessible, community ownership, no tracking or profiling
- **Primary problem:** Social isolation — the absence of authentic human connection in algorithmically mediated social environments

## How It Works

- **Random connection** — participants are connected by voice with a stranger, removing the friction and performance of curated social interaction
- **Community installations** — physical installations bring the experience to public spaces, community centres, and events where digital access may be limited
- **Open-source** — the technology is freely available for communities to deploy and own independently
- **Privacy by design** — no profiles, no recordings, no data retained beyond the call

## LCAA Phase

**Art** — Gold.Phone is a creative technology project where the medium (random voice connection) is the message. The act of connection is the art form. It sits within ACT's Art phase as an expression of the idea that human contact, stripped of performance, is itself transformative.

## See Also

- [[the-confessional|The Confessional]] — complementary project using art and anonymity for healing
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — story capture platform, adjacent in its focus on human voice
- [[dad-lab-25|Dad.Lab.25]] — men's health and community connection
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]]

pages.title: Goods on Country
pages.excerpt: Manufacturing durable household goods from 100% recycled plastic for remote and marginalised Australian communities — where conventional products fail within weeks.
pages.content:
> Manufacturing durable household goods from 100% recycled plastic for remote and marginalised Australian communities — where conventional products fail within weeks.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-GD | **Tier:** Ecosystem

## What It Is

Goods on Country is ACT's circular economy social enterprise. It designs, manufactures, and deploys indestructible household goods for remote Aboriginal and marginalised communities across Australia, where extreme heat, overcrowding, dust, and limited repair infrastructure destroy standard products in weeks rather than years.

The enterprise operates through A Curious Tractor Pty Ltd (ABN: 21 591 780 066) and trades at goodsoncountry.com.au. It is not an Indigenous-owned organisation — it partners deeply with Indigenous-owned organisations (Oonchiumpa, Wilya Janta) and community bodies. Communities are co-designers, not recipients.

**Internal project code:** ACT-GD

## The Problem It Solves

In remote communities, families sleep on floors. Beds last weeks, not years. Appliances corrode, break, and go unreplaced. Standard consumer goods are not engineered for:
- Extreme heat and UV exposure
- High-density occupancy
- Dust and limited sealed flooring
- Lack of repair services or spare parts infrastructure

The resulting housing inadequacy causes exhaustion in children (affecting school outcomes), deteriorating health outcomes, and constant wasteful replacement cycles that drain community resources.

## Products

### Stretch Bed

The flagship product — co-designed with Elders across Central Australia, the Top End, Palm Island, and Kalgoorlie. Specifications:

- **Material:** 100% recycled HDPE plastic, UV-stabilised
- **Weight:** 26kg
- **Load capacity:** 200kg
- **Assembly:** Five minutes, tool-free
- **Cleaning:** Fully washable with a garden hose
- **Repairability:** Every component individually replaceable
- **Lifespan:** Built to last 10+ years
- **Plastic diverted per unit:** 25kg from landfill

The bed was not designed in an office — it was co-designed with Elders in Tennant Creek, tested in Alice Springs, and refined on Palm Island. Fred Campbell (Oonchiumpa, Western Arrernte man) consults on product design and cultural appropriateness.

**Current economics:** Production cost $550–650/unit at small batch; cost reduction pathway to ~$350/unit at scale (5,000+/year). Institutional pricing $700–850/unit yields gross margins of 50–55% at scale.

### Industrial Washing Machine

A fleet of community-deployed industrial washing machines, IoT-instrumented for remote telemetry. Elder Dianne Stokes (Warumungu) named the washing machine in language. 20 machines deployed across communities to date.

The washing machine fleet serves a dual purpose: providing clean laundry infrastructure to communities, and generating IoT telemetry data that feeds ACT's R&D program (fleet management, remote asset monitoring, anomaly detection).

## Scale to Date

As of early 2026:

- **389 products** deployed
- **8 communities** served
- **1,000+ lives** directly impacted
- **9,225kg of plastic waste** diverted from landfill
- **33 community storytellers** documenting experiences through [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]
- **$445,685** in philanthropic funding received (Snow Foundation, FRRR, Vincent Fairfax, AMP Spark, The Funding Network)
- **$537,595** total revenue recorded (Xero, ACT-GD code)

## Community Partnerships

### Palm Island (PICC)

Palm Island Community Company has been a key deployment partner. 141 beds deployed on Palm Island. Palm Island Housing is in active expansion discussions. PICC is also a consortium partner in the REAL Innovation Fund (DEWR) application alongside Oonchiumpa and ACT.

See also: [[picc|PICC]]

### Tennant Creek

Multiple Tennant Creek community organisations engaged:
- **Centrecorp** — approved 107 beds for Utopia Homelands; applications submitted for 100 beds across 4 communities
- **Anyinginyi Health** — requested washing machine fleet; specs in negotiation
- **Julalikari** — introduced ACT to Anyinginyi Health

200 v1 beds were delivered to Tennant Creek communities in early 2025, but were unfunded (~$36K outstanding), creating a cashflow gap that has constrained R&D capacity.

### Central Australia

- **Oonchiumpa Consultancy** (Alice Springs) — 100% Aboriginal-staffed, confirmed manufacturing partner for the Central Australian containerised facility. Two years of co-design collaboration. Fred Campbell (Western Arrernte man) leads cultural consultation.
- **NPY Women's Council** — ongoing relationship; 200–350 beds requested, "always looking for beds"
- **Wilya Janta (Simon Quilty)** — fridges requested for Norm's community; engaged but progressing slowly

### East Arnhem / Top End

- **Miwatj Health** — exploring fleet deployment across 8 clinics; 500+ mattress and 300 washer requests from Groote Eylandt communities documented
- **Groote Eylandt communities** — significant documented demand; Groote Eylandt Aboriginal Trust identified as a capital target
- **Maningrida** — $1.1M demand identified in GHL pipeline
- **Wadeye, Galiwinku, Milingimbi** — high-value demand signals in community pipeline

### Kalgoorlie / WA

Co-design consultations conducted with Kalgoorlie communities during product development.

## Manufacturing Model: Containerised On-Country

The scale vision is not a central factory that ships to communities. It is containerised manufacturing infrastructure that communities own and operate.

Each containerised facility is a self-contained production unit:
- Housed in shipping containers, transportable to regional centres
- Produces 1,000–1,500 durable goods annually
- Employs 4–6 local workers
- Processes locally-sourced recycled plastic as feedstock

**Scale plan:**
- **Year 1 (2026–27):** First facility on Jinibara Country (QLD), producing 1,500 beds, 6 FTE
- **Year 2 (2027–28):** Second facility at Oonchiumpa partnership (Alice Springs). Combined output: 3,500 units, 12 FTE
- **Year 3 (2028–29):** Third facility (Top End or Torres Strait). 5,000+ units/year, ~$3.5–4.2M revenue, 18 FTE

At 5,000 units/year: gross margin ~$1.75M, net operating surplus ~$850K–1.15M.

## Circular Economy Loop

Each facility accepts local plastic waste as feedstock, creating a closed loop — community waste becomes community furniture. Envirobank (Indigenous-owned recycled HDPE supplier) is in active partnership discussions as the supply chain anchor.

The model simultaneously:
1. Diverts plastic from landfill
2. Reduces freight costs for raw materials
3. Creates local employment
4. Keeps manufacturing value on country

## Digital Infrastructure: Asset Register

Every product receives a unique QR code at manufacture, linked to a Supabase-backed asset register (separate Supabase project: `cwsyhpiuepvdjtxaozwf`). The register tracks:

- Deployment location and community
- Condition check-ins (community health workers scan QR codes during visits)
- Repair history and component replacements
- Wash cycle counts (washing machine fleet, via IoT telemetry)
- Support tickets (communities report issues by scanning the QR code)

This telemetry data feeds ACT's broader R&D program — the IoT fleet is an experimental testbed for remote asset monitoring, anomaly detection, and community-managed fleet operations.

The codebase lives at `/Users/benknight/Code/Goods Asset Register/` (GitHub: `Acurioustractor/goods-asset-tracker`). Stack: Static HTML (Netlify), Supabase, CLI tools. Public-facing: product catalogue and community orders. Internal: asset tracking, inventory, delivery management.

## CivicGraph Integration: Goods Workspace

The `goods-workspace` route in [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] (hosted in GrantScope) provides procurement intelligence for Goods on Country. It operates as a buyer and capital discovery layer — not duplicating what GHL CRM does, but adding automated discovery and scoring on top.

### Five Panels

1. **Thesis** — strategic framing, outstanding commitments, cash recovery signals
2. **Buyer Pipeline** — ranked potential buyers by plausibility score (Centrebuild, Centrecorp, Outback Stores, ALPA, Miwatj, Anyinginyi, QIC, Tangentyere, West Arnhem)
3. **Capital Stack** — ranked funders by capital fit score (Snow Foundation, FRRR, VFFF, SEFA, SEDI, Minderoo, Rio Tinto Foundation, Fortescue, Centrecorp Foundation, General Gumala Trust, Groote Eylandt Trust)
4. **Community Need + Proof** — community demand signals, delivery data, and Empathy Ledger story integration
5. **Delivery + Partner Graph** — supply chain partners, manufacturing partners, community partners

### Search Modes

Four ranking modes: Need-led (start from a community's documented needs), Buyer-led (rank buyers by procurement plausibility), Capital-led (rank funders by fit), Partner-led (map delivery ecosystem). Community-first navigation: select a community, see the full procurement picture.

### NT Remote Community Sweep

A dedicated panel audits official NT community coverage — postcode mapping, buyer presence, and service gaps — to surface communities with high need and no existing Goods relationship.

### Data Flow

```
CivicGraph (GrantScope)              ACT Infrastructure
─────────────────────                ──────────────────
Discovers buyers/capital     →       Seeds into GHL + relationship_pipeline
Scores & ranks targets       →       Informs priority of action items
Exports to Notion/CSV        →       Feeds Notion pipeline view
Pushes to GHL via API        →       GHL is shared source of truth
```

CivicGraph's procurement data (1.1M federal contract records, AusTender, state grant portals) connects directly to the Goods buyer pipeline — surfacing which organisations in its coverage area are already spending on housing, health, and community services and therefore plausible bulk buyers.

## Revenue Model

Three streams at maturity:

| Stream | Share | Examples |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Institutional sales | 60% | Centrecorp, Miwatj Health, housing providers, health services |
| Government procurement | 25% | State/territory housing departments replacing disposable mattress programs |
| Retail and corporate | 15% | E-commerce, corporate partnerships (camping, emergency services, defence) |

Community pipeline (from GHL) includes identified demand from Maningrida ($1.1M), Wadeye ($1.09M), Galiwinku ($998K), Wurrumiyanga ($749K), and 15+ additional communities. Total identified demand exceeds $10M.

**FY27 projection:** $585K revenue with path to $900K (from financial strategy modelling).

## Funding & Capital Stack

Philanthropic funding received to date: $445,685 (Snow Foundation, FRRR, Vincent Fairfax, AMP Spark, The Funding Network).

Active capital pursuits as of early 2026:

| Opportunity | Type | Value | Status |
|-------------|------|-------|--------|
| REAL Innovation Fund (DEWR) | Federal grant | $1.2M over 4 years | EOI submitted Mar 2026 (Oonchiumpa consortium lead) |
| QBE Catalysing Impact | Catalytic grant | ~$210K | Shortlisted |
| Snow Foundation | Grant + impact investment | ~$200K | Proposal under review |
| QLD Partnering for Impact (PFI) | Repayable investment | $640K (of $3.2M) | EOI March 2026 |
| Centrecorp | Grant (beds) | ~$150K | March board |
| SEFA | Impact loan | Working capital | Advanced discussion |

REAL Innovation Fund ($1.2M over 4 years via Oonchiumpa consortium) is the primary pathway to the production facility. QBE Catalysing Impact is the single most time-sensitive opportunity — its outcome unlocks Snow Foundation's impact investment track and the social enterprise transition.

## R&D Tax Incentive

Goods on Country is classified as **Supporting R&D** under ACT's FY26 Division 355 claim (ITAA 1997). It supports the core R&D activities (ALMA AI orchestration, IoT fleet telemetry) by providing:

1. **IoT telemetry system** — Particle.io devices on 10 washing machines generate real-time data for the ALMA infrastructure experiments
2. **Remote deployment logistics** — iterating on community infrastructure constraints as an experimental testbed
3. **Community handover protocols** — transitioning from ACT-managed to community-managed fleet operations

FY26 R&D eligible spend (estimated): $65,516 direct, with apportioned benefit of $87,355.

Key R&D finding to date: technology handover is easier than relationship handover — community trust transfers to individuals, not organisations.

## Community Narrative Accountability

Communities don't just receive products — they tell the story of what those products mean. Through [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]], 33 storytellers across 7 communities document their own experiences. Each story is published only with community consent and elder approval where culturally required. Stories syndicate automatically to the Goods on Country website — community voices, not ACT's marketing team, define the public narrative.

This is accountability infrastructure: communities hold the pen.

## LCAA Connection

Goods on Country sits in the **Action** phase of [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] — making things that embody place and cultural knowledge.

But the project spans all four phases:
- **Listen** — Elders in Tennant Creek, Alice Springs, Palm Island shaped every design decision
- **Curiosity** — IoT data and community feedback loops drive ongoing product iteration
- **Action** — manufacturing, deploying, maintaining the fleet
- **Art** — Elder Dianne Stokes naming the washing machine in Warumungu language; community storytellers defining the narrative

It is also ACT's most direct test case for the [[designing-for-obsolescence|Designing for Obsolescence]] methodology — the long-term goal is community-owned and operated manufacturing, with ACT's role progressively diminishing.

## Place-Based Design Philosophy

Goods on Country rejects the model of designing products in offices and shipping solutions to communities. Its principles:

1. **Design with, not for** — every product specification validated through co-design with community members and Elders
2. **Made on country** — containerised manufacturing brings production to community, not community to production
3. **Culturally grounded** — naming, design aesthetics, and protocols shaped by community knowledge holders
4. **Community controlled** — the arc bends toward community ownership of facilities, data, and relationships
5. **Circular by default** — local waste becomes local goods; nothing leaves the loop unnecessarily

## Infrastructure & Operations

### Asset Register Platform

The digital asset register is a two-version system:

| Component | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **V1 (Python)** | CLI scripts for QR generation, CSV processing, SQL seeding |
| **V2 (Next.js)** | Next.js 16.1.4, React 19, TypeScript, Stripe payments |
| **Hosting** | Netlify (goodsoncountry.au + goodsoncountry.netlify.app) |
| **GitHub** | [act-now-coalition/goods-asset-tracker](https://github.com/act-now-coalition/goods-asset-tracker) |
| **Local path** | `/Users/benknight/Code/Goods Asset Register/` |
| **Local dev (v2)** | `npm run dev` in `/v2` → http://localhost:3005 |

### Alert System

The asset register runs automated alerts across four types:

| Alert | Trigger |
|-------|---------|
| Overuse | High usage detected |
| Maintenance | Scheduled check due |
| No Check-in | 6+ months since last QR scan |
| High Priority | Critical ticket submitted via QR |

Severity levels: Low → Medium → High → Critical.

### External Integrations

- **GHL CRM:** Pipeline "Goods", tags: `goods`, `beds`, `washers`, `assets`.

pages.title: Governance & Consent (Operational)
pages.excerpt: Consent is a relationship, not a checkbox. Community authority is the default, not the exception.
pages.content:
> Consent is a relationship, not a checkbox. Community authority is the default, not the exception.

## Overview

This article covers ACT's operational governance practices — how consent commitments are implemented in daily work, the shareability matrix teams use to make decisions, and the OCAP-aligned systems embedded in Empathy Ledger. For the conceptual and architectural argument for consent as infrastructure, see [[consent-as-infrastructure|Consent as Infrastructure]].

The two articles are complementary: consent-as-infrastructure asks "what must be built?" — this article asks "how do we work within it?"

## Core Commitments

| Commitment | What It Means |
|------------|---------------|
| **Consent is explicit** | No assumed permissions |
| **Consent is ongoing** | Renewable, not permanent |
| **Consent is revocable** | Withdrawal respected immediately |
| **Elder review required** | Where cultural protocols demand it |
| **Sacred knowledge protected** | Hard blocks, not warnings |
| **Partner nuance internal** | Sensitive detail stays private until reviewed |

## OCAP in Practice

ACT implements [OCAP principles](https://fnigc.ca/ocap-training/) in code and practice across all platforms:

| Principle | Implementation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Ownership** | Communities own their collective data |
| **Control** | Communities control access and use decisions |
| **Access** | Communities can access their own data anytime |
| **Possession** | Data stays under community custody |

In daily work this means: Elder Review Systems for sacred content, ongoing consent with renewable expiry (6–12 months), cultural protocols configurable per organization, AI analysis only with explicit opt-in, and full data export available at any time.

## Shareability Matrix

Every document, story, or piece of content belongs in one of three categories. When in doubt, default to the more conservative tier.

| Level | Meaning | Examples |
|-------|---------|----------|
| **INTERNAL ONLY** | Working notes, partner nuance, sensitive detail | Draft documents, partner negotiations, personal details |
| **EXTERNAL-LITE** | System-level learnings without identifiers | Anonymized patterns, general insights, methodology |
| **EXTERNAL** | Explicit consent, cultural review, safe-to-share | Published stories, case studies, public reports |

### Before Sharing Externally

Ask:
- Is consent explicit and current?
- Has cultural review happened where required?
- Are identifiers removed or approved?
- Is the purpose clear and appropriate?
- Who benefits from this sharing?

## Community Authority

**Community authority carries the highest weight, even when it complicates delivery.**

| Scenario | Response |
|----------|----------|
| Elder says wait | We wait |
| Partner wants speed over safety | We slow down |
| Community questions approach | We revisit |
| Cultural protocol unclear | We ask, not assume |

## Consent Architecture in Empathy Ledger

### Five-Tier Permission Levels

1. **Sacred** — Hard-blocked, Elder review required
2. **Restricted** — Named individuals only
3. **Community Only** — Organization members
4. **Educational** — Approved educational use
5. **Public** — Open sharing with attribution

### Consent Records

Every story tracks:
- Consent scope (what can be shared)
- Consent giver (who approved)
- Consent date (when approved)
- Renewal date (when to check again)
- Cultural sensitivity level
- Revocation history

## Elder Review Workflow

When cultural protocols require Elder review:

1. **Flag** — Content marked for review
2. **Queue** — Added to Elder review queue
3. **Review** — Elder examines content
4. **Decision** — Approve / Restrict / Request changes
5. **Record** — Decision documented
6. **Apply** — Permissions updated

Elder decisions are final on cultural matters.

## AI and Consent

AI analysis requires explicit opt-in. The default is **No AI**.

| Setting | What It Means |
|---------|---------------|
| **No AI** | No automated analysis of content |
| **Internal AI Only** | ACT tools only, no external services |
| **AI Permitted** | Includes external AI services |

See [[ai-ethics|AI Ethics & Agent Strategy]] for the full AI consent framework.

## Partner Protocols

- Governance agreements before data sharing
- Clear boundaries on use
- Mutual accountability
- Regular review cycles
- Partner-specific nuance marked `[INTERNAL ONLY]`, not shared without partner review

## Project Governance Checklist

Every project should be able to answer:

| Question | Answer Required |
|----------|-----------------|
| Who holds authority here? | Named |
| How do we know? | Evidence |
| Is consent in place? | Yes/No/In progress |
| What's the handover plan? | Documented |
| What stays internal? | Listed |

## Backlinks

- [[consent-as-infrastructure|Consent as Infrastructure]] — the architectural and philosophical argument
- [[alma|ALMA Framework]] — impact model that respects consent boundaries
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the platform where consent architecture lives
- [[ai-ethics|AI Ethics & Agent Strategy]] — AI-specific consent rules
- [[beautiful-obsolescence|Beautiful Obsolescence]] — governance as handover discipline

pages.title: GrantScope (CivicGraph)
pages.excerpt: Decision infrastructure connecting supplier intelligence, place-based funding data, and outcome evidence.
pages.content:
> *Decision infrastructure connecting supplier intelligence, place-based funding data, and outcome evidence.*
> *The agentic insight layer underneath JusticeHub. The Living Brain that makes [[three-circles|Circle One]] real.*

**Status:** Active, partly deployed | **Stack:** Next.js 15 · TypeScript · Tailwind 4 · Supabase Postgres · MCP server · vector embeddings | **Repo:** `/Users/benknight/Code/grantscope` (separate codebase from this wiki) | **Canonical review:** [[../../thoughts/shared/handoffs/staying/grantscope-review|grantscope-review]] (2026-04-08, agent-verified)

## What it is

GrantScope (the codebase name) is **CivicGraph** (the public product name) — a shared data and agentic insight layer that connects every dataset and entity touching the Australian government and social sector. It is the **decision infrastructure** that helps institutions allocate better and communities access fairly. For [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] pitch, GrantScope is the technical reality of *Circle One — The Living Brain*: it is what already exists, what Minderoo would be funding the next layer of, and what the program theory leans on most heavily.

GrantScope holds the agentic + history layer beneath [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]. JusticeHub is the *youth-justice-facing* application; GrantScope is the *cross-sector data substrate and AI agent system* that powers it. They share a Supabase database and enrichment pipelines.

## Repo orientation

| Directory | What lives there |
|---|---|
| `/apps/web` | Next.js 15 frontend, the public CivicGraph application |
| `/data` | 71 source datasets — AIHW, ROGS, BOCSAR, Closing the Gap, AusTender, ACNC, ORIC, AEC, ATO, ASIC, ABR, foundations, grants, social enterprises, Hansard, more |
| `/scripts` | 320+ agentic tasks — scrapers, enrichers, bridgers, verifiers |
| `/migrations` | Schema for the shared Supabase Postgres database |
| `/mcp-server` | MCP (Model Context Protocol) server exposing 6 tools to AI agents |
| `/output` | Intelligence reports — PICC dashboard, philanthropy power briefs, founder intake PRDs |
| `/thoughts/outreach/` | Foundational narrative work including *the-cure-already-exists-v2.md* |

The shared Supabase database is the **same instance** as JusticeHub and Empathy Ledger — three projects, one substrate.

## Live data layer (verified 2026-04-08)

| Asset | Number | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| **Entities resolved** | **100,036** | F1 match precision **94.1%**. Target 150K+. |
| **Relationships mapped** | **199,001** | Funding flows, board overlaps, political donations, ALMA links. Target 200K+. |
| **Geographic coverage** | **96% postcode · 96% remoteness · 95% LGA · 94% SEIFA** | Enables gap analysis showing where alternatives are systematically unfunded |
| **Justice funding rows** | **71,000** in `justice_funding` table | State, recipient, program, amount, year, announcement date — bridged to ALMA via `alma_intervention_id` |
| **AusTender contracts** | **770,000 rows** | Across all sectors; justice subset extractable via contract category |
| **Foundations** | **10,779 rows** | 30% enriched with descriptions; LLM enriching the remaining 7,500 |
| **JusticeHub orgs linked to CivicGraph** | **315 of 556 (57%)** | Bridge in progress; ABN fuzzy-matching enrichment running |
| **ALMA verified interventions** | **1,155** | The most comprehensive map of Australian youth justice alternatives in existence |

## Live youth-justice datasets

- **`rogs-youth-justice/youth-justice-2026.csv`** (2,444 rows) — AIHW Rules of Government Spending youth justice by state, jurisdiction, measure (detention vs community), age 10–17, rates per 10,000. Covers FY 2016–17 through 2024–25. Latest: **3,177 young people under supervision** (2024–25); detention rate **2.7/10,000**; community rate **9.4/10,000**.
- **`closing-the-gap/ctg-youth-justice.csv`** (815 rows) — Closing the Gap youth detention trajectory projections by state and Indigenous status through 2030–31. **Aboriginal/TSI projection: 24.6 / 10,000 by 2030–31** versus 11.9 for all youth.
- **`bocsar/nsw-lga-crime.xlsx`** — NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics LGA crime data; provides crime context for youth justice geography.
- **`prf-reports/`** (5 PDFs) — Maranguka (Bourke) annual report 2024 · JRI Youth Justice SA 2024 · HRLC annual report · NTCOSS annual report. *These are the anchor community organisations documented as PDFs; structured ingestion still pending for some.*

## Named programs in GrantScope's funding data

- **[[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]** (Alice Springs) — *95% diversion* (cited from Oonchiumpa's own programmatic reporting)
- **[[picc|Palm Island Community Company]]** — **78% diversion · $29M annual turnover · 208 FTE**
- **Mountie Yarns** (Mt Druitt)
- **Young Offender Support Service** (QLD DCYJMA)
- **Operation Luna** (NT Police)

## International precedents in the data layer

| Model | Coverage | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **[[diagrama\|Diagrama]] (Spain)** | 13.6% recidivism · €31K/year cost · 5.64:1 cost-benefit ratio. Featured in `/thoughts/outreach/the-cure-already-exists-v2.md` (foundational piece). Appears in PICC dashboard as international partner. | **Narrative + numerical proof points; no schema** |
| **Halt (Holland)** | Referenced in narrative | Narrative only — not in structured data |
| **Norwegian restorative justice** | Mentioned as tour stop | Narrative only |
| **Portuguese diversion** | Mentioned as tour stop | Narrative only |
| **Canadian First Nations sentencing circles** | Mentioned as tour stop | Narrative only |
| **South African community courts** | Mentioned as tour stop | Narrative only |
| **Maranguka (Bourke)** | Annual report PDF (2024); marked as "In ALMA" in PICC dashboard | **PDF only — structured ingestion pending** |
| **Whole System Approach (Scotland)** | Not found in GrantScope | **Gap** |

The international tour data is currently **narrative-only**. Structuring it into the schema is a **Year 1 deliverable** of [[three-circles|Three Circles]] Circle One.

## Live agentic infrastructure

### MCP server — `civicgraph-mcp`

**Live, deployed.** Exposes **6 tools** to any AI agent that connects:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `civicgraph_search` | Full-text + vector search across all 100K+ entities |
| `civicgraph_entity` | Returns full profile + power scores for any entity |
| `civicgraph_power_index` | Cross-system rankings (funding + governance + influence) |
| `civicgraph_funding_deserts` | Surfaces underserved LGAs by sector |
| `civicgraph_revolving_door` | Cross-references lobbying, donations, and contracts |
| `civicgraph_ask` | Natural language interface across all datasets |

This is the **strongest concrete proof** of Circle One — the Living Brain — being real. It is what magistrates, funders, journalists, and communities will eventually query directly. It is operational *today*.

### Hansard scraper

**Live for Queensland**, expanding to other jurisdictions. Scrapes Parliamentary Hansard PDFs from the sitting calendar, filters speeches for justice-relevant keywords (*youth justice, detention, Indigenous, funding, reform*), and ingests them tagged by relevance. This is what makes "every Hansard mention" in the Three Circles pitch real, not aspirational.

### Bridge: JusticeHub ↔ CivicGraph

`bridge-justice-to-graph.mjs` links JusticeHub organisations to CivicGraph entities via ABN fuzzy matching. **315 of 556 matched (57%)** at last count; 241 still to bridge. Closing this gap is one of the **Year 1 hardening deliverables** under Circle One.

### ALMA enrichment pipeline

`enrich-alma-orgs.mjs` and the `link-alma-*.mjs` family enrich ALMA intervention records with CivicGraph entity data — ABN, location, sector, SEIFA, remoteness, revenue. Cascades organisation enrichment backward to interventions. **Live, running.**

### Output reports

Generated weekly by the agent layer to `/output/`:
- `picc-comprehensive-dashboard.md` — $38.9M tracked PICC funding, BAU program map, Station Precinct innovation brief
- `civicgraph-founder-intake-prd.md` — product positioning, data layer documentation
- 15+ philanthropy power briefs — foundation giving profiles, openness scores, geographic focus matched to local orgs

## Why GrantScope matters for Three Circles

GrantScope is what makes Circle One *more than a wishlist*. Without it, the Three Circles pitch would be claiming a queryable national intelligence layer that doesn't exist yet. With it, the pitch is funding the *next layer* on top of an operational system.

**Specifically, GrantScope provides for the pitch:**

1. **The verified data backbone** — 100K entities, 199K relationships, 71K justice funding rows, 1,155 ALMA interventions. These numbers replace the inflated earlier claims.
2. **The live agentic interface** — 6 MCP tools, Hansard scraper, ALMA enrichment, organisation bridging. Proof that Circle One is operational *today*, not vapourware.
3. **The geographic precision** — 96% postcode coverage means a funder can ask "where are the alternatives systematically unfunded by remoteness category" and get an answer in seconds.
4. **The international precedent numbers** — Diagrama, especially. 13.6% recidivism, 5.64:1 cost-benefit, €31K/year vs $1.33M.
5. **The PICC dashboard** — $38.9M of tracked funding, 208 FTE, 78% diversion. The strongest concrete community proof point in the entire pitch.

## Gaps to close before pitching Three Circles

These are the things a sophisticated funder will press on:

1. **JusticeHub ↔ CivicGraph bridge at 57%** — 241 orgs still unmatched. Funder query *"which community-led orgs work on youth diversion in QLD"* may not return Oonchiumpa if the join is incomplete. **Y1 hardening priority.**
2. **Frameworks Institute / Andrea Davidson integration is zero** in GrantScope. Scoped as a **Year 1 deliverable**, not a precondition.
3. **International tour data is narrative-only.** Norway / Portugal / SA / Canada need at least a thin schema before Year 1 — a few weeks of structured work.
4. **Maranguka is PDF only** — needs structured ingestion. Maranguka is one of the strongest community-led precedents in Australia and not having it in the data layer is a real weakness.
5. **Empathy Ledger has 9 live storytellers** (target 226). Either reframe in pitch language or commit to a number we can hit by pitch date.
6. **Foundation enrichment 30% complete** — 7,500 foundations still awaiting LLM descriptions.
7. **ASIC director linkage not yet ingested** — 2.2M companies awaiting selective extraction.
8. **Supply Nation Indigenous business verification** — pending API integration (7,822 → 10K+ target).

## Numbers retired from earlier JusticeHub pitch claims

The earlier JusticeHub Minderoo pitch cited some numbers that **could not be verified** in the GrantScope data layer. These are retired in the canonical [[three-circles|Three Circles]] page:

| Earlier claim | Verified replacement |
|---|---|
| "1,081 verified youth justice programs" | **1,155 ALMA verified interventions** |
| "587,000 entities" | **100,036 entities resolved** (target 150K+) |
| "1.5 million relationships" | **199,001 relationships mapped** (target 200K+) |
| "$114.9B tracked across 35 sources" | **71K rows of justice funding · $1B+ in justice spending mapped · 14 government and philanthropic source categories** |
| "38+ stories published" (Empathy Ledger) | **Empathy Ledger v2 platform live with story sovereignty model; 9 storytellers onboarded, scaling to 226** |
| "1,000+ ALMA interventions" | **1,155** (verified, slightly more than originally claimed) |

See [[three-circles#Data verification status|Three Circles → Data verification status]] for the full reconciliation.

## How GrantScope connects to the rest of ACT

- [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] — GrantScope IS Circle One; the canonical 3-year, $2.9M Minderoo pitch funds the next layer of work on top of GrantScope's existing data substrate
- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the youth-justice-facing application that sits on top of GrantScope's shared Supabase
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the third application sharing the Supabase substrate; provides the story sovereignty layer
- [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] — the public product brand for GrantScope's data layer (codebase name = GrantScope, public name = CivicGraph)
- [[diagrama|Diagrama]] — the international precedent numbers (13.6% recidivism, 5.64:1 cost-benefit) live in GrantScope narrative + PICC dashboard
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — anchor community whose 95% diversion proof point lives in the data layer
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — the strongest community proof point in GrantScope; full dashboard at `/output/picc-comprehensive-dashboard.md`
