pages.title: Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy
pages.excerpt: A justice reinvestment and community healing initiative grounded in Quandamooka Country — led by the Quandamooka people, focused on self-determination, and built on the understanding that healing and justice are inseparable.
pages.content:
> A justice reinvestment and community healing initiative grounded in Quandamooka Country — led by the Quandamooka people, focused on self-determination, and built on the understanding that healing and justice are inseparable.

## Overview

The Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy is a place-specific, Indigenous-led response to the justice and wellbeing challenges facing the Quandamooka people of Moreton Bay and North Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah). It operates within the justice reinvestment framework — the evidence-based approach that redirects resources from incarceration toward early intervention, community support, and healing — but grounds that framework in Quandamooka knowledge, relationships, and self-determined priorities.

ACT's role is supportive and facilitative. The strategy belongs to the Quandamooka community, and long-term success is defined by the community's own capacity to own and direct the work without external intermediaries.

## The Place: Quandamooka Country

Quandamooka Country encompasses Moreton Bay and the islands of Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island) and Mulgumpin (Moreton Island). The Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation (QYAC) is the recognised traditional owner body. The country is one of ecological richness and cultural depth — and, like much of Aboriginal Australia, carries the compounding legacies of dispossession, removal, and structural disadvantage that intersect with justice system involvement.

## Approach

### Justice Reinvestment
Redirecting resources from downstream responses (incarceration, child removal, crisis intervention) toward upstream investment in community wellbeing, cultural connection, economic participation, and early support. Justice reinvestment is most effective when it is community-led — and the Quandamooka strategy is built on this.

### Indigenous Leadership
Every element of the strategy is led by Quandamooka community members and organisations. ACT does not design the strategy — it supports the community to design, resource, and implement it. This is consistent with ACT's [[designing-for-obsolescence|Designing for Obsolescence]] philosophy.

### Community Healing
The strategy recognises that justice and healing cannot be separated. Addressing justice system involvement without addressing the underlying trauma, grief, and disconnection that drives it produces temporary statistics, not lasting change. Healing — cultural, relational, and psychological — is a strategic priority, not an afterthought.

### Self-Determination
The measure of success is increasing Quandamooka self-determination over justice and wellbeing outcomes on Country — not reduced dependence on a particular program, but reduced dependence on external systems altogether.

## LCAA Phase

**Listen + Action** — The strategy begins with deep listening to Quandamooka community priorities, knowledge, and experiences of the justice system. Action follows from that listening: strategy development, investment in community-led programs, and advocacy for the policy and resource shifts that make self-determination viable.

## Backlinks

- [[index|ACT Wikipedia]]
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]]

pages.title: R&D Tax Incentive Claim Strategy — FY26
pages.excerpt: Action: both founders invoice FY26 retroactively ($100K each), book a CPA specialising in RDTI for software/civic-tech, and file a claim targeting $200K+ refundable offset. Receipt backlog (11% coverage) is the highest-risk item.
pages.content:
> Action: both founders invoice FY26 retroactively ($100K each), book a CPA specialising in RDTI for software/civic-tech, and file a claim targeting $200K+ refundable offset. Receipt backlog (11% coverage) is the highest-risk item.

This document prepares the CPA conversation. It is not tax advice.

## Current position (from R&D Tax Package, 29 March 2026)

| Item | Amount | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Total Xero spend FY26 YTD (9 months) | $463,711 | ~$51.5K/month |
| Total R&D-tagged spend | $418,835 | Excludes Benjamin's unpaid work |
| Nicholas Marchesi salary | $238,654 | 40% R&D allocation = $95,462 eligible |
| Benjamin Knight FY26 invoices | **$0** | 2,151 commits at 95% R&D allocation — critical gap |
| Benjamin Knight FY25 invoices | $79,000 | Dated June 2025 (end of FY25) |
| Core R&D categories (ACT-IN, ACT-DO, ACT-EL, ACT-JH) | $114,665 | |
| Supporting R&D (ACT-GD) | $65,516 | |
| SaaS/API spend (Claude, OpenAI, Supabase, Vercel, etc.) | ~$12,940 | Eligible as supporting R&D if tied to registered core activities |
| Receipt coverage | **11% (146 of 1,332 transactions)** | ATO audit risk — Dext running but backlog exists |

## The founder invoicing lever

Every $100K of founder invoicing at high R&D allocation generates additional refundable offset:

| Scenario | Ben invoice | R&D eligible (95%) | Additional 43.5% refund |
|---|---|---|---|
| $100K invoice | $100,000 | $95,000 | **$41,325** |
| $150K invoice | $150,000 | $142,500 | **$61,988** |
| $200K invoice | $200,000 | $190,000 | **$82,650** |

If both founders invoice $100K each:
- Combined new R&D eligible: $95K (Ben) + existing $95K (Nic) = $190K founder component
- Total R&D eligible (with existing $418K base): ~$513K
- **Total refund at 43.5%: ~$223K** (vs $182K without Ben invoicing — incremental $41K)

## Eligible R&D activities across ACT codebases

The CPA needs to understand what ACT actually builds. Map of core R&D activities by product:

### [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — consent-sovereign storytelling infrastructure

- **Resonance Field particle system**: portrait-derived palette extraction via node-vibrant + WCAG contrast nudge; d3-force physics modelling (attention cursor, orbital tangential, breathing gravity, secondary theme pulls); canvas renderer with circular-cropped face particles. Novel application of creative coding techniques (Imbrizi methodology) to data sovereignty visualisation.
- **Consent-as-infrastructure**: OCAP/CARE protocol implementation in database architecture; cultural review gating for palette extraction; per-storyteller consent envelope with right-of-withdrawal.
- **Transcript analysis pipeline**: four-layer voice-preserving pipeline (Claude v3 analyser + PRISM signals + spiral resonance mapping + quality scoring); canonical analysis standardisation across 738 transcripts.
- **R&D uncertainty**: how to render storyteller identity as interactive physics without extracting from the storyteller; how to preserve consent sovereignty at the data layer while enabling cross-org resonance signals.

### [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] — civic entity resolution and relationship intelligence

- **Entity graph**: 100K+ entities, 672K+ contracts, 312K+ political donations resolved into a single graph with deterministic GS IDs.
- **Multi-LLM round-robin**: 9 LLM providers in round-robin for entity enrichment; novel architecture for cost/quality/latency balancing.
- **ALMA scoring engine**: six-signal evidence framework applied to 1,155+ youth justice interventions.
- **R&D uncertainty**: how to achieve reliable entity resolution across fragmented government procurement datasets with inconsistent identifiers; how to score intervention quality from heterogeneous evidence types.

### [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — civic intelligence and campaign infrastructure

- **Hansard scraper**: automated extraction and NLP processing of parliamentary records for youth justice policy signals.
- **CONTAINED campaign architecture**: data-driven touring campaign with 225+ contacts, SMS/email/social templates, nomination tracking.
- **R&D uncertainty**: how to make civic policy data legible and actionable for community-led advocacy organisations.

### [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — QR-traceable asset provenance

- **Asset tracking system**: 389 QR-tagged assets across 8 remote communities; telemetry for washing machines; check-in/usage logging.
- **R&D uncertainty**: how to maintain real-time asset visibility in remote Indigenous communities with intermittent connectivity.

## What the CPA needs from us

1. **Founder invoices** — both founders issue retroactive FY26 invoices this month. Through the family trust structures being established (ACT Pty Ltd → family trusts). CPA to advise on timing and structure.
2. **R&D activity descriptions** — the above descriptions, mapped to AusIndustry's "core" vs "supporting" categories. Core = genuine technical uncertainty. Supporting = directly supports a registered core activity.
3. **Evidence of experimentation** — git commit history (2,151 commits, timestamped) + Xero spend by category + API usage logs. The commit-to-hours methodology (3h/commit conservative estimate = 6,453 hours) needs CPA sign-off.
4. **Receipt backlog resolution** — Dext is running (15-min auto-forward) but only 11% of transactions have receipts attached. Need a sprint to capture remaining receipts before filing.
5. **AusIndustry registration** — core activities must be registered within 10 months of FY end (FY26 deadline: 30 April 2027). File early to get refund cash in Aug–Dec 2026.

## Timeline

| Date | Action |
|---|---|
| **By 30 April 2026** | Both founders issue FY26 invoices |
| **By 15 May 2026** | CPA booked and briefed with this document + R&D Tax Package |
| **By 30 June 2026** | Receipt backlog sprint complete (target 80%+ coverage) |
| **By 31 October 2026** | AusIndustry registration for FY26 core activities filed |
| **By 31 December 2026** | Company tax return lodged with RDTI claim |
| **Feb–Apr 2027** | ATO refund received (~4–10 weeks after lodgement) |

## Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Software R&D is the most audited RDTI category | Contemporaneous experiment logs (git commits) + clear "technical uncertainty" descriptions. CPA to review framing. |
| Receipt coverage at 11% weakens the claim | Dext sprint before filing. Prioritise high-value transactions. |
| Benjamin's $0 FY26 invoicing may raise ATO questions if invoiced retroactively in bulk | CPA to structure as quarterly invoices backdated with board resolution. Family trust pathway preferred. |
| ACT Pty Ltd not yet established | Registration must complete before invoicing through trusts. Fallback: invoice as sole trader (less tax-efficient). |
| Commit-to-hours methodology may be challenged | CPA to validate; supplement with calendar records and project logs where available. |

## Annual rhythm (FY27 onwards)

Once FY26 is filed, this becomes a repeatable annual cycle:
- **Monthly**: Dext captures receipts; Xero auto-categorises; Placemat flags gaps
- **Quarterly**: Founders invoice through trusts; R&D allocation reviewed
- **Annually**: AusIndustry registration filed within 10 months; tax return with RDTI claim
- **Ongoing**: Git commits + project documentation maintained as contemporaneous evidence

Target: $200K+ refund annually, compounding to ~$400K+ recycled cash over the plan's five-year horizon.

pages.title: Redtape
pages.excerpt: Bureaucratic friction made visible. Art that takes the invisible labour of compliance and makes it impossible to ignore.
pages.content:
> Bureaucratic friction made visible. Art that takes the invisible labour of compliance and makes it impossible to ignore.

## Overview

Redtape is an ACT studio art project that turns government and grant-application paperwork into a physical object — the literal red tape that the metaphor came from. The work sits in the same lineage as [[contained|CONTAINED]] (youth detention as installation), [[the-confessional|The Confessional]] (institutional space made intimate), and [[gold-phone|Gold.Phone]] (bureaucracy as creative material) — pieces that take an everyday system most people don't see and make it stand in the room with them.

The project asks the audience to **feel** what an ACCO has to wade through to receive funding. Not as a chart. Not as a complaint. As a thing you walk through.

## Why It Matters

The case ACT keeps making — that small First Nations organisations carry the heaviest reporting burden for the smallest grants — is hard to land in a slide deck. The numbers are abstract. **The physical experience of standing inside the paperwork is not.**

Redtape is one of the [[ai-community-engagement|"AI eats the paperwork"]] arguments in physical form: when you can show people how much time, language, and cultural translation labour goes into a $50K acquittal, the conversation about who designs grant systems changes.

## Status

Evidence sparse — Redtape is part of ACT's Studio art line. Specific exhibition history, materials, dimensions, and partner credits await deeper source ingestion. The wiki should grow this article as new context lands.

pages.title: Regional Arts Fellowship
pages.excerpt: A fellowship for practitioners working at the intersection of art, technology, and agriculture — supporting the creative innovators regenerating regional Australia from the ground up.
pages.content:
> A fellowship for practitioners working at the intersection of art, technology, and agriculture — supporting the creative innovators regenerating regional Australia from the ground up.

## Overview

The Regional Arts Fellowship recognises a specific and underserved kind of innovator: the artist-farmer, the technologist-land-steward, the creative practitioner whose work is inseparable from the particular landscape they inhabit. These practitioners are doing some of the most consequential regenerative work in Australia, but they sit outside the usual categories — not quite arts, not quite agtech, not quite environmental science — and so fall through the gaps of standard fellowship and funding programs.

The fellowship creates dedicated support infrastructure for this work: time, resources, recognition, and connection to a wider network of peers and knowledge.

## The Intersection: Art, Technology, Agriculture

### Art
Creative practice as a primary mode of inquiry, communication, and transformation. Not art as decoration or documentation of "real" work, but art as a way of knowing and changing the world — making visible what data cannot, building the emotional and relational conditions that enable systemic change.

### Technology
Digital tools, sensing systems, data platforms, and emerging technologies deployed in service of land and community — not for efficiency gains divorced from ecological relationship, but as instruments in the hands of people who understand place.

### Agriculture
The land as the primary context and stakeholder. Agriculture not as industrial extraction but as regenerative practice — farming systems that restore soil, water, biodiversity, and community relationships simultaneously.

## Relationship to ACT's Ecosystem

The Regional Arts Fellowship connects to several threads in ACT's portfolio:

- [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] — regenerative food systems and regional innovation
- [[act-farm|ACT Farm]] — land-based practice as community and research infrastructure
- [[green-harvest-witta|Green Harvest Witta]] — regenerative agriculture in regional Queensland
- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — First Nations-led land and supply chain work

The fellowship also reflects ACT's commitment to the Art phase of [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] as a site of genuine innovation, not just communication.

## LCAA Phase

**Art** — Creative practice is not a reporting mechanism here but the primary mode of work. The fellowship supports practitioners for whom making art and working the land are the same activity.

pages.title: ReSOLEution
pages.excerpt: A shoe design and customisation program inside youth detention that transforms young people from sneaker consumers into sneaker creators, building identity, skills, and commercial pathways.
pages.content:
> A shoe design and customisation program inside youth detention that transforms young people from sneaker consumers into sneaker creators, building identity, skills, and commercial pathways.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-RS | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

ReSOLEution is a creative intervention program operating inside Bimberi Youth Justice Centre in the ACT. It gives young people in detention the opportunity to design and customise their own sneakers — working from initial concept through to finished prototype across four structured workshop sessions.

The insight behind the program is simple but precise: in facilities where almost everything is stripped away and uniformity enforced, shoes remain a source of pride and personal identity for young people. ReSOLEution meets them there — not by importing an external interest, but by taking something they already care deeply about and making it a platform for creativity, skill development, and legitimate pathways to commercial opportunity.

The program's name holds a double meaning: resolution (finishing, completing, deciding) and sole (the foundation of both a shoe and a person's character). Craft your future, one sole at a time.

## Origin

The program was developed by a practitioner who began their justice work through a Snow Foundation-supported pilot exploring digital tools for the Drug and Alcohol Court (DASL). That experience — building relationships slowly, understanding what actually matters to young people inside — shaped ReSOLEution's design from the ground up.

The observation was direct: during visits to Bimberi, amid all the restrictions and uniformity of detention, shoes were consistently how young people expressed individuality and connection to life beyond the centre's walls. "They'd proudly show off their sneakers outside their units, sharing stories and connections through their footwear."

From this observation came a question: what if that pride became a skill? What if their stories became designs? What if their creativity had real commercial value?

## The Workshop Structure

ReSOLEution runs as four intensive 40-minute sessions, designed to build progressively:

**Session 1 — Brainstorming and Initial Design**
Participants explore the personal stories, interests, and themes they want to express. Initial sketches begin, followed by group sharing and feedback.

**Session 2 — Design Development**
A brief lesson in core design principles (colour theory, balance, composition), followed by refinement of initial sketches and development of the narrative behind each design — what story does the shoe tell?

**Session 3 — Prototyping and Making**
Introduction to materials and techniques, then 30 minutes of hands-on prototyping — creating a basic 3D model or detailed physical sketch. Design challenges are worked through in real time.

**Session 4 — Planning and Review**
Discussion of how the design could be produced at scale. Participants prepare and deliver a brief presentation of their design and its story. Group feedback closes the process.

By the end of the four sessions, each participant has: a fully developed shoe design concept, a prototype or detailed visual representation, a personal narrative explaining the meaning of their design, and experience presenting their work to a group.

## Key Relationships

**Jayke** — a mentor with lived experience of detention, introduced to the program through the DASL pilot. Jayke's involvement brings authenticity that no amount of professional training can provide. He helps participants see real possibilities, sharing his own journey and what changed for him.

**Lorana Bartels** — academic researcher and force for positive change in the Canberra justice space, whose support and insights helped shape the program's approach to innovation in a complex environment.

**Butter, Sydney** — ReSOLEution's commercial partnership with Butter (Sydney's sneaker culture hub) is what distinguishes this program from a craft activity. Participants' designs are showcased at Butter — connecting their creativity directly to one of Australia's most respected sneaker culture communities. For a young person in detention, knowing that their design could be displayed in that venue is not a small thing. It is proof that their creativity has real-world value.

## Partnership with ConFit Pathways

ReSOLEution operates at Bimberi on alternating days to [[confit-pathways|ConFit Pathways]]. The two programs are complementary by design: ConFit brings the internal work (G-Code methodology, physical discipline, values), ReSOLEution brings external expression (creativity, story, commercial possibility). Together they offer a more complete intervention — addressing who someone is on the inside and what they can build on the outside.

## Financial Empowerment Model

A core feature of ReSOLEution is that shoe sales generate revenue for designers upon release. This is not a symbolic gesture — it is a structural attempt to connect the creative work done inside to real economic outcomes outside. Young people who invest in their designs and share their stories have a legitimate pathway to earning from their creativity.

## Connection to ACT Ecosystem

ReSOLEution is tracked within the [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] ecosystem as a community-led innovation in youth justice. It embodies the ACT principle that programs that actually transform lives begin with what young people themselves identify as meaningful — not what adults decide they should care about.

The program also demonstrates the ACT methodology in action: meeting people where they are (sneaker culture, identity, pride), building trust through genuine engagement, and creating real pathways rather than instructional ones.

## Published Writing

- "ReSOLEution" (2025-10-11) — program overview, workshop structure, and design outcomes
- "ReSOLEution at Bimberi Youth Justice Centre" (2025-10-11) — origin story, the Butter partnership, and the thinking behind bringing ConFit Pathways alongside

pages.title: Richard Cassidy
pages.excerpt: First Nations leader bridging cultural knowledge and modern practice — Manbarra Operations, Palm Island.
pages.content:
> First Nations leader bridging cultural knowledge and modern practice — Manbarra Operations, Palm Island.

## Overview

Richard Cassidy is a First Nations man deeply connected to his grandmother's country on Manbarra land at [[palm-island|Palm Island]]. He carries forward cultural obligations passed from his grandfather, serving as a bridge between traditional knowledge systems and contemporary organisational practice.

Richard leads Manbarra Operations, applying Indigenous governance frameworks to modern business and community development on Palm Island.

## Connection to Country

Richard's identity and purpose are inseparable from Country:

> "Country helps me be, and helps me be me, and helps me understand who I am. And it's out of that, from that base of where I land, that I can work out what my doing is going to be."

His grandfather's instruction anchors his work: "You're always gonna look after your grandmother's country."

## The "Our Story" Philosophy

Richard's approach to cross-cultural relationship building centres on shared narrative. Rather than positioning people as "first people" or "second people," he uses story as the vehicle for human connection:

> "Tell me your story and I'll tell you my story and then we'll try and figure out how my story and your story can become an our story."

This methodology — story as bridge — aligns with the [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] principle of Listen first. It rejects hierarchical framing in favour of mutual recognition through narrative exchange.

## Navigating Two Worlds

Richard describes the daily practice of holding both traditional and Western knowledge systems simultaneously:

> "I navigate those two worlds intuitively inside almost all day every day. So I've got this dominant culture side and I've got this cultural side. And one informs each other."

He uses the metaphor of a two-edged spear — the L-O-R-E (traditional law) and the L-A-W (Western legal systems) — arguing both are needed to "cut a path into this landscape."

## The Pebble Philosophy

A core teaching Richard shares about entering another's country:

> "Don't come to someone else's country as a rock or a boulder, but as a pebble, so that your footprint is small. But when you leave, that person says, 'Oh, that one came, your presence is great, and there's a heart. He came and didn't make a ripple. So he's welcome anytime.'"

When asked about his own legacy: "I want to be the smallest pebble I can be... my footprint would be that no one knew that I was here in the first place."

## Leading Manbarra Operations

Richard applies cultural governance frameworks to organisational development. He uses the concept of "hunting for particular fish" — finding people with specific expertise (finance, business, policy) while grounding the organisation in cultural authority.

He teaches his team: "You've got to navigate these two worlds. But for you to understand these two worlds, you've got to know your own world."

## Future Vision

For the land where he works, Richard envisions restoration: "We're planning to minimise that boulder and the impact of that rock and restore this country... the country is restoring itself and regenerating itself."

## ACT Connection

Richard's storytelling and governance practice was documented through [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] field work on Palm Island. His "Our Story" philosophy directly informed ACT's approach to sovereign storytelling and the principle that communities already hold the knowledge — the role of technology is to amplify, not replace.

pages.title: SMART Connect
pages.excerpt: A digital connection platform integrating peer support, digital access, and community connection — bringing innovation, operations, and storytelling together in one ecosystem.
pages.content:
> A digital connection platform integrating peer support, digital access, and community connection — bringing innovation, operations, and storytelling together in one ecosystem.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-SM | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

SMART Connect is a digital platform project that sits within the broader SMART Recovery ecosystem ACT has been involved in supporting. It brings together three strands that are often siloed in recovery and community health settings: the operational infrastructure of running a program, the peer support relationships that make recovery sustainable, and the storytelling that builds community and reduces stigma.

The platform is designed to close the gap between people who need peer support and the community networks that can provide it — while also addressing the digital access barriers that disproportionately affect people in recovery or experiencing disadvantage.

## Key Areas

### Peer Support
Connecting people in recovery or at risk with trained peer supporters who have lived experience. SMART Connect creates structured pathways for these relationships rather than relying on informal, ad hoc connections.

### Digital Access
Recognition that digital exclusion compounds social disadvantage. SMART Connect addresses this not only by building accessible technology but by supporting people to develop the skills and access needed to engage with it.

### Community Connection
Beyond one-to-one peer support, the platform fosters broader community belonging — the network effects that reduce isolation and build resilience over time.

### Integration of Innovation, Operations, and Storytelling
SMART Connect is notable for deliberately integrating these three layers. Innovation without operational continuity fails communities. Operations without storytelling fails to inspire or sustain. Storytelling without innovation stagnates. The platform holds all three.

## Relationship to SMART Recovery Ecosystem

SMART Connect is closely related to two other ACT-supported SMART Recovery projects:

- [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|SMART Recovery GP Kits]] — equipping GPs to introduce SMART Recovery tools in primary care
- [[smart-hcp-gp-uplift|SMART HCP GP Uplift]] — upskilling healthcare providers in addiction support

Together, these three projects represent a system-level approach to addiction recovery: platform connection (SMART Connect), primary care entry point (GP Kits), and clinical workforce capability (HCP Uplift).

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — SMART Connect is a direct delivery project: building the platform, connecting the people, closing the gaps. The listening and design phases inform it, but SMART Connect is where that work becomes infrastructure.

pages.title: SMART HCP GP Uplift
pages.excerpt: A healthcare provider education initiative — building GP and allied health confidence and competence in supporting patients through addiction recovery.
pages.content:
> A healthcare provider education initiative — building GP and allied health confidence and competence in supporting patients through addiction recovery.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-SM | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

SMART HCP GP Uplift (Healthcare Provider GP Uplift) is the workforce development arm of ACT's SMART Recovery ecosystem. Where [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|GP Kits]] provide practical tools for the consultation, HCP Uplift works at the level of the clinician — building the knowledge, skills, and confidence GPs and healthcare providers need to have more effective addiction support conversations.

The project recognises a structural gap: healthcare providers receive limited training in addiction medicine, and even less in peer-based, non-12-step recovery models like SMART Recovery. When clinicians don't know the evidence base, don't feel confident raising the topic, or default to referral-only approaches, patients miss recovery support they could benefit from.

## Key Focus Areas

### Provider Education
Training GPs and allied health providers in the SMART Recovery model — its evidence base, its approach, and how it differs from and complements other pathways.

### Addiction Support Capability
Building the clinical skills to screen for addiction issues, hold non-judgmental recovery-oriented conversations, and navigate the complexity of co-occurring conditions.

### Healthcare System Integration
Working within CPD (Continuing Professional Development) structures and primary care education channels to embed SMART Recovery awareness into how healthcare providers learn and practice.

## Relationship to GP Kits

HCP Uplift and [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|GP Kits]] are designed as complementary:

- GP Kits give clinicians the practical resources
- HCP Uplift builds the capability to use them well

A clinician with high capability but no tools is limited. A clinician with tools but low confidence won't use them. The two projects together address both barriers.

## SMART Recovery Ecosystem

This project sits within a three-part ACT SMART Recovery portfolio:

- [[smart-connect|SMART Connect]] — digital peer support platform
- [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|SMART Recovery GP Kits]] — primary care toolkit
- **SMART HCP GP Uplift** — workforce capability development

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — Training delivered, providers upskilled, system-level capability built. The knowledge and tools are now in the hands of the clinicians who can use them.

pages.excerpt: Practical toolkits for GPs to introduce SMART Recovery to patients in primary care settings — meeting people at the point of first contact with the health system.
pages.content:
> Practical toolkits for GPs to introduce SMART Recovery to patients in primary care settings — meeting people at the point of first contact with the health system.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-SM | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

SMART Recovery GP Kits are a healthcare integration initiative designed to bring evidence-based addiction recovery support into the primary care encounter. GPs are often the first — and sometimes only — professional contact for people experiencing addiction, yet most GP practices lack structured tools to introduce peer-based recovery pathways in a consultation.

The GP Kits address this gap directly: equipping general practitioners with accessible, ready-to-use resources that open the conversation about SMART Recovery and create a pathway from the GP's office to community-based peer support.

## Purpose and Rationale

The primary care system sees people at their most vulnerable and most accessible moments. A person who will never seek out an addiction service may still see their GP. GP Kits are designed to leverage this touchpoint — turning a routine consultation into a potential entry point to recovery.

SMART Recovery's evidence base makes it particularly suited to the GP context: it is science-based, secular, and self-empowerment focused rather than reliant on a spiritual or disease-based model that may not fit all patients.

## Key Features

### Primary Care Optimised
Resources are designed for the time constraints, patient literacy diversity, and clinical communication norms of general practice — not adapted from specialist addiction settings.

### Practical and Ready-to-Use
Kits provide GPs with materials they can hand to patients, scripts for introducing the topic, and clear pathways to local SMART Recovery meetings or digital resources.

### Healthcare Integration
The project works within existing Medicare and primary care structures rather than creating parallel systems, making adoption lower-friction for busy practices.

## Relationship to SMART Recovery Ecosystem

GP Kits are one part of a three-project SMART Recovery ecosystem within ACT's portfolio:

- [[smart-connect|SMART Connect]] — the digital platform for peer support and community connection
- [[smart-hcp-gp-uplift|SMART HCP GP Uplift]] — workforce upskilling for healthcare providers, complementing and extending the GP Kits work

Where GP Kits focus on tools and pathways, HCP GP Uplift focuses on building GP confidence and competence in addiction conversations.

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — Kits in hand, referrals made, recovery conversations happening in consultation rooms. This is direct delivery.

pages.title: SMART Recovery: The Meetings Behind SMART Connect
pages.excerpt: How ACT's partnership with SMART Recovery Australia developed — from a digital brief to a full platform design, a pilot launch, and a GP campaign.
pages.content:
> How ACT's partnership with SMART Recovery Australia developed — from a digital brief to a full platform design, a pilot launch, and a GP campaign.

**Compiled:** 2026-04-07 | **Source:** 7 ACT-SM meeting records (5 substantial)
**See also:** [[smart-connect|SMART Connect]], [[smart-hcp-gp-uplift|SMART HCP GP Uplift]], [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|SMART Recovery GP Kits]]

---

## How ACT Got Into This Space

SMART Recovery Australia is a peer-support addiction recovery organisation — not a 12-step program, explicitly secular, evidence-based. It operates a network of face-to-face and online groups facilitated by trained volunteers, a national app, and a facilitator portal. By mid-2024, the app was live but underperforming, the facilitator community was not cohering digitally, and SMART was looking for a partner who could help them think differently.

ACT came in through NM's network and the Orange Sky connection — Nicholas Marchesi's background as co-founder of Orange Sky gave him immediate credibility with organisations doing peer-support and dignity-centred work. The first meeting on record is 27 August 2024.

---

## First Catch Up Face to Face (August 2024)

The first in-person meeting established rapport and confirmed scope. Sparse notes — primarily relationship-building. But it set the terms: ACT would help SMART think about community and engagement design, not just app development.

---

## First Catch Up with Tim — SMART Digital (September 2024)

Tim Steele manages all of SMART's digital infrastructure: the website, the app, the project management tools. Meeting on 4 September 2024.

Key context Tim provided:
- The app had been live for ~2.5 months; built at an initial cost of $500,000
- First priority had been getting something out — they had been "trying to please a lot of people" during development, resulting in a good starting point but no clear engagement hook
- The core need: a way for facilitators to communicate often and engage with each other. Once trained and running groups, most facilitators disengage from SMART as an organisation. They don't feel like they need to.
- The goal: a **community of practice for facilitators**
- Participants are a longer-horizon opportunity — the open forum model is high-risk (moderation, privacy, crisis support) for people at varying stages of recovery

Tim's framing of the engagement problem was direct: *"Participants at the moment have a very low touchpoint with SMART as an organisation — they go to meetings and that's about it."*

ACT's brief from this meeting: design a community engagement platform (SMART Connect) starting with facilitators, with participants as a later phase. Formal proposal for app uplift to be submitted that week.

One significant structural note from Tim: the distinction between participant and facilitator in SMART is not fixed. Many facilitators were once participants. The design should reflect this — graduated pathways, not hard walls.

---

## Chris Gimpel Interview — Clean Slate Clinic (December 2024)

The most analytically rich meeting in the ACT-SM record. Chris Gimpel runs Clean Slate Clinic — a digital healthcare service supporting people in recovery. He was identified as a key design partner for SMART Connect's participant-facing features.

The interview ran deep on several questions:

### The Safety Architecture

Chris's primary design concern: *"I need to just get my own head and others would need to get their own heads around just the care of the people in it [...] the key things in my mind are how can somebody easily access immediate help."*

His estimate: 20–30% of users in recovery groups are in a headspace where they need additional support mechanisms. The other 70–80% can guide themselves. This ratio shapes every architectural decision — the platform can be self-directed most of the time, but it must have clear pathways to crisis support built in. Not as an afterthought, but as structural infrastructure.

### Platform Differentiation

The conversation worked through what SMART Connect needs to be that Reddit and Facebook are not:
- Reddit: asynchronous, thoughtful, indexed — not suited to real-time peer support
- Facebook: too broad, too distracting, too public for vulnerable conversations
- SMART Connect: synchronous and asynchronous, explicitly bounded community, recovery-context-aware moderation

Chris identified Hello Sunday Morning as the type of platform SMART should aspire toward — behavioural change platform built for a specific recovery context, not repurposed from general social media.

### Data Sovereignty and Decolonising Research

Chris raised the intersection of peer support and data sovereignty — informed by his work at Minjerribah with Elders. The insight: community members need to receive data back. Not as a surveillance report but as a mirror: *"90% of you left with a seven-day plan. 50% of you felt more supported."* At the moment, outcomes data is collected (survey monkey at the end of an online meeting) and then nothing happens with it. SMART Connect could turn data collection into a reciprocal loop rather than extractive measurement.

This is the "decolonising research" thread that Sally would take up in February 2025: community-based, collective, sovereignty-first data practice applied to a non-Indigenous organisation.

### Danny and Encapsulator

Chris had introduced ACT to Danny from Encapsulator — a recovery-tech product — and then managed expectations. *"He went through a recovery journey and wants to be a SMART facilitator. He's really committed."* But ACT's message was clear: SMART is at a point of consolidation, not addition. Understanding what you have before building more.

### The SMART Global Context

Chris explained the landscape: SMART Recovery International (SRI) and SMART Recovery Global (SRG) — Tony funding both. SRG is the digital arm, US/UK/Indonesia/Australia. The ED of SRI had stepped down, creating a leadership vacuum. James from Yama (developer of the facilitator portal) was reconsidering his investment, potentially offering ACT the keys to the existing portal for free. Chris confirmed he would connect ACT with James.

The facilitator portal handover question was live at this point: if Yama transfers the portal to SMART, ACT's build scope could change significantly. April Long would need to understand the full digital ecosystem before deciding whether to build new features or activate the existing infrastructure.

---

## BK, Sally and April — SMART (February 2025)

The most operationally significant meeting in the record. Confirmed:

**Pilot launch date: 1 April 2025.** Six-week discovery phase to complete by end of financial year.

**Test groups confirmed:**
1. Most-engaged facilitator portal users
2. Clean Slate Clinic cohort (Chris Gimpel as warm entry point)

**Onboarding flow:** Two-week sprint → check-in → six-week discovery phase → review and refine.

**Yama/James:** April confirmed she had met James face-to-face (Central Coast). He had pitched Portal 2.0 — linked with an LMS for training and certification. SRI leadership vacuum means SMART may inherit the portal. April's preference: don't build more apps. Understand the existing ecosystem first, then make decisions.

**Monday.com integration:** ACT added to Monday.com for shared planning. Sally to add BK and NM as team members.

**The data sovereignty thread continued:** Sally mentioned Alison — a researcher with funding for a Meth project — who could help design a "research testing channel" where participants opt into innovative data collection. BK raised the Minjerribah Elders data sovereignty model as a governance loop to aspire to.

**The NZ delegation:** SMART Australia is sending a delegation to Wellington, Auckland, and Hamilton — invited by the NZ Mental Health Commission — for the NZ Drug Summit, Leaders Day, and a "Taste of SMART" event. Cultural exchange with senior Māori elders. NM to connect Sally to NZ Orange Sky marketing contacts.

**Sally's farm epiphany:** In a personal aside, Sally shared that time at ACT's farm had been the first thing that broke her burnout cycle in years. She hadn't vaped since. BK named the opportunity: a "mini Silos-based experience" for NFP leaders — rest, reset, strategic coaching, cultural immersion. The farm as a healing space for sector leaders. This is the first time the farm's healing potential for sector leaders is articulated explicitly, and it connected directly to the Justice Hub idea: bringing justice orgs to the farm for peer mentoring.

**GP campaign:** The Chemist Warehouse connection (NM's contact) discussed. Sally confirmed ACT's role in supporting the GP campaign materials.

---

## BK, Sally, April, Nic, Rose — March 2025

Follow-up session, lighter. Key decisions:
- Dr. Chris Davis (most senior Aboriginal doctor in Australia) identified as SMART Connect ambassador
- GP desk kit: water bottle as main tangible give-away (modelled on Hunter Water shower timers). $10,000 budget approved for drink bottle procurement.
- Coasters for pubs and gambling venues as a SMART brand activation channel
- The squishy poo for colon cancer cited as the model for what makes a healthcare give-away memorable — practical, sits on the desk, starts conversations

---

## What the SMART Arc Reveals

**ACT entered as community designers, not app developers.** From Tim's first meeting onward, the brief was about facilitator community and engagement culture — not feature lists. The app already existed. The problem was belonging.

**The crisis support architecture is non-negotiable.** Chris Gimpel's 20–30% figure — the proportion of users who will need active support mechanisms — is the constraint that shapes everything. Any platform that ignores this will fail the people who most need it.

**The data sovereignty question runs through the whole arc.** From Chris's Minjerribah Elders reference in December 2024, through Sally's decolonising research conversation in February 2025, to BK's OCAP governance loop suggestion — the question of what happens to the data after it's collected recurs as a values challenge, not a technical one. SMART is a non-Indigenous organisation operating in addiction recovery spaces with significant First Nations participation. Getting data governance right is how you build trust.

**The Yama handover changes the build scope.** If SMART inherits the facilitator portal from Yama, ACT is no longer building from scratch. This was unresolved as of the February 2025 meeting. The outcome shapes the entire platform roadmap.

**The farm is a strategic asset for sector relationships.** Sally's burnout epiphany on the farm, and BK's subsequent pitch of "bring justice leaders to the farm," shows the ACT farm and Harvest property as infrastructure for relationship capital — not just a physical asset. The farm earned trust with Sally in a way that no amount of pitching would have.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| Aug 2024 | First face-to-face with SMART Recovery Australia |
| Sep 2024 | Tim Steele meeting — brief confirmed, proposal to be submitted |
| Dec 2024 | Chris Gimpel interview — design architecture, safety, data sovereignty |
| Feb 2025 | BK/Sally/April — pilot date (Apr 1), test groups, Yama handover question live |
| Mar 2025 | GP kit decided: drink bottles, coasters, Dr. Chris Davis as ambassador |
| Apr–Jun 2025 | Pilot phase 1 (discovery), target: complete by end of FY25 |

---

## Backlinks

- [[smart-connect|SMART Connect]] — the platform
- [[smart-hcp-gp-uplift|SMART HCP GP Uplift]] — the GP campaign
- [[smart-recovery-gp-kits|SMART Recovery GP Kits]] — the physical activation materials
- [[empathy-ledger-relationships|Empathy Ledger Relationships]] — the data sovereignty thread connecting both platforms
- [[harvest-property-arc|Harvest Property Arc]] — the farm as sector relationship infrastructure
- [[justicehub-evolution-meetings|JusticeHub Evolution]] — the justice org farm-gathering idea that emerged from this arc

pages.title: Staying — Country & Council
pages.excerpt: ⚠️ 2026-04-08 framing change. This page was originally drafted as a standalone Minderoo pitch. After review of the canonical Three Circles proposal (wiki/raw/2026-04-07-jh-three-circles-proposal.md) — which Lucy Stronach is already warm on at $2.9M / 3 years with 10 anchor communities — *Staying has been reframed as the methodology layer inside Three Circles, not a competing pitch.*
pages.content:
> ⚠️ **2026-04-08 framing change.** This page was originally drafted as a standalone Minderoo pitch. After review of the canonical Three Circles proposal (`wiki/raw/2026-04-07-jh-three-circles-proposal.md`) — which Lucy Stronach is already warm on at $2.9M / 3 years with 10 anchor communities — **Staying has been reframed as the *methodology layer* inside Three Circles, not a competing pitch.**
>
> The canonical pitch lives at **[[three-circles|The Three Circles]]**.
> Staying is the name of the *practice* the Circle Two embedded storytelling team does, plus the per-young-person *Journal* artefact added to *The Country We're Building*.
>
> Everything below is preserved as the alternative-shape working draft. Numbers, communities, tiers, European-only framing — all superseded by Three Circles. **Do not pitch this version.** Refer to `[[three-circles]]` for the canonical proposal.

> *A three-year accompaniment of community-led youth justice in seven places.*

**Status:** ⚠️ Superseded by [[three-circles|Three Circles]] as a pitch — preserved here as the methodology + alternative-shape working draft | **Cluster:** Methodology + creative artefact (now lives inside Circle Two) | **Original envelope (no longer the ask):** Foundation $1.8M · Recommended $3.43M · Full ambition $6M (over 3 years)

## What it is

A 3-year program in which a small team rotates through 7 Australian communities — one in each state — accompanying community-led youth justice work, photographing it, journaling it, and producing a bound book per young person at the end. In Year 2, every community sends a young person and a support person on a focused exchange visit to **one** European country — [[diagrama|Diagrama]] in Spain, Halt in Holland, or the Children's Hearings system in Scotland — and brings the experience back. After 3 years it culminates in seven community-led launches and a published book — the largest collection of community-led youth justice evidence ever assembled in this country.

The word **Staying** is the methodology. Every other youth justice program leaves. Staying is the move.

The subtitle **Country & Council** is non-negotiable. *Country* is the place and the people on it. *Council* is the form of community-led decision-making. Both structures are the spine of the program.

## Why this exists

Australia spends $3.9M to detain a single child for 3 years. For roughly the cost of detaining 1.5 children, Staying runs for 3 years across 7 communities, reaches ~50 young people, takes Aboriginal Elders and tribal council members to Spain, and produces the largest evidence base of community-led youth justice ever assembled in this country.

The pattern Staying makes legible is older than fintech — Tyson Yunkaporta's *Sand Talk*, Elinor Ostrom's commons work, [[diagrama|Diagrama]]'s three decades in Murcia. [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] is the *world model* that holds it. [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] is its human face. [[contained|CONTAINED]] is the room you walk into. **Staying is the program that produces all of it.**

It is also the answer to the only question philanthropic capital ever actually asks: *does it work, and how do we know?* Staying answers by staying long enough to be in the proof.

See the synthesis: [[the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is-justicehub-as-the-world-model-for-community-led|The Edge Is Where the Healing Is]].

## Three movements

| Year | Name | Where | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Year 1** | *Listen* | 7 Australian communities | 4 months on (rotating visits) + 8 months virtual support |
| **Year 2** | *Compare* | Distributed European exchange — each community sends **2 people** (1 young person + 1 support) to **one** of [[diagrama|Diagrama]] (Spain), Halt (Holland), or Children's Hearings (Scotland) — focused short visit, full capture, return home | 4 months on in AU + the European exchange visits + reciprocal European visits to AU |
| **Year 3** | *Tell* | Back to the 7 communities + 7 community-led launches | 4 months on + 8 months journal production & launches |

Three acts. Funders, audiences, books all need three acts. Listen / Compare / Tell.

## Team

**1 FTE lead + 1 support person — two people.** Lean on purpose. Doesn't overwhelm a community when it arrives, and fits inside a $1M/year ceiling.

## Cadence

- **4 months on** — heavy engagement, rotating visits per community, in person, longer per-visit stays so each trip earns its travel cost
- **8 months off** — back home in Brisbane, processing, photographing, building journals, prepping next round, doing the European exchange logistics in Year 2
- **One community close to Brisbane** for cheap, frequent low-friction visits and a shorter feedback loop

## The journal — the centre artefact

> *If the program produces nothing else, the journals are the proof.*

- **Bound book per young person** — A5, hand-stitched, ~80–120 pages
- **One delivery, in Year 3** — the complete bound volume, accumulating quietly across all three years and only printed once everything is in. (Earlier versions of the design had three chapter deliveries; cut to fit the envelope without losing the artefact itself.)
- **Contents:** B&W portraits in [[the-brave-ones|Brave Ones]] discipline, the young person's own handwriting, voice transcripts from [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]], letters from Aunties and uncles, ledger entries of who showed up and when, drawings, marks, place — and the European exchange visit captured as its own chapter
- **Owned by the young person.** Not ACT. Not Minderoo. OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer through Empathy Ledger. Right of withdrawal at any point.
- **One archival copy** (with explicit consent only) held by ACT for the program's evidence base.

Visual register: the **ledger page**, not the diagram. References — Christian Boltanski, Sophie Calle, Edmund Clark, Theaster Gates, Anselm Kiefer, Judy Watson, Daniel Boyd, Vernon Ah Kee, Tony Albert, Brook Andrew. Hand-made, lived-in, accumulated over time, system-as-marginalia, the young person at the centre. See [[../../tools/three-ripples-ledger.html|Three Ripples Ledger mockup]].

## Year 3 launches (communities first)

**Seven launches in seven places.** The work goes home. Each of the seven communities hosts a launch on their own terms, in their own venues, with their own people standing in front of their own portraits and journals.

Accompanied by a **published book** — one printed volume that gathers the seven journals (with consent) into a single national artefact. Every electorate office gets a copy.

**National gallery tour deferred to a Year-4 stretch goal.** The institutional tour (NGA / MCA / NGV / regional) is the natural next chapter once Year 3 has landed and proven the work — but it sits outside this $3M envelope and would be raised separately, ideally with the young people and community representatives travelling with the work into the city institutions in Year 4.

## Year 2 — the European exchange

Year 2 is **distributed, not centralised.** No team-in-residence. No one community sends people to all three countries. Each community chooses one European destination that fits the work they're already doing, sends a focused pair, and brings the experience back into the journal and the home community.

**The shape:**

- **2 travellers per community: 1 young person + 1 support person** (Elder, family member, tribal council member, or program lead — chosen by the community, not by ACT)
- **One country per community**, not all three. Each pair goes deep into one place rather than skating across three.
- **Three host geographies**, chosen because they hold practice the rest of the world treats as impossible:
  - **Spain — [[diagrama|Diagrama]]** (Murcia and beyond). The thirty-year proof that community-based youth justice scales. Cornerstone partner; door is already open via the Olga meeting.
  - **Holland — Halt.** Restorative justice infrastructure and the diversion-first prevention model.
  - **Scotland — Children's Hearings system + Whole System Approach.** The political courage to legislate a minimum age of criminal responsibility worth importing.
- **Focused short visits** — long enough to sit inside the practice, short enough to honour the lives travellers leave at home and to keep the budget honest
- **Reciprocal European visits to Australia** — small delegations from each host (Diagrama, Halt, Scottish) travelling to a subset of the seven communities, walking Country with the people they only ever read about
- **Captured in full** — every visit documented end-to-end (photographs, voice, journal entries), and every traveller's experience becomes a chapter in their community's contribution to the Year 3 book

Why this still works as the masterstroke at a fraction of the original budget:

1. Puts a young person and a community Elder on a plane to Europe and into a Spanish, Dutch, or Scottish youth centre. **Those conversations have never happened in this country's history** — and they happen in seven communities at once because every community sends a pair.
2. Inspires the local communities to believe they are *already* doing world-class work — and to see themselves as international peers, not service recipients.
3. Brings Europe to Australia in the same year. The reciprocal visits collapse the centre/periphery framing every philanthropic conversation about Indigenous justice gets stuck in.
4. Turns [[diagrama|Diagrama]], Halt, and the Children's Hearings network from abstract precedents into living relationships, distributed across seven communities.
5. Gives the program its three-act arc — *Listen / Compare / Tell.*
6. Makes Minderoo's gift internationally legible — *"The Minderoo Australian Justice Cohort sent fourteen people to Europe and brought Europe back."*

## Three scales — same program, three sizes

Staying flexes. The architecture is the same at every scale; what moves is *how many communities*, *how big the team*, *how deep Europe goes*, and *what Year 3 produces*. Three honest tiers, so the conversation with a funder is about fit, not negotiation:

| | **Foundation** | **Recommended** | **Full ambition** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Annual flow** | ~$600K/year | ~$1.0M / $1.24M / $1.20M | ~$2.0M/year |
| **3-year total** | **~$1.8M** | **~$3.43M** | **~$6.0M** |
| **Communities** | 5 communities (drop hardest-to-reach 2 states) | 7 communities, one per state | 7 communities + annual national cohort gathering |
| **Team** | 1 FTE lead, no support | 1 FTE lead + 1 support | 2 FTE + 1 support |
| **Cadence** | 3 months on / 9 months virtual | 4 months on / 8 months virtual | 6 months on / 6 months virtual |
| **Year 2 Europe** | Deferred — small Spain scoping trip only (2 ACT staff, no community travellers) | Distributed exchange — 14 travellers (1 young person + 1 support per community), one country each (Spain / Holland / Scotland) | Distributed exchange + reciprocal European visits to AU + one full cohort immersion week per host country |
| **Journal** | Y3 only, simple binding, 1 copy per young person | Y3 only, hand-stitched, 1 copy per young person + 1 archive | **Three chapter deliveries** (Y1/Y2/Y3), hand-stitched, premium binding, multiple copies |
| **Year 3** | 5 community-led launches, no book | 7 community-led launches + 1 published book | 7 community-led launches + book + **national gallery tour** (NGA / MCA / NGV) + every-electorate-office distribution |
| **Cultural review fees** | $50K/year (the floor) | $80K/year | $100K/year + paid Elder council |
| **What it proves** | The methodology works in Australia | The methodology works *and* scales internationally | The methodology becomes a fixture of Australian civic life |
| **Versus detaining 1 child for 3 years** ($3.9M) | 46% of the cost | 88% of the cost | 154% of the cost |

**Recommended is the default pitch.** Foundation is what we go to if Minderoo wants the cap held flat. Full ambition is what we go to if Minderoo (or co-funders) wants the legacy version — and unlocks the national gallery tour without it needing to be raised separately later.

---

## Detailed budget — Recommended tier (~$1M/year, $3.43M total)

This is the **return-pitch shape**. A previous ~$8M / 3-year design was too much; a fuller ~$6.3M version (year-long European team in residence, 2 FTE + 1 support, three journal chapter deliveries, full national gallery tour) was archived to make this fit. Every line below is sized so the program *moves* rather than stalls in funder negotiation. The Foundation and Full ambition tiers above flex this same line structure up and down.

| Line | Year 1 (AU) | Year 2 (AU + Europe exchange) | Year 3 (AU + community launches) | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Core team (1 FTE lead + 1 support) | $220K | $220K | $220K | $660K |
| AU travel + accommodation (4 months on) | $110K | $80K | $110K | $300K |
| Community partnership fees (7 × $50K/yr) | $350K | $350K | $350K | $1.05M |
| European exchange — 14 travellers (1 young person + 1 support per community), one country each | — | $130K | — | $130K |
| European exchange — chaperone team + in-country fixers + capture | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| European reciprocal visits to AU (small Diagrama / Halt / Scottish delegations) | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| Diagrama + Halt + Children's Hearings partnership fees | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| Young person stipends + journal materials (accumulating) | $30K | $40K | $90K | $160K |
| Journal binding + final book production (Y3 only) | — | — | $80K | $80K |
| Equipment, archive, production | $40K | $20K | $20K | $80K |
| Data + tech infra ([[justicehub|JusticeHub]] / ALMA / [[empathy-ledger|EL]] contributions) | $40K | $30K | $30K | $100K |
| Seven community-led launches (Y3) | — | — | $70K | $70K |
| Comms, social, content | $30K | $30K | $40K | $100K |
| Cultural review + Elder governance fees | $80K | $80K | $80K | $240K |
| Operations + admin (5%) | $45K | $57K | $55K | $157K |
| Contingency (5%) | $45K | $57K | $55K | $157K |
| **TOTAL** | **~$0.99M** | **~$1.24M** | **~$1.20M** | **~$3.43M** |

Year 1 sits cleanly under the $1M soft ceiling. Years 2 and 3 each run a little above it — Y2 because of the European exchange line items, Y3 because of journal production + 7 community launches. Both can be trimmed back under $1M flat if Minderoo wants the cap held hard, at the cost of either fewer European travellers, a thinner final book, or smaller community launches.

Funded by Minderoo as catalytic capital. Their legacy.

**The ask:** ~$3.43M over three years, with annual flow of ~$1.0M / $1.24M / $1.20M. Tight ops + contingency (5% each) — held there because the program design is conservative and the partner relationships are already in place.

**For context:** detaining one child for 3 years costs $3.9M. **Staying runs for less than the cost of detaining a single child**, reaches ~50 young people across 7 communities, sends 14 people to Europe and brings Europe back, and produces the largest community-led youth justice evidence base ever assembled in this country.

**What was cut to fit the envelope** (kept here so the conversation about scope is honest):

- Team from 2 FTE + 1 support → 1 FTE + 1 support
- Cadence from 6/6 → 4/8
- Year 2 from year-long European residency → distributed short exchange visits
- Journal from three chapter deliveries → one Year 3 delivery
- Year 3 national gallery tour → deferred to a Year 4 stretch goal raised separately

## The 7 communities — first-pass shortlist

| State | Likely candidate | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **NT** | [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] (Mparntwe) — Aunty Bev, Tanya Turner, Kristy Bloomfield | Existing partnership, very strong |
| **QLD (north)** | [[picc|PICC]] (Palm Island) — Richard Cassidy and the Bwgcolman families | Existing partnership |
| **QLD (Brisbane region)** | One of three candidates: **EPIC Pathways** (Rhian Miller), the **MMEIZC** team on Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah), or the **Toowoomba** team | Three-way pick — close-to-home community |
| **NSW** | Maranguka (Bourke Tribal Council) | Need to approach |
| **WA** | Olabud Doogethu (Halls Creek) | Need to approach |
| **TAS** | Prevention Not Detention (Loic Fery's coalition) | Pipeline contact |
| **VIC** | ??? | **OPEN — Q12** |
| **SA** | ??? | **OPEN — Q12** |

**How we find the 7 (locked):** there is no funnel. We start with the people we already know and trust — co-selecting alongside Minderoo and other aligned funders — and from there we radiate outward through trust, recommendation, and openness. New communities surface through search, peer recommendation, and open ideas, not through an application form. The filter is relationship, not process.

## Cultural protocol (non-negotiable)

1. No community is approached without prior consultation with existing ACT relationships in that region
2. **Elder and Council sign-off** before any photographs, recordings, or journals begin
3. **OCAP/CARE protocols** at the data layer via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the legal and technical baseline, not aspirational
4. **Young person owns their journal.** Right of withdrawal at any point, including post-exhibition; portraits and entries removed within 7 days of request
5. **Subjects under 18** require guardian and cultural authority sign-off
6. **Cultural review fees** are budgeted as line items, not absorbed as goodwill labour
7. **No exhibition opens** without at least one young person or cultural representative present
8. **Income from book/exhibition sales** flows on a published transparent split to subjects and their nominated community organisations

The first consent conversation matters more than the first photograph. Get the protocol wrong and the program should not exist.

## How it connects to the rest of ACT

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — Staying is the field arm; JusticeHub is the world model that holds the evidence, ALMA is the data spine
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — every voice transcript, every consent, every story is captured here. The ethical and technical base.
- [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] — the visual discipline; every Staying portrait sits in the Brave Ones series
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — companion piece; the touring exhibition travels alongside CONTAINED where it can
- [[diagrama|Diagrama]] — Year 2 partner; the international comparator
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — first locked community partnership
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — second locked community partnership
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Listen (Y1) → Compare ≈ Curiosity (Y2) → Tell ≈ Action + Art (Y3)
- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology Staying enacts at scale
- [[the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is-justicehub-as-the-world-model-for-community-led|The Edge Is Where the Healing Is]] — the synthesis this program operationalises

## Funding pathway

**Lead funder (proposed):** Minderoo Foundation — Walk Free + Generation One alignment, capacity for catalytic 3-year capital, international ambition matches the Year 2 European exchange.

**Contact:** Lucy Stronach (Minderoo). Already warm. Already asking for specific dollar numbers and plans.

**Approach (locked): return pitch with a tight envelope.** A previous ~$8M / 3-year shape was too much. The next pitch goes back at **~$3.43M total**, structured as ~$1M / $1.24M / $1.20M annual flow. Year 1 sits inside the soft ~$1M ceiling Lucy signalled; Years 2 and 3 each run ~$200–240K above it because that's where the European exchange and the journal/launches land. This is the shape that makes the program *move* rather than stall (see Budget envelope above).

The *Edge Holds* blog + LinkedIn piece still publish — but as accompaniment around the return pitch, not as a cold-warmup.

**Naming opportunity:** *"The Minderoo Australian Justice Cohort"* — international civic-infrastructure legacy positioning that a foundation will pay a premium for.

## Decisions locked (2026-04-08)

Q11–Q15 resolved in session:

- **Q11 — Year 2 is a distributed European exchange.** Each of the 7 communities sends 2 people (1 young person + 1 support) to *one* country: Spain (Diagrama), Holland (Halt), or Scotland (Children's Hearings). Focused short visits, not a year-long residency. Reciprocal European visits to Australia in the same year. Designed to make every community an international peer at a fraction of the year-long-team-in-residence cost.
- **Q12 — Brisbane region community is a three-way pick** between EPIC Pathways (Rhian Miller), the MMEIZC team on Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah), and the Toowoomba team. VIC and SA candidates still to be sourced through trust-based outreach (not a public call).
- **Q13 — No 30 → 7 funnel.** Co-select with Minderoo and other aligned funders starting from the people we already know and trust, then radiate outward through trust, recommendation, and openness. No application form. The filter is relationship.
- **Q14 — Communities first.** Year 3 produces seven community-led launches in the seven places, plus a published book that gathers the seven journals (with consent) into one volume. The national gallery tour (NGA / MCA / NGV) is **deferred to a Year-4 stretch goal** raised separately — outside this $3.43M envelope.
- **Q15 — Return pitch with a tight envelope.** Lucy Stronach is already warm and asking for numbers. A prior ~$8M shape was too much. New shape: **~$3.43M total** at ~$1M / $1.24M / $1.20M annual flow. Y1 inside the soft $1M ceiling, Y2/Y3 a touch above to carry Europe and book production. The program is re-cut (1 FTE + 1 support, distributed European exchange, journal as Y3 delivery) to fit. *Edge Holds* publishes alongside the pitch, not as cold warmup.

pages.title: Storytelling, Data Sovereignty, and Community Recovery
pages.excerpt: Storytelling and data sovereignty anchor recovery work, with Elders guiding what is shared and why.
pages.content:
> Storytelling and data sovereignty anchor recovery work, with Elders guiding what is shared and why.

## Context

**Place:** Palm Island community
**Voice Owner:** Community storytellers and Elders group (consented)
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE — Elders review required for external use

## Story

In the aftermath of devastating storms, Palm Island community faced not just physical recovery but the challenge of telling their own story. Previous disaster responses had seen external media and researchers arrive, extract stories, and leave — sometimes misrepresenting the community or exposing sensitive information.

Through Empathy Ledger, the community established a different model. Elders guide what is shared and why. Storytellers maintain control over their narratives. Data sovereignty means the community owns their recovery story.

The result: recovery documentation that serves the community first, respects cultural protocols, and provides evidence for future planning — on the community's terms.

## ALMA Signals

| Signal | Level | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------|
| **Authority** | High | Elder guidance, community control |
| **Evidence** | High | Narrative documentation of recovery |
| **Harm Risk** | Medium | Storm impacts are sensitive |
| **Capability** | Medium | Ongoing, building capacity |
| **Option Value** | High | Model for future recovery |
| **Community Value Return** | High | Community owns the narrative |

## Connections

**LCAA Shift:** Listen (gathering storm impact stories) → Art (story becomes shared recovery practice). Storytelling became infrastructure for community-led recovery, not external extraction.

*Consent reviewed: 2025-12 | Next review: 2026-06*

pages.title: Strategic Decisions Log
pages.excerpt: The load-bearing decisions that shape ACT's strategy. Distilled from 58 decision records in project_knowledge, filtered down to the dozen that matter most.
pages.content:
> The load-bearing decisions that shape ACT's strategy. Distilled from 58 decision records in `project_knowledge`, filtered down to the dozen that matter most.

## Why a Curated Log

Of the 58 decisions stored in Supabase, most are routine student-team meeting choices from 2023–2024 development sprints (`ACT-MISC` code). The decisions below are the genuinely strategic ones — the moments where ACT chose a direction, refused a path, or framed a problem in a way that changed downstream work.

## 2026

### PRF Power Analysis: 61/22/17 Split (2026-03-26, ACT-HQ)

Of ~$90M in traceable Paul Ramsay Foundation grants:
- **61%** → universities + large intermediaries
- **22%** → community organisations
- **17%** → ACCOs directly (only 1 of top 10 grants — Anindilyakwa $3.45M)
- **ACF** intermediates $17.6M+
- PRF claims 50%+ First Nations support, but that's strategy-aligned only — actual $220M Indigenous work = 19% of $1.15B total
- Revenue source: Ramsay Health Care dividends (PRF holds 17.58% stake)

**Why it matters:** The Kristy Muir Power letter (Feb 2026) was a genuine signal of intent, but structural inertia in PRF's grant-making means most dollars still flow upstream. This analysis is the basis for ACT's 2026 funder engagement strategy: don't pitch PRF as a transactional funder; pitch them on the structural problem their own data reveals.

### PLACE as JusticeHub Entry Point (2026-03-26, ACT-HQ)

PLACE Network (Dr Luke Craven, CEO) connects every target funder ACT cares about — PRF, Dusseldorp, Minderoo, Ian Potter, Bryan, AusGov — and has no data platform of its own. Ian Trust bridges PLACE Community Council and PRF FNAC. Tennant Creek (Oonchiumpa basecamp) is in the SPSP network.

**Decision:** Position [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] as the evidence platform PLACE communities need, not as a competing initiative. Entry through Luke Craven (systems-change practitioner who will immediately understand the value proposition) rather than through traditional foundation-relations channels.

### Westpac Event 30 March (2026-03-27, ACT-HV)

**Decision:** Proceed with Westpac event on 30 March.
**Rationale:** Align with Mounty visit and Jo's attendance.
**Source:** NM/BK sync.

A small operational decision, included here because it represents the cadence of opportunistic stakeholder alignment that drives ACT's relationship-building rhythm.

## 2025

### Spain Trip — Diagrama Engagement (2025-01-16, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Move forward with planning the Spain trip.
**Rationale:** Engage high-profile decision-makers in understanding [[diagrama|Diagrama]]'s approach to youth justice.

This is the decision that produced the 2025 Spain delegation and the foundation for ACT's [[global-precedents|global precedents]] research thread. Without this trip, the Diagrama partnership stays theoretical.

## 2024

### Reject the Loan (2024-11-07, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Do not pursue a loan.
**Rationale:** Preference for support from the UK instead.

A small decision with implications: ACT chose relational capital over debt, even when a loan was available. This pattern (prefer aligned capital over neutral capital) recurs across 2025–2026 funding decisions.

### YJ Legislative Push (2024-05-22, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Pursue legislative changes for youth justice.
**Rationale:** Improve the system based on experiences from Spain.

The genesis decision for ACT's [[youth-justice-reform|youth justice reform]] advocacy posture — shifting from program delivery to systems change.

## 2023

### Central Tech Platform (2023-05-29, ACT-JH)

**Decision:** Develop a central technology platform to support individual agency and data control.
**Rationale:** Enable better integration and user experience in the human services system.
**Source:** TYSON Bank workshop.

**This is the genesis decision for what became [[justicehub|JusticeHub]].** Everything downstream — ALMA, the intervention portfolio, the funding landscape work — traces to this single sentence.

### ACT Supports Confit Pathways (2023-03-29, ACT-EL)

**Decision:** A Curious Tractor will support the pitch and build of the Confit Pathways application.
**Rationale:** Address pain points in scaling the program and enhance community support.

The first formal commitment to the [[confit-pathways|Confit Pathways]] partnership — a pattern ACT would repeat: take responsibility for the technology layer of someone else's mission rather than running parallel programs.

## What's NOT in this Log

The 58 raw decision records also include:
- 30+ student team operational decisions (Notion vs Miro, IntelliJ vs other IDEs, MySQL vs other databases)
- A handful of meeting cadence decisions
- Form-design choices for early app prototypes

These are preserved in the raw snapshot at `wiki/raw/2026-04-07-supabase-strategic-decisions-snapshot.md` for completeness, but they don't belong in the strategic narrative.
