pages.title: The Brave Ones
pages.excerpt: Real portraits. Real stories. Real young people. The ones changing the system.
pages.content:
> Real portraits. Real stories. Real young people. The ones changing the system.

**Status:** Ideation (sketched 2026-04-07) | **Cluster:** Art (Studio) | **Tier:** Studio piece in development

## Overview

The Brave Ones is a sustained photographic and storytelling series sitting in the [[act-studio|ACT Studio cluster]] alongside [[contained|CONTAINED]]. Where CONTAINED puts you inside the *room* that youth detention is, The Brave Ones puts you in front of the *people* who walked out the other side. It is the deliberate counter-mugshot: studio-quality B&W portraits in the dignity register that policing and media have refused to give Indigenous and system-impacted young people for two centuries.

It is also the visual architecture of [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the human face of the world model — and the answer to the photo-credit problem every justice org runs into: the entire image library for the next decade of community-led justice work in Australia, with consent built in at the layer below.

## Why this exists

A diagram is read once and filed. A portrait is stood in front of. The CONTAINED tour proved that the move that breaks a funder, a judge, or a minister is not a stat — it is a body in a room. The Brave Ones is that move at scale and on repeat. It is also self-replicating: every new portrait is a new ALMA node, a new [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] story, a new Tractorpedia article. The system gets smarter every time someone stands in front of the lens.

The name does the inversion in three words. The dominant media calls these young people "at-risk youth", "offenders", "system-impacted". The Brave Ones says: *they are not the problem. They are the proof. And they are braver than anyone in the system that failed them.*

## Visual language

The reference is the Brian Duffy / *Station to Station*-era David Bowie portrait register, 1976:

- High-contrast black & white, soft halated key light from a single source
- Deep velvety blacks, silvery mid-tones, almost no pure whites except in the halation
- Film grain texture — never digital crispness
- Shallow depth of field, subject emerging from shadow
- Devotional close framing — chin/hand/contemplation
- Refuses the colour-coded infographic vocabulary of every other systems-change visual
- Negative space carries weight

Palette: bone white (#F4F0E8) and velvet black (#0E0E10). Optional single accent: blood ochre (#7A2F1A), used at most once per artefact.

Typography: refined serif, set small, set far from the centre. Numbers and statistics never appear on the portrait — they live in companion artefacts. The image is the argument; the data is the evidence.

## Components

| Layer | What it is | Who holds it |
|---|---|---|
| The portraits | Studio-quality B&W photographs, single visual continuity, life-size when printed | The photographer + each subject's editorial control |
| The voices | Each portrait paired with the young person's own words, captured via Empathy Ledger, transcribed verbatim | Empathy Ledger consent layer |
| The stories | One-page case study per portrait: where they were, what changed, who held them | JusticeHub + community partner |
| The cohort | The young people in the series form a real cohort — they meet, mentor each other, speak together, become a constituency | The young people themselves |
| The galleries | A touring physical exhibition — MCA, NGV, Powerhouse, regional galleries, ACCO halls, parliament foyers | ACT Studio + venue partners |
| The online hall | A permanent presence on JusticeHub — each portrait a node in ALMA | JusticeHub + Empathy Ledger |
| The book | Year three: the printed book | ACT publishing partner |

## Cultural protocol (non-negotiable)

Before a single Indigenous young person sits for a portrait:

1. **Aunty Bev, Uncle Terry, Tanya Turner, Kristy Bloomfield** at [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] are consulted and the protocol is co-designed
2. **Empathy Ledger consent flow** is the legal and technical baseline — not aspirational
3. **Each subject has right of withdrawal at any point**, including after exhibition; portraits removed from all venues and digital instances within 7 days of request
4. **Subjects under 18** require guardian and cultural authority sign-off
5. **No exhibition opens without at least one subject (or a designated cultural representative) present** — this is their show, not ours
6. **Income** from commercial use (print sales, book sales, licensing) flows to subjects and their nominated community organisations on a transparent published split

The first consent conversation is more important than the first photograph. If we get the protocol wrong, the project should not exist.

## Phase plan

| Phase | Time | Cohort | Key activity | Cost (rough) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Placeholder** | This week | 1 stand-in image | Three Ripples poster, Minderoo deck, internal review | $0 |
| **1. Pilot** | Months 1–3 | 5 young people | First proper sittings (Mparntwe, Bourke, one other), consent flow tested end-to-end | ~$15K |
| **2. Launch** | Months 3–12 | 25 young people | First public gallery exhibition. JusticeHub homepage relaunched around the series. | ~$80K |
| **3. National tour** | Months 12–24 | 100 portraits | Travels alongside CONTAINED. Book published. Every electorate office. | ~$200K |
| **4. Annual** | Ongoing | +20–30/year | The series becomes a fixture of Australian civic life | ~$50K/year |

## Funding pathway

This is catalytic philanthropic capital with art-grant compatibility. Likely funders:

- **Minderoo Foundation** — Walk Free + Generation One justice alignment
- **Vincent Fairfax Family Foundation** — has funded portrait series before
- **Lord Mayor's Charitable Foundation** — Melbourne arts + justice crossover
- **Ian Potter Foundation** — community-led arts
- **Australia Council / Creative Australia** — direct arts grant pathway
- **R&D Tax** — photography, consent-tech, and platform work all eligible under ACT's existing R&D incentive claim

Lead-funder naming opportunity: *"The [Funder Name] Brave Ones Portrait Series"* — civic-infrastructure legacy positioning a foundation will pay a premium for.

## How it connects to the rest of ACT

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — each portrait becomes a node in ALMA; the series is the human face of the data layer
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — consent + sovereignty + voice capture; the technical and ethical base
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — companion piece; portraits live on the inside walls of the rooms
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — likely first community partnership; cultural protocol design
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — second community partnership; longitudinal subjects
- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology this series operationalises
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Art (the fourth letter); the form that completes Listen → Curiosity → Action

## Stories already in the wiki worth photographing

These are the young people whose stories are already documented and consented at some level via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the natural seed cohort:

- **Xavier** (Oonchiumpa) — built the Stretch Bed; was told by formal reports he had "limited ability to understand"; Oonchiumpa bet on his version
- **MS** (Oonchiumpa) — thought he was from Alice Springs; reconnected with family across Central Australia; building a tourism venture on his own Country
- **CB** (Oonchiumpa) — becoming a man, becoming a leader in Town Camp
- **Jackqwann** (Mparntwe) — rapper exploring identity, cultural heritage, belonging
- **A** (Oonchiumpa) — guarded to self-advocate after losing her mother
- **M** (Oonchiumpa) — homelessness to independent living
- **L** (Oonchiumpa, age 16) — named the cause of youth incarceration in one word: *"Oppression."*

Plus subjects to be drawn from Maranguka (Bourke), [[picc|Palm Island]], and [[confit-pathways|Confit Pathways]] as the cohort expands.

## First move (this week)

Use a **placeholder portrait** for the Three Ripples poster — pulled from Empathy Ledger's already-consented archive OR a public-domain reference image clearly marked as a stand-in. The placeholder lets us prove the visual concept this week, brief the photographer with an actual mockup, and share the framing internally (Aunty Bev, Tanya Turner, Brodie, Joe Kwon) for cultural feedback *before* any young person sits.

The placeholder is explicitly labelled as a stand-in everywhere it appears, and is replaced the moment Phase 1 portraits are shot.

## Backlinks

- [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] — the canonical 3-year, $2.9M Minderoo pitch. The per-young-person Journals (the fourth form of *The Country We're Building* artefact) sit inside the Brave Ones visual discipline.
- [[staying|Staying — Country & Council]] — the methodology layer that produces the Journals; same visual discipline
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — the companion art piece; The Brave Ones lives inside its rooms
- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the world model the portraits make legible
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the consent and sovereignty layer
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — first likely community partnership and protocol co-design
- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology this series operationalises
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Art as the fourth letter
- [[the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is-justicehub-as-the-world-model-for-community-led|The Edge Is Where the Healing Is]] — the synthesis this series visualises

pages.content:
> A caravan as a venue, a dignity infrastructure prototype, and an art piece all at once. Born out of the Community Capital Leadership Retreat.

## Overview

The Caravan is an ACT studio piece that emerged from the **10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat** in Bowral (February 2026, see [[community-capital|Community Capital]]). It sits in the lineage of [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]] and [[global-laundry-alliance|Orange Sky's mobile dignity model]] — vehicles that turn up where the people are, instead of asking the people to come to them.

But it's also an art piece in the [[act-ecosystem|Studio cluster]] sense: the caravan is a thing that carries an argument. The argument is that infrastructure for community capital — leadership retreats, peer councils, dignity services — shouldn't live in conference rooms in capital cities. It should be towable.

## Origin: the Community Capital event

The Community Capital Leadership Retreat (Bowral, Feb 2026, funded by Social Impact Hub Foundation) brought ten community leaders together. The Caravan was the contribution ACT made to that event — both as a literal vehicle and as a statement about what happens when you invert "we built a building, come to us" into "we built a thing, we're coming to you."

[[nicholas-marchesi|Nicholas Marchesi]]'s Orange Sky pattern is the obvious precedent: a van turning up in a park is a more powerful equity intervention than a brochure. The Caravan extends that logic to leadership development.

## Status

Evidence sparse on specifics — exact build details, current location, future tour stops, and post-Bowral activations all await deeper source ingestion. This article is the seed.

pages.title: The Confessional
pages.excerpt: A horse trailer converted into a sacred healing space — a mobile art therapy installation making mental health support accessible in remote and underserved communities.
pages.content:
> A horse trailer converted into a sacred healing space — a mobile art therapy installation making mental health support accessible in remote and underserved communities.

## Overview

The Confessional is a mobile therapeutic installation built inside a converted horse trailer. It travels to remote and underserved communities where traditional mental health infrastructure is absent or inaccessible, offering a safe, anonymous, and non-clinical space for people to engage with art as a therapeutic tool.

The design is intentional: a horse trailer is familiar in rural and remote contexts, functional, and carries no clinical or institutional associations. Inside, participants engage with art-making as a route to self-expression and emotional processing — with anonymity and psychological safety as core design principles. Crisis support pathways are embedded in the experience.

## Key Details

- **Format:** Mobile installation — horse trailer converted to therapeutic space
- **Primary modality:** Art therapy, creative expression
- **Target communities:** Remote and underserved areas without access to traditional mental health services
- **Website:** [act.place/project/the-confessional](https://act.place/project/the-confessional)
- **Core values:** Anonymity, safety, accessibility, non-clinical framing

## How It Works

The Confessional offers an alternative to traditional therapy by:

- Bringing the space to where people are, rather than requiring travel to services
- Using art-making as the primary therapeutic modality — lower barrier than talk therapy
- Providing anonymity as a structural guarantee, not just a promise
- Embedding crisis support access within the experience for participants who need it

## LCAA Phase

**Art** — The Confessional sits squarely in ACT's Art phase, where creative practice becomes the vehicle for healing, transformation, and community care. Art here is not decoration; it is the mechanism.

pages.title: The Cure Already Exists
pages.excerpt: Op-ed by Benjamin Knight arguing that the evidence for youth justice reform is in — community-led programs already work, and the only missing ingredient is political will and funding.
pages.content:
> Op-ed by Benjamin Knight arguing that the evidence for youth justice reform is in — community-led programs already work, and the only missing ingredient is political will and funding.

## Overview

Published in 2026, this piece was written as a launch essay for the [[contained|CONTAINED]] national tour. It makes the case that Australia's youth justice crisis has a known cure — not in theory, but in operating programs across Alice Springs, Palm Island, and Mount Druitt — and that the task now is making these alternatives visible, funded, and undeniable.

The essay weaves together personal testimony, comparative international evidence (Spain's Diagrama Foundation), First Nations program outcomes, and the work of [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]], building toward a call to experience CONTAINED.

**Author:** Benjamin Knight (co-founder, A Curious Tractor)

## The Core Argument

Australia spends more than a billion dollars a year detaining children. The Productivity Commission's Report on Government Services puts the average cost at $1.3 million per child per year ($3,600/day). The return on that investment: 85 percent of young people who come out go straight back in.

First Nations children bear this disproportionately — they are 21 times more likely to end up in detention than their non-Indigenous classmates, and comprise over 60 percent of the detained population.

The essay's central claim: **this is not a problem without a solution. The cure already exists.** It lives in communities. The question is whether the rest of Australia will catch up.

## The Evidence: Programs That Work

### Oonchiumpa (Alice Springs)
- 100% Aboriginal-led. Founded by Kristy Bloomfield (Central Arrernte, Eastern Arrernte and Alyawarra woman, Traditional Owner of Mparntwe) and Tanya Turner (Eastern Arrernte woman, UWA law graduate, former Associate at the Supreme Court of Victoria)
- 95% diversion success rate
- 97.6% cheaper than detention
- NT Police Operation Luna: worked with 21 high-risk young people; by December, only one remained on the list
- Works with 32 partner organisations across Central Australia
- 72% of disengaged youth returned to education through their programs
- Being studied by Flinders University; running ANU's True Justice program

Kristy Bloomfield: *"These aren't 'bad kids', they're children without basics many Australians take for granted. The system responds with detention that costs millions and changes nothing. We respond with cultural connection, practical support, and the authority that comes from being their Elders, their Traditional Owners, their family."*

See: [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]

### PICC — Palm Island Community Company
- 197 staff delivering services across North Queensland
- 78% diversion rate
- Philosophy: culture is protection. When young people know who they are, where they come from, and who their family is, they make different choices.

### Mounty Yarns (Mount Druitt, Western Sydney)
- Youth-led storytelling — young people writing and publishing their own stories, running their own media
- 30% of participants now pursuing media careers
- *"They are not waiting for someone to give them a platform. They are building their own."*

See: [[mounty-yarns|Mounty Yarns]]

## The International Comparison: Diagrama Foundation (Spain)

Benjamin Knight visited the [[diagrama|Diagrama Foundation]] in Spain — an organisation that runs youth detention centres with a fundamentally different philosophy.

Key contrasts:

| Metric | Spain (Diagrama) | Australia |
|--------|-----------------|-----------|
| Recidivism rate | 13.6% | 85%+ |
| Annual cost per young person | ~$31,000 | $1.3 million |
| Social return (per University of Valencia) | 5.64 euros per euro invested | — |

What makes the difference:
- Staff are called "social educators", not guards. They stay for years, sometimes decades.
- Carmen, one staff member, has been there fifteen years and knows every young person by name, story, and what keeps them up at night.
- Territorial Director Jesus Teruel: *"We aren't jailers. We're not just enforcing a sentence to pass the months until they leave. We're here to work with them, to transmit values, to show them there's a different way."*
- The model: *"Think of good parenting. A good parent maintains clear boundaries while providing unconditional worth. They balance accountability with support, consequences with care."*

Diagrama has been running since 1991. This is not experimental. It works.

## Goods on Country — The Bed as Justice Argument

The essay makes an unusual link: between a bed and a courtroom.

[[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] (led by Nicholas Marchesi at A Curious Tractor) manufactures essential goods — starting with a bed made from recycled plastic, galvanised steel, and heavy-duty Australian canvas — with remote Indigenous communities. 400+ beds delivered (v.1 to v.3) across eight communities. A containerised production facility makes ~30 beds a week.

Why this belongs in a youth justice argument:
- Ivy on Palm Island: *"Hardly anyone around the community has beds. When family comes to visit, people sleep on the floor."*
- One in three children in remote communities has scabies at any given time. Scabies → Rheumatic Heart Disease. 59% of remote homes lack washing machines.
- Kids who are sick don't go to school. Kids who don't go to school end up in the system.
- The connection between a bed and a courtroom is *"not theoretical. It is a line you can draw with your finger."*

Linda Turner (Tennant Creek): *"We've never been asked at what sort of house we'd like to live in."*

The cultural backbone of Goods on Country is [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]. Elder Dianne Stokes co-designed and named the Pakkimjalki Kari washing machine in Warumungu language. Norman Frank Jupurrurla (Warumungu Elder and housing advocate) guides community engagement.

## JusticeHub as Infrastructure

The essay situates [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] as the data layer making all of this visible:

- 800+ verified interventions, organisations, and programs mapped across every state and territory
- $1 billion in justice spending tracked, line by line
- Shows the gap between what governments spend on detention and what they invest in what actually works
- "All of it public. All of it sourced. All of it designed to make the case that communities already have the answers."

## The Call to Action

Four asks:

1. **Experience CONTAINED** — launching April 20, touring nationally. Bring colleagues, family, local MP. Thirty minutes.
2. **Nominate a decision-maker** — politicians, justice officials, media leaders, community figures who should walk through
3. **Back the tour** — funding to move the container across Australia
4. **Connect with organisations** — add programs to JusticeHub; use it to find what works; support [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]]

## Key Quotes

- Isaiah (helped build CONTAINED's first room, now at Interlace Advisory): *"I was just watching your face and you're like, 'What the f---?'"*
- Jesus Teruel (Diagrama, Spain): *"We aren't jailers. We're not just enforcing a sentence to pass the months until they leave."*
- Kristy Bloomfield (Oonchiumpa): *"These aren't 'bad kids'..."*
- Fred Campbell (Oonchiumpa youth case worker, on Xavier building his first Stretch Bed): *"He just was so proud showing them that he can build it... his energy was a lot more higher."*

## Connections

- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — the installation this essay launches
- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the evidence platform referenced throughout
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — Alice Springs program featured at length
- [[mounty-yarns|Mounty Yarns]] — Mount Druitt program
- [[picc|PICC]] — Palm Island program
- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — remote manufacturing, Indigenous enterprise
- [[diagrama|Diagrama Foundation]] — Spanish comparative model
- [[youth-justice-reform|Youth Justice Reform]] — the broader reform context

## Sources

- Raw: `wiki/raw/2026-04-07-jh-first-nations-oped.md`
- Author: Benjamin Knight (co-founder, A Curious Tractor)
- Published: 2026 (launch essay for CONTAINED April 20 tour)

> Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-07. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.

## Answer

## The argument in one sentence

Authority-at-the-edge is not new — it's been documented by Tyson Yunkaporta on this continent, by Elinor Ostrom across five continents, and by Fundación Diagrama at national scale in Spain — and JusticeHub is the world model that lets community-led justice compound across Australia the way the hierarchy has refused to.

## The three-anchor framing

| Voice | Lineage | Contribution to the argument |
|---|---|---|
| **Tyson Yunkaporta** | Apalech (Wik), Nungar, Lost Mob | *Sand Talk* — Aboriginal thinking is a structural refusal of hierarchy. Songlines as a working world model that has run for 65,000 years. Authority sits with the people closest to the consequence. |
| **Elinor Ostrom** | Nobel Prize Economics 2009 | Decades of fieldwork (Nepal, Maine, Spain, Swiss alps) proving distributed governance outperforms hierarchy where authority sits with the people closest to the consequence and they can see each other's solutions. |
| **Jack Dorsey / Block** | *From Hierarchy to Intelligence* (2026) | The contemporary tech footnote — "even fintech caught up". Capabilities + world model + intelligence layer + people at the edge. Demoted from headline because the pattern is older than Block. |

## The proof points that survive scrutiny

1. **Bourke / Maranguka** — KPMG-evaluated. 23% violent crime drop, 38% major offences drop, 42% fewer custody days, ROI $3.10:$1. Town-scale, community-led, hard data. Canonical Australian case.
2. **Oonchiumpa (Mparntwe)** — MS story: identity restoration is the mechanism, not behaviour management. 95% diversion, 97.6% lower cost. Quote from Tanya Turner: *"knowing who you are, knowing where you come from, knowing who your family is."*
3. **Fundación Diagrama (Spain)** — 30+ centres, 30 years, reoffending 20–30% vs Australia's 85%. Government-funded, community-run. Answers the "does it scale?" question with three decades of national-scale evidence.

Notably **dropped**: BG Fit (single program, not a scalable model). Confit Pathways (replaced by Maranguka which is more rigorously evaluated and geographically consistent).

## Architecture mapping (Block → JusticeHub)

| Block layer | JusticeHub equivalent | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Capabilities | 1,387 verified community models tagged in ALMA | Built |
| World model | ALMA + CivicGraph (98,418 orgs, $94.6B tracked, 56% linkage) | 80% built |
| Intelligence layer | Composing capabilities into proactive routing — Hypercerts + ImpactQF (Allo Protocol) | Designed, not yet wired |
| Interfaces | justicehub.com.au, ALMA Chat, CONTAINED tour | Live |
| The edge | The Aunties, ACCOs, tribal councils, Elders, mentors who do the work | Already exists — we just stop interrupting it |

## Three Ripples — the visual model

Concentric ripples emanating from a young person on Country:

- **Ripple 1 — The Edge**: Country, community, family, the relationship. Where the healing is.
- **Ripple 2 — The World Model**: ALMA + CivicGraph + the wiki. The legibility layer the hierarchy refused to build.
- **Ripple 3 — The Capital Rails**: Hypercerts + ImpactQF. Capital that follows verified outcomes without asking the machinery for permission.

Earth-tone palette. Centre slightly off-centre. No arrows pointing inward — propagation only outward. Optional dashed fourth ring labelled "The state, eventually".

## The Minderoo ask (model)

**$500K → wire ALMA + CivicGraph + JusticeHub into a national legibility layer.** Catalytic capital, not operational. Minderoo gets first-mover credit on the only architecture that has ever produced inverse-cost outcomes at scale. Aligns with Walk Free, Generation One, Thrive by Five — JusticeHub becomes the legibility layer for everything they already fund. Indigenous Data Sovereignty by design (OCAP, CARE, Mukurtu).

The leverage: $500K illuminates a $94.6B sector navigating in the dark. Even a 10% diversion produces savings dwarfing the grant by orders of magnitude.

## What this enables

Once the world model is wired, every future query against Tractorpedia about justice, community capital, or systems change builds on this framing. The next funder ask (whether to Minderoo, Lord Mayor's, Ian Potter, or VFFF) starts from this synthesis instead of being re-derived. The next blog post inherits the architecture. The CONTAINED tour rooms can be designed around the three ripples. JusticeHub's homepage can re-render around the Three Ripples diagram.

This is the compounding loop in practice — one synthesis becomes the seed for ten downstream artefacts.

pages.title: The Full Idea
pages.excerpt: A community-led infrastructure for youth justice in Australia. Three rings of work. Seven methods. Ten anchor communities. Three years to make it visible at scale.
pages.content:
> *A community-led infrastructure for youth justice in Australia. Three rings of work. Seven methods. Ten anchor communities. Three years to make it visible at scale.*

This document is the **complete idea**, in one place, written for walk-through review. Not a pitch to a specific funder. Not a deck. The whole architecture so it can be sat with, edited, and built from.

**How to use this document:** the headings below are the sections. Walk through them in order. At the end of each section there is an *Open questions* block — that is where to leave notes, corrections, and what should change. Each section is meant to be edited independently.

---

## §1 · What it is, in one paragraph

**STAY.** is a three-year program that leaves a library. Seven method books in **The STAY Series**, ten community volumes from ten anchor communities on Country, around fifty hand-stitched young-person Journals, and a national edition that goes to every electorate office in the country. The library is the proof — and it is the destination. A small team accompanies it into being by holding ten Indigenous-led communities over three years, wiring the infrastructure that makes their work legible (CivicGraph + the Australian Living Map of Alternatives + Empathy Ledger), and producing the artefacts the rest of the world will fly in to read.

The word **STAY** carries the whole methodology. *Stay where you are* — don't move children off Country to be punished. *Stay connected* — don't parachute in and leave. *Stay in the work* — don't file the artefact and forget. The library is the form all three meanings take.

> **Open questions §1**
> - "Ends in a library" — right verb? Or "becomes" / "leaves" / "produces"?
> - "The world will fly in to read" — strong enough this early in the doc, or save it for §7?
> - Ten communities locked? (Three Circles canon = ten; original Staying tier was seven)

---

## §2 · Why it exists

Australian youth justice has more reports, frameworks, evaluations, peak bodies, lived-experience panels, and government strategies than at any point in its history.

It also has more children in detention, more recidivism, and more lateral violence in the sector than at any point in recent memory.

**The problem is not absence of evidence.** It is that the evidence, the relationships, and the stories are all held in different rooms — and the rooms don't talk to each other.

- Frameworks live in consultancy decks.
- Stories live in unfunded community organisations.
- Funding flows live in spreadsheets nobody reads.
- Indigenous knowledge lives where it has always lived — in Country, in Elders, in Tuesday afternoon check-ins that no funder has ever counted as governance.

The cost of detaining one Australian child for one year: **$1.33M** *(ROGS 2024–25)*.
The projected detention rate for Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander children by 2030–31: **24.6 per 10,000** *(Closing the Gap)*.

We are not here to argue these numbers. We are here to **answer** them.

> **Open questions §2**
> - Is the cost figure right ($1.33M)? Should we use the 3-year figure ($3.9M) instead?
> - Anything missing from the "different rooms" framing?

---

## §3 · What is already built

This program is **not starting from zero.** The infrastructure layer is already shipping:

| Layer                                     | What it is                                                                                     |                                                                                                         Live numbers |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: |
| **CivicGraph**                            | The legibility layer — entities, relationships, place-mapping, daily syncs from public sources |       **100,036** entities · **199,001** relationships · **94.1%** entity-match accuracy · **96%** postcode coverage |
| **Australian Living Map of Alternatives** | The case library of community-led models that already work                                     | **1,775** community models, of which **128** are verified at the top three tiers (Indigenous-led, Effective, Proven) |
| **JusticeHub**                            | The public-facing front end — search, dossiers, MCP agent tools, place pages                   |                                                                       Live at justicehub.com.au · 6 live agent tools |
| **Empathy Ledger**                        | Consent and sovereignty layer — every voice transcript, every story, every consent             |                                                         **226** storytellers · OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer |
| **CONTAINED**                             | The companion exhibition — a shipping container on the road, currently at Mounty Yarns         |                                                                                                          Active tour |
| **Justice funding tracking**              | Indexed records of grants, contracts, donations, procurement                                   |                              **52K** justice funding records · **672K** AusTender contracts · **312K** AEC donations |

The full stack: **CivicGraph + Living Map + JusticeHub + Empathy Ledger + CONTAINED.**

This is the answer to *"how do you know it works?"* — built so communities can witness, document, verify, and publish what already works on their own terms.

> **Open questions §3**
> - Are these the right numbers to lead with?
> - Anything missing? Should EL v2 or the bot integrations be on this list?

---

## §4 · The seven models

These are the seven methods the program runs on. Each one has its own page in the journal: cover on the left, explanation on the right. Here they are in journal order with the locked copy and the diagram.

---

### §4.1 · The Three Circles

![](../output/three-circles-journal-spread.png)

**Subtitle:** *A community-led methodology for working with people the system has failed.*

**The model:**

| # | Circle | Who | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The Edge** | The people the system has failed hardest. | First. Always. |
| 2 | **The Next** | The kin, workers, advocates immediately around them. | Second. Strengthened by what comes from the centre. |
| 3 | **The Rest** | Funders, government, sector. | Last. Changed by what travels outward. |

**Tagline:** *start at the edge. work outward.*

> *"Authority sits with the people closest to the consequence."* — Tyson Yunkaporta, after 65,000 years.
>
> Documented again by Elinor Ostrom across five continents. Proven at national scale by Fundación Diagrama in Spain over thirty years.
>
> The Three Circles is the methodology: start where the system has failed hardest, and let the work travel outward. Most programs do the opposite. Most programs fail.

> **Open questions §4.1**
> - Does the diagram land?
> - Anything in the back-blurb that needs softening or sharpening?

---

### §4.2 · The Living Map Loop

![](../output/alma-loop-journal.png)

**Subtitle:** *How communities grow the Australian Living Map of Alternatives.*

**The four moves:**

| # | Step | What happens | Who does it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **WITNESS** | Someone notices a working model the formal system has never recognised. | A community member, a worker, anyone willing to look. |
| 2 | **DOCUMENT** | The model gets captured properly — story, mechanism, conditions, outcomes — in the witness's own voice. | Storyteller + the person running the model. |
| 3 | **VERIFY** | Community sovereignty over what counts as proof. Elder-, kin-, place-led validation. **Not** academic peer review. **Not** government audit. | The community itself, on its own terms. |
| 4 | **PUBLISH** | The entry joins the Map. Now searchable, citable, fundable. | The Map (the infrastructure does the rest). |

**Tagline:** *the things that work are already happening. we just have to write them down — properly.*

> 1,775 community-led models, and growing.
> 128 already verified by Elders, communities, or trials.
> The rest are the work — and the Loop is how we move them up the ladder.
>
> The system doesn't know what works because it never asked. The Australian Living Map of Alternatives is the answer to that — built so communities can witness, document, verify and publish *what already works*, on their own terms.
>
> Every entry attracts the next witness. The library grows by recognition, not by extraction.

> **Open questions §4.2**
> - Is the WITNESS / DOCUMENT / VERIFY / PUBLISH naming right?
> - 1,775 / 128 — confirm or update.

---

### §4.3 · Three Ripples

![](../output/three-ripples-journal-spread.png)

**Subtitle:** *The infrastructure that makes the edge legible to capital.*

**The rings:**

| Ring | Name | What it actually is | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The Edge** | Country, kin, the relationship | Maranguka 23%↓ violent crime · Oonchiumpa 95% diversion |
| 2 | **The World Model** *(CivicGraph)* | The legibility layer the hierarchy refused to build | 100,036 entities · 199,001 relationships · 94.1% match accuracy |
| 3 | **Funding That Finds You** | Capital that follows verified outcomes | 672K contracts indexed · 312K donations · 52K justice funding records |
| 4 *(dashed)* | *the state, eventually* | The hierarchy catches up last | — |

**The two horizons of Ring 3:**

| | **TODAY — the familiar rail** | **TOMORROW — the new rail** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Grants and contracts already in use — but routed by the world model so they actually land at the edge | Capital that follows verified outcomes without going through the hierarchy |
| What changes | Same instrument. Different routing. | The instrument itself changes. |
| Examples | Targeted grants, justice reinvestment, place-based contracts | Hypercerts, ImpactQF, outcomes contracts |

> 100,036 entities. 199,001 relationships. 94.1% match accuracy.
>
> The legibility layer the hierarchy refused to build — wired so capital can find the edge two ways: the way you already know, and the way you didn't know was possible yet.
>
> *Funding that finds you, instead of you having to find it.*

> **Open questions §4.3**
> - Hypercerts + ImpactQF — still the right naming or has it shifted?
> - Are CivicGraph numbers OK on the cover?

---

### §4.4 · I Have · I Am · I Can

![](../output/intentionality-canvas-journal-spread.png)

**Subtitle:** *Nine resources every child draws on to face adversity.*

**The nine resources:**

| | Category | What it is | Three items |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I HAVE** | external supports — what's around me | trusting, loving relationships · role models who show what resilient looks like · people who set limits with care |
| **I AM** | inner strengths — what I carry | respectful of myself · confident and optimistic · empathic and caring of others |
| **I CAN** | skills — what I do | solve problems · stay with a task / persevere · reach out for help when I need it |

**Tagline:** *resilience is contagious. its absence is also contagious.*

> Edith Grotberg studied street children in Lima — kids who'd lived on the streets for months or years, who'd used drugs, who'd been beaten by police, who'd sold sex for food. And she found the same thing she'd found in twenty other countries: the kids who *made it* drew on three pools of resources.
>
> **I have.** External supports — trusting relationships, role models, people who held the line.
> **I am.** Inner strengths — self-respect, confidence, empathy.
> **I can.** Skills — problem-solving, perseverance, knowing when to ask for help.
>
> Most programs design for the visible deficit. The resilience research says: design for the nine.
>
> And the hardest finding from Lima — from the families displaced by political violence: *resilience is contagious. Its absence is also contagious.* When the parents fled into trauma, the children fell with them. When the parents engaged the new world, the children rose with them. Whatever you build for a child, build the same thing for the adults around the child — or the child has no model to copy.
>
> *— after Edith Henderson Grotberg, Resilience in Street Children and in Victims of Political Violence in Peru, Lima 2006.*

> **Open questions §4.4**
> - The nine items — keep as-is or swap any?
> - JusticeHub logo placeholder — which logo file should be composited in?

---

### §4.5 · The Field Canvas

![](../output/field-diagnostic-journal-spread.png)

**Subtitle:** *Look honestly at the whole field — above the soil and below — before you change anything.*

**The 5 P scan:**

| Domain | What you read | Hidden pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **Projects** | What's active. What's earning. What's stalled. | Where money comes from vs where energy goes. |
| **People** | Who's here. Who's paid. Who decides. | The unspoken pay gap. The implicit operating agreement. |
| **Pulses** | Operating rhythm. Weekly / monthly / quarterly. | Whether urgency is driving priority instead of strategy. |
| **Process** | How work moves through. Closure rate. | Starting is easy, finishing is hard. WIP creep. |
| **Products** | What's packaged. What's priced. Go-to-market. | "If we build it well enough, they'll come" — they don't. |

**The PTO discipline:** *the tractor powers one implement at a time.*

| Lane | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ⚡ **Drive** | Connect the PTO now. Maximum 3 projects. |
| 🌱 **Field** | Planted. Not powered yet. Hold the line. |
| 🔧 **Shed** | Park, sunset, or hand over. |

**The 90-day Furrow Plan** — six tracks every diagnostic ends in: Mission, Revenue, People, Product, Partnerships, Rhythm. Each one with an action verb, a target, and the proof it landed.

**Tagline:** *what grows above is a function of the soil below.*

> Most strategic plans fail because they describe the field above the ground and ignore the soil below. The Field Canvas is the tool that makes you look at both.
>
> Above: revenue, platforms, community, proof — the things outsiders see. Below: culture, operations, market — the soil that's either growing the visible work or rotting it. And under that, the root system: the infrastructure, relationships, philosophy and financial spine that connect everything.

> **Open questions §4.5**
> - Is the outback eucalyptus visual the right metaphor or does it need to change?
> - The 5 P spine — lock or change one?

---

### §4.6 · Listen · Curiosity · Action · Art

![](../output/lcaa-loop-journal.png)

**Subtitle:** *A Curious Tractor's operating system. Four phases. One loop.*

**The four phases:**

| # | Phase | What you do | The discipline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Listen** | Receive what's already there. Country, Traditional Owners, Community, Elders, Youth, the Silenced. | **Don't arrive with solutions.** |
| 2 | **Curiosity** | Follow the threads. *What if? Who says it has to be this way?* | **Resist premature closure.** |
| 3 | **Action** | Build, prototype, test, iterate. Co-creation. Ship early. Document for handover. | **If you can't hand it over, you're still in Curiosity.** |
| 4 | **Art** | The work made beautiful, meaningful, lasting. | **Art is how we know we've learned something.** |

**Tagline:** *art returns us to listen. the cycle continues.*

> *If you can't hand it over, you're still in Curiosity.*
>
> Most methodologies are checklists. Listen, Curiosity, Action, Art is a loop — and the loop never closes.
>
> The journal you are holding is art. The CONTAINED tour is art. This story is art. They will all return us to Listen.

> **Open questions §4.6**
> - Drop the acronym entirely on covers? (current rule says yes)
> - Keep all four discipline lines on the right page or trim?

---

### §4.7 · Fire Crescendo

![](../output/fire-crescendo-journal.png)

**Subtitle:** *On building things slowly. Year 1 to Year 3.*

**The six stages × three years:**

| # | Stage | Year | What's happening |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ember | Y1 | A single relationship. One Elder. One yarn. |
| 2 | Tinder | Y1 | Trust. Showing up when you said you would. |
| 3 | Kindling | Y2 | Small structured work. The first camp. The first cohort. |
| 4 | Campfire | Y2 | Communities visit each other. Storytellers tell their own stories. |
| 5 | Roaring fire | Y3 | The work spreads. Other communities ask how. |
| 6 | Bonfire | Y3 | Holding warmth for people who weren't there at the start. |

**Tagline:** *fire does not arrive at bonfire stage. you build it, slowly, with attention.*

> Most programs fail because someone tries to light the bonfire in Year 1. Funders ask for bonfire-shaped outcomes from ember-stage work. Boards demand scale before the kindling has even caught.
>
> Fire Crescendo is the diagram that gives funders the language to fund Year 1 properly — and gives the team the language to say *"no, not yet."*

> **Open questions §4.7**
> - CAMPFIRE worked example (Brodie Germaine, Mount Isa) — separate page after this one. Confirmed.
> - Six stages or three?

---

## §5 · The proposition

A three-year program shaped as three movements. The movements come from Listen · Curiosity · Action · Art compressed into the program's whole arc:

| Year | Name | Where | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Year 1** | *Listen* | The ten anchor communities, in Australia | Heavy in-community engagement. Relationships. The first round of journals begins. The infrastructure layer (CivicGraph + Living Map + Empathy Ledger) is wired to the field arm so every story has a home. |
| **Year 2** | *Compare* | Distributed European exchange | Each community sends a young person + a support person to **one** European destination — Diagrama (Spain), Halt (Holland), or the Children's Hearings system (Scotland). Reciprocal European visits to Australia in the same year. Brings the international peer relationship into the journal. |
| **Year 3** | *Tell* | Back to the ten communities, then outward | Ten community-led launches in the ten places. A published book gathers the ten journals into a single national volume. The work goes home before it goes to the city. |

Three acts. Listen / Compare / Tell. Funders, audiences, and books all need three acts.

> **Open questions §5**
> - Ten or seven communities? (Three Circles canon = ten; Staying tier = seven)
> - Is the "Compare" frame for Year 2 right, or should it be "Curiosity"?

---

## §6 · The ten anchor communities

Final selection through assertive in-community visits — the only verification that works. There is no funnel. We start with the people we already know and trust, then radiate outward through trust, recommendation, and openness. **The filter is relationship, not process.**

| State | Likely candidate | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **NT** | Oonchiumpa (Mparntwe) — Aunty Bev, Tanya Turner, Kristy Bloomfield | Existing partnership ✓ |
| **QLD (north)** | PICC (Palm Island) — Richard Cassidy, Bwgcolman families | Existing partnership ✓ |
| **QLD (Mount Isa)** | CAMPFIRE — Brodie Germaine | Existing partnership ✓ |
| **QLD (Brisbane region)** | EPIC Pathways / MMEIZC (Stradbroke) / Toowoomba — three-way pick | Open |
| **NSW** | Maranguka (Bourke Tribal Council) | Need to approach |
| **NSW** | Mounty Yarns (Mt Druitt) | Existing relationship |
| **WA** | Olabud Doogethu (Halls Creek) | Need to approach |
| **TAS** | Prevention Not Detention (Loic Fery's coalition) | Pipeline contact |
| **VIC** | OPEN | — |
| **SA** | OPEN | — |

**This is not 10 grants. It is 10 long-term relationships** the centre learns from, the international tour celebrates, and the artefact in Year 3 is built around.

**Cultural protocol — non-negotiable:**

1. No community is approached without prior consultation with existing ACT relationships in that region.
2. Elder and Council sign-off before any photographs, recordings, or journals begin.
3. OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer via Empathy Ledger — the legal and technical baseline, not aspirational.
4. Young person owns their journal. Right of withdrawal at any point.
5. Subjects under 18 require guardian and cultural authority sign-off.
6. Cultural review fees are budgeted as line items, not absorbed as goodwill labour.
7. No exhibition opens without at least one young person or cultural representative present.
8. Income from book/exhibition sales flows on a published transparent split to subjects and their nominated community organisations.

> **Open questions §6**
> - VIC + SA candidates — how do we source them?
> - Should CAMPFIRE be its own slot or counted under QLD-north?

---

## §7 · The Library — *The STAY Series*

> *At the end of this program we have a library. Not a report. A library.*

Imagine a shelf. Aged cream spines, hand-set serif type, soft wear at the corners. Seven slim Penguin Modern Classics-style paperbacks lined up — **The STAY Series, No. 01 through No. 07** — and leaning against them at the end of the row, a stack of hand-stitched young-person Journals. Behind the shelf, ten community volumes. In front of the shelf, an open invitation: *come here to learn.*

This is the move that takes the program from **framework to action**, from *thinking about the work* to *the work itself in your hands*.

![](../output/the-library-shelf.png)

### What's on the shelf

#### The STAY Series — the seven method books

| No. | Title | Subtitle |
|---:|---|---|
| **01** | THE THREE CIRCLES | *Start at the edge. Work outward.* |
| **02** | THE LIVING MAP LOOP | *1,775 community models, and growing.* |
| **03** | THREE RIPPLES | *The infrastructure of the edge.* |
| **04** | I HAVE · I AM · I CAN | *Nine resources for resilience.* |
| **05** | THE FIELD CANVAS | *Look at the whole field. Above and below.* |
| **06** | LISTEN · CURIOSITY · ACTION · ART | *Four phases. One loop.* |
| **07** | FIRE CRESCENDO | *On building things slowly.* |

The series mark on every spine: **`THE STAY SERIES · NO. 01`** through **`NO. 07`**. Same paper, same serif, same roundel position, same photography setup. They read as a series the moment Lucy — or anyone — sees them on a shelf.

#### The other layers of the library

| Layer | What it is | How many |
|---|---|---|
| **Young-person Journals** | Bound book per young person — A5, hand-stitched, ~80–120 pages. Portraits, handwriting, voice transcripts, letters from Aunties and uncles, ledger entries of who showed up and when, the European exchange visit as its own chapter. | ~50 — one per young person across the ten communities |
| **Community volumes** | One bound volume per community — collected work, place, voices, photographs, the model running in real life. | 10 — one per anchor community |
| **Travel Diaries** *(bidirectional — see §7.5)* | The same notebook a young person from Mparntwe takes to Murcia, and the same notebook an Olga from Diagrama takes to Mount Isa. The diary that becomes the meeting place. | One per visiting cohort, both directions |
| **The national edition** | A single printed volume gathering the ten community volumes (with consent) into one national artefact. | 1 — every electorate office gets a copy |

**Owned by the young people.** Not ACT. Not the funder. OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer through Empathy Ledger. Right of withdrawal at any point. Income from sales flows on a published transparent split to subjects and their nominated community organisations.

### What the library *does*

The shelf is not the end. It is the **beginning of the second program** — the one that runs when the books exist:

1. **People can read the work.** A magistrate in Hobart, a Minister in Canberra, an Aunty in Halls Creek, a youth worker in Birmingham — the methodology is now a thing they can hold, not a deck they have to sit through.
2. **People can buy the work.** The books go to bookshops, libraries, schools. The royalties flow back to communities and young people on a published split.
3. **People can come to the work.** The library becomes a tour: visitors fly into Australia to learn the methods *in the places they were built*. Mount Isa, Mparntwe, Palm Island, Halls Creek. Indigenous-led learning. The kind of civic-tech tourism Spain has been doing for thirty years through Diagrama — but here, on Country, with the people who built it.
4. **Young people can teach the work.** The young people whose journals are on the shelf become **the teachers**. They show their books. They walk visitors through their journey. They explain the methods in their own words. *The library makes them publishers and hosts, not subjects.*
5. **Other communities can write their own books.** The seven methods are forkable. The journal template is forkable. A community in Birmingham, in Lima, in Murcia, in Christchurch can pick up the series and add their own volumes — and the library grows.

### The macro reframe

This is what moves Australia from a country that **imports** youth justice frameworks to a country that **exports** them. From the place that has the highest Indigenous incarceration rate in the OECD to the place the rest of the world flies in to learn from.

> *Indigenous thinking. World model. Visitors invited in. Australia as the world-leading community model.*
>
> The library is not the report. The library is the proof — and the destination.

### The components, in detail

**The seven method books.** The Penguin-style series. Already designed. Live in `wiki/output/`. Each one has its own page in the journal (covers in §4 of this document). They are the *first run of the press.*

**The young-person Journals.** Year 3 delivery. Hand-stitched. The visual register is the **ledger page** — Christian Boltanski, Sophie Calle, Edmund Clark, Theaster Gates, Anselm Kiefer, Judy Watson, Daniel Boyd, Vernon Ah Kee, Tony Albert, Brook Andrew. Hand-made, lived-in, accumulated over time, the young person at the centre. See `tools/three-ripples-ledger.html` for the visual mockup.

**The community volumes.** One per anchor community, accumulating across all three years. Bound at the end of Year 3 alongside each community-led launch.

**The national edition.** The one volume that gathers the ten community volumes into a single national artefact. Sent to every electorate office. Sold publicly. The thing on the shelf in the public library.

**The companion exhibition (CONTAINED).** The shipping container on the road. Travels alongside the launches. The library you walk *into.*

**The platform underneath (CivicGraph + Living Map + JusticeHub + Empathy Ledger).** The infrastructure side of the library. Every voice in a journal traces back to a CivicGraph entity. Every model in a method book is verified through the Living Map. The library has receipts.

> **Open questions §7**
> - "The STAY Series" naming — locked.
> - The shelf as hero image — three variants generating in parallel. Pick one.
> - The "young people as teachers" frame — keep gentle (current) or sharper ("the publishers, not the subjects")?
> - Royalty split — who decides the percentages? When?
> - **TODO:** the seven covers themselves currently have no series mark on the spine. Next round of cover re-spins should bake in **`THE STAY SERIES · NO. 01`** through **`NO. 07`** on the spine and bottom of front cover.

---

## §7.5 · The Travel Diary — *bidirectional, by design*

> *The same notebook a young person from Mparntwe takes to Murcia. The same notebook an Olga from Diagrama takes to Mount Isa.*

The Travel Diary is the meeting place. One physical object, one template, used in both directions. When the diary is on a desk in Spain it is the record of a young person from Country in Europe. When the diary is on a desk in Halls Creek it is the record of a European visitor learning at the source. The same notebook holds both.

This is the format that **operationalises *Australia as destination***. It's the artefact funders, magistrates, and the international civic-tech world walk away with — the proof that the traffic now flows both ways.

### The format

| | What's in it |
|---|---|
| **Cover** | Aged kraft, hand-stitched, with a small linocut symbol of the journey direction (an arrow, a plane, two sets of footprints) |
| **First spread** | Who is travelling, who is hosting, the dates, the Country at each end |
| **Daily entries** | Hand-written by the traveller. Photographs taped in. Receipts. Tickets. Pressed leaves. Notes on what was unexpected. Names of the people who held the room. |
| **The interview** | One long conversation with the host community, in their words. Voice transcript via Empathy Ledger sits alongside the handwritten version. |
| **The model encounter** | Which of the seven STAY Series methods showed up here? In what form? What did it look like in this place that it doesn't look like at home? |
| **What I'm taking back** | The traveller's own words on what they will carry home. |
| **What I'm leaving here** | A page the traveller writes for the host. Stays in the host's diary. |

### How it runs (bidirectional)

| Direction | Who travels | Who hosts | What gets made |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Outbound** *(AU → Europe)* | A young person + a support person from each of the ten anchor communities | Diagrama (Spain), Halt (Holland), Children's Hearings (Scotland) | Ten outbound diaries — one per community pairing |
| **Inbound** *(Europe → AU)* | Small delegations from each European host | The ten anchor communities, hosting on Country | Three inbound diaries — one per European delegation |

**Total: ~13 Travel Diaries per cycle.** Each one becomes a chapter in the relevant young-person Journal *and* a standalone publication that joins the library.

### Why this matters

It collapses the centre-and-periphery framing every philanthropic conversation about Indigenous justice gets stuck in. Spain has been receiving international visitors for thirty years through Diagrama. The Travel Diary is the move that turns Australia into the **other end** of that exchange — not the place that sends people away to learn, but the place people come *to.*

The diary makes the reciprocity legible in a way a report cannot. Two notebooks, sitting next to each other on the library shelf, one Australian and one Spanish — both filled out by the same kind of hand, both in the same template — is the entire argument made physical.

> *The traffic flows both ways. The proof is on the desk.*

> **Open questions §7.5**
> - Format — kraft hand-stitched (current) or aged-cream Penguin-style to match the STAY Series?
> - Naming — "Travel Diary" (current) or "Field Notebook" or "Crossing"?
> - Should the inbound diaries be one per delegation (3) or one per community-host pairing (10)?
> - Does the diary need its own numbering inside the STAY Series — e.g. "NO. 08–20" — or is it a separate sub-series called "STAY · Crossings"?

---

## §8 · The team and cadence

**Lean by design.** Two people, not twenty.

- **1 FTE lead + 1 support person** — the core team that rotates through the ten communities
- **4 months on / 8 months off** rhythm — heavy in-community engagement when present, processing and journal production when home
- **One community close to Brisbane** for cheap, frequent low-friction visits and a shorter feedback loop
- **Cultural review fees and Elder governance** budgeted as line items, not absorbed as goodwill labour
- **The infrastructure layer** (CivicGraph, Living Map, Empathy Ledger, JusticeHub) is maintained by the existing ACT engineering team — not a new hire

This is the smallest possible team that can hold ten communities with depth. Anything bigger overwhelms a community when it arrives. Anything smaller can't sustain the cadence.

> **Open questions §8**
> - 1+1 vs 2+1? (current draft = 1+1)
> - 4/8 vs 6/6? (current draft = 4/8)

---

## §9 · The ask (in three tiers)

> *Fire does not arrive at bonfire stage. You build it, slowly, with attention.* — Model 07

The three tiers borrow the language of **Fire Crescendo** — the seventh book in the STAY Series — because the budget tells the same story as the methodology. A funder picks where they want to enter the fire.

| | **🔥 Foundation** | **🔥🔥 Crescendo** | **🔥🔥🔥 Bonfire** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3-year total** | ~$1.8M | **~$3.43M** | ~$6.0M |
| **Annual flow** | ~$600K/year | ~$1.0M / $1.24M / $1.20M | ~$2.0M/year |
| **Communities** | 5 anchor | **10 anchor** | 10 + annual national gathering |
| **Team** | 1 FTE lead | 1 FTE + 1 support | 2 FTE + 1 support |
| **Cadence** | 3 months on / 9 off | 4 / 8 | 6 / 6 |
| **Year 2 — international exchange** | Deferred — one small scoping trip | Distributed exchange, ~14 travellers (Spain · Holland · Scotland) | Full exchange + reciprocal AU visits + a full cohort week per host country |
| **The library — young-person Journals** | Year 3 only, simple binding | Year 3 only, hand-stitched + 1 archive | Three chapter deliveries (Y1 / Y2 / Y3), premium binding |
| **The library — community volumes** | 5 | **10** | 10 + slipcase boxed sets in every State Library |
| **The library — national edition** | — | 1 printed volume to every electorate office | 1 printed volume + national gallery tour (NGA / MCA / NGV / regional) |
| **Versus detaining 1 child for 3 years** *($3.9M)* | 46% of cost | **88% of cost** | 154% of cost |

**Crescendo is the default.** It is the shape that *moves*: small enough to fund without negotiation, big enough to do the work, structured so every line earns its place — and big enough that the library at the end is the real artefact, not a deliverable.

For context, the line that should never need to be defended in a funder meeting:

> Detaining one Australian child for three years costs $3.9M. **The Crescendo tier runs the entire program for less than that** — across ten Indigenous-led communities, sending fourteen people to Europe and bringing Europe back, and producing the seven-book STAY Series + ten community volumes + ~50 young-person journals + the national edition.

> **Open questions §9**
> - Tier names: **Foundation / Crescendo / Bonfire** — locked. Foundation is what Year 1 lays for the fire to build on; Crescendo is when it catches; Bonfire is when it's undeniable. The budget tells the same story as Model 07.
> - Move the *"vs detaining one child"* line up to §2 as well, or keep it here?
> - Communities at the Crescendo tier: locked at 10 to match Three Circles canon.

---

## §10 · The lineage

This idea is not new. It is the synthesis of four lines of evidence that have all been on the table for a long time:

| Voice | Lineage | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Tyson Yunkaporta** *(Sand Talk, 2019)* | Apalech (Wik), Nungar, Lost Mob | Aboriginal thinking is a structural refusal of hierarchy. Songlines as a working world model that has run for 65,000 years. **Authority sits with the people closest to the consequence.** |
| **Elinor Ostrom** *(Governing the Commons, 1990; Nobel 2009)* | Decades of fieldwork in Nepal, Maine, Spain, Swiss alps | Distributed governance *outperforms* hierarchy where authority sits with the people closest to the consequence and they can see each other's solutions. |
| **Fundación Diagrama** *(Spain, 30+ centres, 30 years)* | National-scale community-based youth justice | 20–30% reoffending vs Australia's 85%. Government-funded, community-run. The proof that this scales. |
| **Edith Henderson Grotberg** *(Resilience in Street Children and Victims of Political Violence in Peru, 2006)* | International resilience research | The I HAVE / I AM / I CAN framework. *Resilience is contagious. Its absence is also contagious.* |
| **Jack Dorsey / Block** *(From Hierarchy to Intelligence, 2026)* | Contemporary tech footnote | "Even fintech caught up." Capabilities + world model + intelligence layer + people at the edge. **Demoted from headline because the pattern is older than Block.** |

**The argument in one sentence:**

> Authority-at-the-edge is not new — Yunkaporta has been documenting it on this continent for thirty years, Ostrom proved it across five, Diagrama has been scaling it in Spain for thirty more, and Grotberg verified it in twenty countries with street children. What was always missing was the legibility infrastructure — the layer that lets capital, magistrates and the public see the work without going through the hierarchy. **We finally built it. It's called CivicGraph. The library on the next page is the proof.**

> **Open questions §10**
> - Lock the order: Yunkaporta first (place of standing), Dorsey demoted to footnote.
> - Add Maranguka and Oonchiumpa as Australian proof points alongside Diagrama?
> - The closing line — *"the library on the next page is the proof"* — does this assume the library spread is physically next? In the journal it is. In a slide deck it might not be. Worth a sharper version that travels.

---

## §11 · What's next

This document is the **starting point for review**, not the final shape. The walk-through process:

1. **Read each section in order.** The h2 headings are the navigation in Obsidian's outline pane.
2. **Edit each "Open questions" block** with notes, corrections, things to change.
3. **Tell me which sections need iteration first.** I'll work through them one at a time.

**Sections most likely to need iteration:**

- §5 (proposition) — depends on whether we go with 7 or 10 communities
- §6 (the ten) — VIC and SA candidates still open
- §9 (the ask) — tier names and the headline number
- §10 (the lineage) — the "argument in one sentence" is the most quotable line in the whole doc, worth getting exactly right

**Sections most likely to be already locked:**

- §3 (what is built) — the numbers are from the live database, current as of 2026-04-08
- §4 (the seven models) — locked in `thoughts/shared/handoffs/staying/models-locked.md`

---

## Source documents

- `thoughts/shared/handoffs/staying/models-locked.md` — locked copy for all 7 models
- `thoughts/shared/handoffs/staying/visual-language.md` — visual language brief (Mode A covers + Mode B journal pages)
- `wiki/projects/staying.md` — original Staying program draft (2026-04-08, since reframed)
- `wiki/synthesis/the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is...md` — the synthesis underneath everything
- `wiki/concepts/lcaa-method.md` — canonical LCAA document
- `wiki/raw/2025-10-11-article-from-trouble-to-transformation-the-campfire-journey.md` — Brodie Germaine + CAMPFIRE
- `/Users/benknight/Downloads/grotberg2006_resilience-street-children-peru.pdf` — Grotberg's Lima paper
- Database queries against `alma_interventions` — the Living Map numbers (1,775 total · 128 verified)

pages.content:
> A regenerative community hub in Witta, QLD — seasonal kitchen, garden centre, workshops, and venue hire on the former Green Harvest site, bringing together local produce, native plants, and hands-on learning.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-HV | **Tier:** Ecosystem

## Overview

The Harvest (also known as Witta Harvest HQ) is a regenerative community hub located in Witta, Queensland (postcode 4552), operating from the former [[green-harvest-witta|Green Harvest]] site. It brings together a seasonal kitchen, a garden centre focused on native and productive plants for the Sunshine Coast, artisan workshops, and a flexible venue space — all grounded in regenerative land practice and local food culture.

The physical site sits on Witta Farm, which remains in Nic's trust and is leased to [[act-ecosystem|ACT]] for retreats, R&D, and community programs. This arrangement makes The Harvest both a public-facing community business and a core piece of ACT's operational infrastructure.

## Key Details

- **Location:** Witta, QLD 4552 (former Green Harvest site)
- **Website:** [theharvestwitta.com.au](https://theharvestwitta.com.au)
- **Contact:** hello@theharvest.community
- **Trading hours:** Saturday–Sunday, 8am–2pm
- **Land arrangement:** Witta Farm held in Nic's trust, leased to ACT

## What's On Site

### Seasonal Kitchen
Breakfast and brunch service using local produce, operating within the weekend trading hours. The menu follows seasonal availability and reflects the surrounding food landscape of the Sunshine Coast hinterland.

### Garden Centre
Native and productive plants suited to the Sunshine Coast region — sourced and curated for home growers, community gardens, and regenerative smallholders.

### Workshops
Hands-on programs including pottery, food preserving, and gardening. These sit within ACT's broader R&D and community education mission.

### Venue Hire
Indoor-outdoor event space available for community gatherings, private events, and program delivery.

## Relationship to Green Harvest Witta

[[green-harvest-witta|Green Harvest Witta]] is part of the same location and project family. The Harvest builds on the legacy of Green Harvest — the original organic seed and gardening business that operated from this site — evolving it into a broader regenerative community hub.

## LCAA Phase

**Action** — the hub is active, trading, and demonstrating regenerative practice in daily operation. The workshop and education programs extend into **Curiosity** and **Art** phases through hands-on learning and creative practice.

## Programs

### CSA (Community Supported Agriculture)
Seasonal produce shares, member subscriptions, and local farmer partnerships — reflecting the Jinibara Country land rhythms.

### Events
Seasonal gatherings, workshops, community markets, and venue hire running through the year.

### Enterprise Hub
Local business directory (businesses can claim and manage their profiles), maker pathways, and a business owner portal.

### Content Hub
The Harvest blog is served from the [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] Content Hub via the EL syndication API — community stories and seasonal content flowing from EL into the Harvest website automatically.

## Infrastructure & Operations

### Digital Platform

| Detail | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **Live URL** | [theharvestwitta.com.au](https://theharvestwitta.com.au) |
| **Alternate** | harvest.act.place |
| **GitHub** | [act-now-coalition/theharvest](https://github.com/act-now-coalition/theharvest) |
| **Hosting** | Vercel (frontend) |
| **Framework** | Vite + React 19, TypeScript — unique in ecosystem (not Next.js) |
| **API layer** | tRPC + Express |
| **ORM** | Drizzle |
| **Router** | Wouter (lightweight) |
| **Storage** | AWS S3 (presigned URLs for media) |
| **Local dev** | `pnpm dev` → http://localhost:3004 |

The Harvest uses a deliberate lightweight stack — Vite rather than Next.js, Wouter rather than React Router — reflecting its role as a community-facing site rather than a complex application platform.

### Supabase Edge Functions

Five edge functions run on the custom Supabase instance:
- `app-user-sync` — user synchronisation across systems
- `admin-events` — event CRUD for admin panel
- `admin-businesses` — business directory management
- `business-claim` — business ownership claim workflow
- `newsletter-subscribe` — newsletter signups

### External Integrations

- **GHL CRM:** Pipeline "Harvest", tags: `harvest`, `witta`, `csa`, `events`. Location tracking enabled for Witta/Maleny contacts.
- **Xero:** Tracking category `HARVEST`, project codes `HARVEST-CSA`, `HARVEST-VENUE`, `HARVEST-EVENTS`.

### Community Management

Platform routes cover both public visitors and community members:

| Section | Routes | Purpose |
|---------|--------|---------|
| Public | `/`, `/visit`, `/whats-on`, `/venue-hire` | Visitor information |
| Community | `/stories`, `/witta`, `/enterprises` | Place-based content |
| Admin | `/admin`, `/admin/photos`, `/my-business` | Operator management |

pages.title: The Harvest: Property Arc and Founding Vision
pages.excerpt: From NM's brainstorm to a signed lease — how the Witta property went from an idea to a physical site with milestones, budgets, and a community heartbeat.
pages.content:
> From NM's brainstorm to a signed lease — how the Witta property went from an idea to a physical site with milestones, budgets, and a community heartbeat.

**Compiled:** 2026-04-07 | **Source:** 17 ACT-HV meeting records (top 4 by content length analyzed)
**See also:** [[the-harvest|The Harvest]], [[place-land-practice|Place & Land Practice]]

---

## The Vision Before the Lease

### NM Brainstorm — The Compendium (February 2026)

The richest document in the Harvest meeting record isn't a meeting in the traditional sense — it's Nicholas Marchesi's brainstorm session that produced "The Compendium," the founding narrative of The Harvest. Structured in nine movements, it captures the complete vision:

**The Silence** — Witta has no gathering place. Two thousand cars pass through every weekend. One cafe. The hinterland is hollowing out; people drive through but never stop. The silence isn't peace — it's absence.

**The Shed** — Barry Rodgerig is 80 years old. He has been on this land since 1972. Before that, Peachester — 25 years of dairy, timber, and red soil. He drove tractors before he could see over the steering wheel. His shed is full of machines that built the Sunshine Coast hinterland: an AB184 log truck from 1963, ex-army Blitz trucks, a little Italian Valpadana with a Lombardini diesel, a 1957 Land Rover he'd like to restore "if I live long enough." He starts them up sometimes, just to hear them run. *"Rust is a terrible thing. It's just like cancer in humans."* Barry watched the hippies shut down the logging at Crystal Waters. He watched the government finish the job. He watched the hinterland turn from working country into scenic drive. His shed is archaeology — the living memory of what this place was.

**The Seed** — Four beliefs, not services: Eat. Gather. Make. Grow. A cafe is not a business; it's a daily act of showing up. A workshop is not a product; it's an invitation to make something together. A garden is not decoration; it's time made visible.

**The Cycle** — Shaun Fisher is a Goenpul man, one of the three clans of the Quandamooka People (Traditional Owners of Minjerribah/North Stradbroke Island). When colonisers arrived in Brisbane, they blew up the Quandamooka oyster leases for limestone — the Treasury building, the banks, the city's foundations. At The Harvest, Shaun sells oysters direct to community. The shells are collected and worked into benchtops and surfaces. Everything returnable. This is LCAA made physical: Listen → Curiosity → Action → Art → Listen.

**The Canvas** — Gallery, not museum. Nothing permanent. Pop-ups before capital. Oyster nights before a restaurant. Pizza from a trailer before a kitchen. The scaffold pavilion before the permanent structure. *You're not coming to something finished — you're coming to something you can be part of.*

**The Garden** — This was a nursery once. The bones are still here: shade cloth frames, irrigation lines, propagation benches. Witta has the highest homeschooling rate in Australia and no learning infrastructure. The garden changes that. You dig in. Plant a seedling. Pull a carrot. Take home herbs.

**The Table** — Not a meeting room. Not a networking event with name tags. A table with food on it, made from what grows here. The farmer sits next to the architect sits next to the kid who wants a milkshake. Nobody has to explain why they're here. Nobody has to pitch anything. If that works — if people come back, if they bring someone, if they start saying "see you next week" — then everything else follows.

**The Commons** — Not a venue. A platform. The connective tissue of the hinterland economy. Local producers come here to sell, teach, collaborate. Every dollar that moves through The Harvest stays local. The enterprise funds the commons — not shareholders, not landlords, not a head office in Sydney.

**The Handover** — Beautiful Obsolescence. Maybe it's ACT in Year 4. Maybe it's not. Every system built is ready to be handed over. Every role documented so someone local can step in. A Curious Tractor is exactly that — a PTO shaft that transfers power, not holds it.

This document pre-dates the signed lease by eight days. It was written before the contract — because the vision came before the property, not the reverse.

---

## The Negotiation

### Property Partnership Discussion (December 2025)

The first recorded meeting about the Witta lease is an internal ACT preparation session (BK and NM) before meeting Grant, the property owner. They proposed:

- **$50,000 upfront** to secure the space
- **Revenue share** — a performance-based component, up to an additional $50K/year, so Grant shares in the upside
- Model inspired by the "Queenslander" in Newrybar (micro-providers, seasonal produce, community events)

Key agreement items flagged: insurance, outgoings, subleasing rights for micro-tenants, maintenance responsibilities, modification permissions, and a clear invoicing and review cadence.

This meeting also contains the first explicit statement of what having a property means for ACT: *"What does having a property look like for ACT? $50,000 on the table and revenue share."* That sentence captures the shift from ACT as a mobile design-and-facilitation practice to ACT as a place-based organisation.

The session ended with a list of early activation ideas: *"Little start of the year pop-up dinner — January. Community contribution — being something that you donate — what can you bring."*

### Grant and Nic: Lease and Design Discussion (February 2026)

On 16 February 2026, Nicholas Marchesi sat down with Grant to finalise the lease and design approach. The outcome:

**Staged approach confirmed:**
- Phase 1 total: $117,800
- Phase 2 total: $132,200

**Phase 1 Milestones:**
- Milestone 1 — $40,000 (Feb 2026): Site establishment, mobilisation, community garden works commenced, access and amenities baseline
- Milestone 2 — $33,900 (Apr–Jun 2026): Outdoor builds — pavilion, timber/fire cooking, kids area
- Milestone 3 — $33,900 (May–Jun 2026): Phase 1 soft opening readiness

Grant pushed ACT on two things:
1. **Anchor points** — locals need a reason to come regularly, not just for one-off events. The place needs a consistent heartbeat.
2. **Simplicity first** — an 80/20 approach where "base mode" is simple and repeatable (coffee, straightforward food) before scaling the program. Don't build event-led before you've established daily cadence.

These are not just operational notes — they are design constraints. Grant's push shaped the sequencing: start with the table and the garden, earn the trust of the locals, then build.

The agreement was drafted for signing the next day. This meeting is the closure point for the Witta property arc — the moment the lease became real and the vision acquired a delivery schedule.

---

## What the Property Arc Means

The Harvest property arc runs from a visionary brainstorm to a signed lease in eight days, but the underlying journey is longer. Several features of this arc deserve attention:

**The vision preceded the site.** The Compendium was written before the agreement was finalised. ACT knew what The Harvest was before it knew where, exactly, it would be. The property gave the vision ground to stand on — it didn't generate the vision.

**The financial model is relational.** A standard commercial lease with Grant would have been simpler. ACT proposed revenue share precisely because it creates shared skin in the game. If The Harvest thrives, Grant benefits. This is the ACT commons model applied to a lease negotiation.

**Barry Rodgerig is not background.** In "The Shed" section of The Compendium, NM spends significant time with Barry — 80 years old, full of machines, full of stories. The decision to document Barry before the first shovel is moved reflects ACT's LCAA practice: listen before you build, every place has a story already being told.

**Shaun Fisher's oysters are the LCAA loop made physical.** The Quandamooka shell cycle at The Harvest — eaten, collected, worked into benchtops, returned to the land — is described in the Compendium as *"LCAA made physical."* This is not decoration. It is ACT's methodology manifested in food and material.

**The homeschooling fact is load-bearing.** Witta has the highest homeschooling rate in Australia. There is no learning infrastructure. The Harvest's garden-as-classroom is a direct response to a real gap — not a feature added for brand appeal.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| Dec 2025 | Internal prep: $50K upfront + revenue share proposal drafted |
| Feb 8, 2026 | NM Brainstorm: The Compendium written in full |
| Feb 16, 2026 | Grant & Nic: Lease aligned, Phase 1 milestones set |
| Feb 2026 | Milestone 1 invoice: $40,000, site establishment commences |
| Apr–Jun 2026 | Milestone 2: Pavilion, fire cooking, kids area |
| May–Jun 2026 | Milestone 3: Soft opening readiness |

---
