pages.title: Ways of Working
pages.excerpt: Our way of working is part of the output. How we show up is the first signal of trust.
pages.content:
> Our way of working is part of the output. How we show up is the first signal of trust.

## Overview

ACT's internal working practices aren't administrative procedures — they're expressions of values. The process is the product. If the way we work isn't respectful, the outcomes won't be either. This article documents the daily rhythms, meeting practices, media governance, and decision-making principles that keep the team aligned.

## Daily Practice

| Practice | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| **Listen first** | If in doubt, pause and return to community voice |
| **Use LCAA** | Structure planning and delivery through the phases |
| **Use ALMA** | Check ethics and learning quality |
| **Ground language** | Keep it non-extractive, honest, no savior framing |
| **Mark nuance** | Tag high-nuance partner details as `[INTERNAL ONLY]` |

## ACT Voice in Daily Work

When writing and communicating, hold these qualities:

| Quality | What It Means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Warm** | Approachable, human, inviting |
| **Grounded** | Based in practice, not theory |
| **Humble** | We don't have all the answers |
| **Visionary** | We see what's possible |
| **Professional yet rebellious** | Serious about the work, questioning the system |

**Do:** Use regenerative metaphors with restraint, ground claims in lived practice, acknowledge uncertainty, center community voice.

**Don't:** Corporate jargon, savior framing, overclaiming, speaking for communities.

See [[voice-guide|ACT Voice Guide]] for the full language system.

## Recurring Calls to Action

Small, repeatable actions that keep the model real:

1. Apply the [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] framework to every project plan and update
2. Route impact learning through Empathy Ledger and [[alma|ALMA]]
3. Keep enterprise pathways practical and community-led (The Harvest, Goods on Country)
4. Protect consent and cultural protocols at every stage
5. Review claims before external sharing

> If a call to action cannot be done this week, it is not a call to action.

## Meeting Practice

### Before
- Clear purpose documented
- Right people invited
- Materials shared in advance

### During
- Listen before speaking
- Note who holds authority
- Capture next actions clearly

### After
- Actions distributed within 24 hours
- Consent confirmed where needed
- LCAA phase noted

## Knowledge Capture

Weekly rhythms:
- Update the agent system with project slugs and ALMA signals
- Capture learnings in the appropriate space (Telegram or Discord)
- Review shareability before any external communication

## Media Governance

Empathy Ledger is the source of truth for stories, photos, video, and consent records.

Before using any media:
1. Check consent status
2. Verify current (not expired)
3. Confirm appropriate scope
4. Attribute properly

## Data Hygiene

Every record should have:
- Clear ownership
- Version tracking
- Consent flags
- Review date

## Infrastructure Philosophy

> "If a system is loud, it is not doing its job. Quiet systems create room for people to show up."

- Fewer tools, clearer pathways
- Faster handover
- Quiet reliability
- Infrastructure serves the work, not the other way around

See [[act-architecture|ACT Technical Architecture]] for how this applies to systems.

## Conflict Navigation

When principles seem to conflict, prioritize in this order:

1. **Country sets the pace** — Land and community readiness come first
2. **Community authority comes first** — Their voice, their decision
3. **Share with care** — If uncertain, keep internal

## Process Is Product

How we work reflects what we believe. Every interaction is an expression of values. There is no "once we scale, we'll do it properly" — the way we work now is the standard.

- [[governance-consent|Governance & Consent]] — consent practices embedded in daily work
- [[voice-guide|ACT Voice Guide]] — language guidance for writing and communication

pages.title: Y1 Art Release Program — 2026/27
pages.excerpt: Eight art projects across the first year, following the Daft Punk release cadence: each project is a "release" — a finished body of work that drops, gets one campaign push, then silence until the next. No daily content. No thought leadership. The work IS the marketing.
pages.content:
> Eight art projects across the first year, following the Daft Punk release cadence: each project is a "release" — a finished body of work that drops, gets one campaign push, then silence until the next. No daily content. No thought leadership. The work IS the marketing.

Total estimated budget: ~$200K. Funded from: existing grant runway + a Y1 Art Program application (Ian Potter / Creative Australia / Copyright Agency Cultural Fund) + customer co-funding where appropriate.

## The releases

### Release 1 — Brave Ones Phase 1 (April–May 2026)

Five studio-quality B&W portraits of Indigenous and system-impacted young people. The visual counterpoint to [[contained|CONTAINED]]. Brian Duffy / *Station to Station* register: high contrast, soft halation, film grain, deep blacks, silvery mid-tones.

- **Budget**: ~$15K (sittings, studio hire, printing, consent process)
- **Output**: 5 portraits + consent envelopes in [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] + gallery-ready prints
- **Trigger**: launches alongside CONTAINED Mount Druitt (April 20, 2026)
- **Revenue model**: co-funder naming rights ("The [Funder Name] Brave Ones Portrait Series"). Print sales + licensing income flows to subjects and nominated community organisations on transparent published split.
- **Reference**: `wiki/projects/justicehub/the-brave-ones.md`

### Release 2 — Extraordinarily Ordinary (JCF) (May–August 2026)

10–15 portraits of "ordinary people who change lives in simple ways" — the June Canavan Foundation's philosophical centre. Anne Gripper's mother. Ben's grandmother. JCF grantees from Sunshine Coast + East Africa.

- **Budget**: ~$15–30K (lower production value than Brave Ones; environmental portraits not studio, warmth over drama)
- **Output**: portrait series + interview excerpts in EL + a printed broadsheet or zine for JCF's board
- **Tone**: warm, soft, exploratory. "Acknowledgement is free."
- **Funded by**: JCF relationship (no direct ask; production costs absorbed or offset by other customer revenue)

### Release 3 — World Tour Travelogue (June–October 2026)

Ben's photographs and recordings from the Empathy Ledger Tour: Kenya safari → Uganda working week → Lesotho (STAY leg 1) → Amsterdam YOPE. Personal, observational, not promotional.

- **Budget**: ~$20K (travel already funded; this is production — editing, sequencing, printing)
- **Output**: photo book (self-published, 80–120 pages) OR short film (15–20 min) OR exhibition of 30 prints
- **Tone**: travelogue, intimate, no institutional voice. Ben as photographer, not as founder.
- **Decision**: book vs film vs exhibition — decide after the trip based on what the material wants to be

### Release 4 — Resonance Field Installation (August–October 2026)

A gallery show where visitors walk into a room and the Resonance Field is projected on walls — 738 faces drifting, cursor interaction, ambient drone. The brand made physical.

- **Budget**: ~$20–50K (venue, projection, AV hire, opening night, documentation)
- **Output**: 1–2 night exhibition in Brisbane or Sydney. Video documentation for future touring.
- **Venue targets**: IMA Brisbane, Carriageworks Sydney, or a shipping container (CONTAINED crossover)
- **Technical**: the observatory canvas rendered to high-res video (skia-canvas server path from the Resonance Field Phase 3 proposal) + a live interactive station

### Release 5 — STAY Journal Chapter 01 (September–December 2026)

The first bound journal artefact from the [[staying|STAY methodology]]. One community (Oonchiumpa or PICC). A5, hand-stitched, 80–120 pages. Contains: young person's own handwriting, voice transcripts from Empathy Ledger, portraits in Brave Ones register, letters from Aunties/Uncles, drawings, marks, place.

- **Budget**: ~$20–40K (photography, transcription, design, printing, cultural authority sign-off)
- **Output**: 50–100 copies of a physical journal. Owned by the young person. Right of withdrawal at any point. OCAP/CARE at the data layer.
- **Funded by**: Minderoo STAY if funded (EL studio budget $60K Y1); otherwise self-funded from EL customer revenue

### Release 6 — The Buttery: Fifty Years of Coming Home (October–February 2027)

200-page hardcover anthology documenting The Buttery's 50-year history — interviews, archival photos, Paul Kelly connection, timeline, program data, staff/alumni voices.

- **Budget**: ~$50–80K (design, photography, printing, editing, distribution)
- **Output**: printed book (500–1000 copies) for capital campaign distribution to funders, staff, alumni, community
- **Funded by**: The Buttery engagement budget + potential co-publication with a small press
- **Note**: the cinematic documentary (already in build at port 3031) launches alongside or slightly before

### Release 7 — The Buttery Cinematic Documentary (November 2026)

Short documentary (~15–20 minutes) using the cinematic/scrapbook design direction already locked. Supersonic-style, Paul Kelly soundtrack permission pending.

- **Budget**: ~$30K (editing, sound design, music licensing, colour grade)
- **Output**: screened at The Buttery's capital campaign launch event + embedded on the documentary site
- **Status**: already in build (design direction locked 2026-04-02, site at port 3031)

### Release 8 — Resonance Field Public Embed Campaign (ongoing)

Partner with 5 orgs to embed their Resonance Field on their public websites. An ACT-branded "Participating Voices" directory at act.place links all the fields together.

- **Budget**: ~$0 extra production cost (infrastructure already shipped)
- **Output**: 5 live Resonance Fields on external sites + a directory page on act.place
- **Targets**: JCF, PICC, The Buttery, SMART Recovery, Orange Sky
- **Value**: every embed is proof-of-brand and a reference for future customers

## Release cadence (Daft Punk rhythm)

| Month | Release |
|---|---|
| Apr–May | Brave Ones Phase 1 + CONTAINED |
| May–Aug | Extraordinarily Ordinary (JCF) |
| Jun–Oct | World Tour Travelogue (in-field capture → post-production) |
| Aug–Oct | Resonance Field Installation |
| Sep–Dec | STAY Journal Chapter 01 |
| Oct–Feb | Fifty Years of Coming Home (book) |
| Nov | Buttery Documentary screening |
| Ongoing | Resonance Field Public Embed Campaign |

Three major "drops" in the year: Brave Ones (Apr/May), Resonance Field Installation (Sep/Oct), and Fifty Years book (Jan/Feb). Each gets one campaign push then silence.

## Funding strategy

| Source | Amount | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| Ian Potter Foundation (application) | $50–80K | Brave Ones + STAY Journal + Installation |
| Creative Australia (application) | $30–50K | Brave Ones + Installation |
| Copyright Agency Cultural Fund | $10–20K | Fifty Years book production |
| JCF engagement budget | $30–50K | Extraordinarily Ordinary |
| Buttery engagement budget | $50–75K | Book + documentary |
| Minderoo STAY EL studio allocation | $60K | Journal Chapter 01 |
| Self-funded from EL customer revenue | $20–40K | World Tour travelogue + Resonance Field embeds |

## What makes this "art" and not "marketing"

The test: would this work survive the removal of every ACT logo and URL? If yes, it's art. If no, it's marketing pretending to be art.

Every release in this program passes that test. Brave Ones is a portrait series that stands on its own. The Buttery book is a history that exists for the community, not for ACT. The Resonance Field installation is a room you walk into and feel something. The travelogue is Ben's personal photographic record.

The fact that these also serve ACT's brand is a consequence of the [[lcaa-method|LCAA]] principle: art is the first form of revolution. Not the other way around.

## Context

**Place:** Murcia, Spain
**Voice Owner:** Young people in Diagrama programs (identity protected)
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE — identity protected

## Story

During ACT's learning journey to Diagrama in Spain, young people in the youth justice system shared their experiences directly. Their insights cut through policy debates to reveal what actually matters:

**What helps:**
- Being treated with respect, not suspicion
- Staff who see potential, not just problems
- Having responsibility, not just restrictions
- Connection to education and skills
- Clear pathways back to community

**What harms:**
- Environments designed around control, not care
- Staff who keep distance
- No clear future after release
- Isolation from family and community
- Being defined by worst moments

These aren't policy recommendations — they're lived experience. They inform JusticeHub's approach to documenting what alternatives need to include.

pages.title: Youth Justice Reform
pages.excerpt: ACT's thesis on why Australia's youth justice system fails, what actually works, and how to shift the system — synthesised across evidence, policy submissions, and field experience.
pages.content:
> ACT's thesis on why Australia's youth justice system fails, what actually works, and how to shift the system — synthesised across evidence, policy submissions, and field experience.

**Status:** Active | **Type:** Concept

## Overview

Australia spends more than a billion dollars a year locking up children. The Productivity Commission puts the average cost at $1.3 million per child per year — over $3,600 a day. In Victoria it is $2.6 million. The system's "success rate" is 15.5%: 84.5% of young people reoffend within 12 months of release.

This is not a disputed finding. Every inquiry has said it. Every report confirms it. The question — ACT's animating question across [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[contained|CONTAINED]], and the satellite programs it supports — is not whether the approach is broken. The question is what you do about it.

ACT's answer is grounded in the evidence: **the cure already exists**. Community-led alternatives operate at 95% lower cost than detention and achieve 78% success rates. Programs like [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] in Alice Springs run entire operations — cultural mentorship, on-Country camps, school re-engagement, justice navigation, family support — at 97.6% less cost than one child in detention. The problem is not knowledge. It is political will and funding allocation.

## The Costs and the Gap

The numbers that power ACT's advocacy are drawn from JusticeHub's tracking of 145,000+ justice funding records:

| Approach | Annual Cost per Child | Success Rate |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------|
| Youth detention (national avg) | $1.1–1.3 million | ~15% |
| Community-led alternatives | ~$58,000 | ~78% |
| Diagrama Foundation (Spain) | ~$31,000 | 86.4% |

Queensland spends over $760,000 per youth annually in detention. The state has simultaneously committed $225 million (Staying on Track and Regional Reset programs) to rehabilitation and early intervention — but the allocation between grassroots organisations and large administrative bureaucracies remains a critical pressure point. Small community organisations, which are most effective, risk being passed over for established agencies whose administrative overhead consumes a significant share of grant funds before they reach young people.

## Who Is Most Affected

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people are dramatically overrepresented. They comprise roughly 60% of those in detention despite being approximately 6% of the youth population. First Nations children are 21 times more likely to end up inside than their non-Indigenous peers (some analyses put this at 24 times). The 1991 Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody made 339 recommendations; most remain unimplemented.

This overrepresentation is not incidental — it is the direct and ongoing consequence of colonial dispossession, the removal of cultural authority, and the deliberate underfunding of community-controlled responses in favour of state enforcement mechanisms.

## The "Cure Already Exists" Argument

The most direct statement of ACT's thesis: the solutions are not waiting to be invented. They are already running, often on volunteer hours and short grant cycles, in communities across Australia.

**[[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]** — Alice Springs, 100% Aboriginal-led (Kristy Bloomfield and Tanya Turner). When NT Police ran Operation Luna targeting 21 high-risk young people, Oonchiumpa worked with them; by December, only one remained on the list. 95% diversion success. 72% of disengaged youth returned to education. Working with 32 partner organisations across Central Australia.

**PICC (Palm Island Community Company)** — 197 staff, 78% diversion rate. Philosophy: culture is protection. When young people know who they are, where they come from, and who their family is, they make different choices.

**Mounty Yarns** — Mount Druitt, Western Sydney. Youth-led storytelling and media. 30% of participants pursuing media careers. Young people building their own platforms rather than waiting for someone to hand them one.

**[[campfire|CAMPFIRE]]** — Mount Isa. Cultural immersion, fitness, and mentorship led by Brodie Germaine. Documented reduction in youth police contact. Operating in the same geography as some of Australia's worst watchhouse overflow.

**[[confit-pathways|ConFit Pathways]]** — Fitness and boxing-based program using mentors with lived incarceration experience. 60% reduction in recidivism among participants.

**[[diagrama|Diagrama Foundation]]** — Spain. Recidivism rate 13.6%. Cost ~$31,000 per young person per year. Staff called "social educators", not guards. A woman named Carmen has worked there for fifteen years; she knows every young person by name, by story, by the thing that keeps them up at night. This model has been running since 1991. It is not a theory. It exists.

## Gold-Standard Program Design

ACT has articulated what a genuinely effective youth justice intervention looks like — drawn from evidence synthesis and the Queensland Kickstarter grants context:

**Evidence-based strategies** — built on approaches proven to reduce offending or its risk factors, including family therapy (which has cut reoffending by 25–50%), cognitive-behavioural techniques for decision-making, and school re-engagement.

**Holistic and multi-faceted** — no single issue leads a young person to crime; no single intervention pulls them out. Gold-standard programs combine family engagement, education support, mentoring, mental health services, and positive recreational outlets.

**Early and targeted** — using data-driven risk assessment to focus intensive support on highest-risk young people at critical turning points (school transitions, first minor offence, family breakdown).

**Intensive and sustained** — not one-off workshops. International best practice shows results come from daily or weekly contact, individualised to each young person, sustained over months or years. Better to thoroughly transform 100 high-risk young people than to briefly touch 1,000 with no lasting change.

**Youth-centred and culturally informed** — for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander youth, this means working with Elders and community leaders, centering cultural identity, and recognising that community-controlled responses consistently outperform externally designed programs on every measurable outcome.

**Co-designed** — local non-profits and youth workers know what resonates. Involving young people with lived experience in program design is not a courtesy; it is how you avoid designing programs for the wrong problem.

## Why the System Persists

The youth justice system is not irrational from the perspective of those who benefit from it. Political incentives run toward "tough on crime" policies that are legible to voters shaped by media sensationalism. The narrative that punishment equals safety has deep cultural purchase even where the evidence clearly contradicts it.

The system is also self-reinforcing: high staff-to-budget ratios in detention facilities create institutional constituencies for their own continuation; procurement processes favour large established agencies over grassroots community organisations; and measuring "success" by detention rates rather than community health makes invisible the programs that actually work.

ACT's framing, drawing on Plato's allegory of the cave, argues that most Australians are looking at shadows: "youth crime waves," "tough on crime" policies, dehumanising narratives that reduce young people to their worst moments. [[contained|CONTAINED]] is the mechanism for turning people away from the wall — making the real cost of the current system felt in the body, then showing what exists beyond it.

## The Queensland Context

Queensland has been the focus of significant ACT advocacy activity. Key pressure points:

- Queensland's recidivism rate among released young people is 84–96% within 12 months — among the worst in Australia
- The state spends over $760,000 per youth annually in detention
- $100 million was committed to "gold standard early intervention" without adequate design criteria for what counts as gold standard
- The Making Queensland Safer Bill 2024 presented an opportunity for fundamental reform toward rehabilitation; ACT made a formal submission arguing for adaptation of the Diagrama model, a dedicated 12-month post-detention transition program, a Youth Justice Co-Lab, and refocusing resources from new detention infrastructure toward community-based programs

The submission explicitly named [[campfire|CAMPFIRE]] (BG Fit, Mount Isa) and the Stradbroke Islander Justice Reinvestment program as models worth replicating — programs already working that need funding to scale, not programs that need to be invented.

## The Role of JusticeHub

[[justicehub|JusticeHub]] is ACT's intelligence platform underpinning this reform thesis. It has mapped more than 800 verified interventions, organisations, and programs across every state and territory. It tracks where public money goes — more than $1 billion in justice spending, line by line. It shows the gap between what governments spend on detention and what they invest in what actually works. All of it public. All of it sourced.

JusticeHub makes the argument that communities already have the answers. The data layer — 145,242 justice funding records, 1,357 evidence-based interventions in ALMA, 57,435 crime statistics records — is the empirical foundation for everything CONTAINED campaigns for.

## The Role of CONTAINED

[[contained|CONTAINED]] is the campaign layer: an immersive shipping-container experience that translates these numbers into felt experience. Three rooms, thirty minutes:

- **Room 1** — what the current system does to a child. You sit in it.
- **Room 2** — what works instead. The Diagrama Foundation. The proof.
- **Room 3** — the community already doing it, in whatever city the container has arrived in.

The chalk question wall: *"What could $1.55M do instead?"* Communities write their own answers. It photographs. It travels. It shifts the conversation in rooms that matter.

## Key Figures and Concepts

- **$1.3M per child per year** — national average cost of youth detention (Productivity Commission)
- **13.6%** — Diagrama Foundation recidivism rate vs Australia's 80%+
- **97.6% cheaper** — Oonchiumpa's cost relative to one child in detention
- **84–96%** — Queensland young people who reoffend within 12 months of release
- **60%** — First Nations children's share of the detained population (6% of youth population)
- **Justice reinvestment** — the policy framework for redirecting detention spending into community programs
